## Medical records request tracking for personal injury firms
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/medical-records-request-tracking-personal-injury/

Medical records request tracking means knowing, for every client and every provider, what you asked for, when you asked, and what has come back. A simple workflow can keep one log, send follow-ups to providers on a schedule you set, file what arrives and give each case manager a weekly list of open requests. A person still reviews every authorization, every request and every record.

Medical records request tracking is where a personal injury case slows down. A client treated with six providers, and each one needs a request for records and a request for bills. Some take a portal upload, some want a fax, some use a records vendor, and one says the request never arrived. The case manager is supposed to follow up, but there are forty other files. The demand can't go out until the last record is in. Sending the request, checking on it and filing the result is the same routine for every provider, so it can run on a schedule while your team does the legal work.

### Where requests stall
- Requests are sent from individual inboxes and fax lines, and the only record is a note in the file
- Records and billing are separate departments at many providers, and only one of them was asked
- A provider rejects the authorization or asks for a fee, and the letter sits unopened
- Follow-up happens when someone remembers, not on a date
- The client mentions a new provider on a call, and it never reaches the list
- Records arrive, but nobody checks that the dates of treatment are all there

### A request log you can copy
Keep one row per provider per request type. For illustration, as it might look for one client:
| Provider | Request | Sent | How | Status | Next action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hospital emergency department | Records | 3 March | Provider portal | Received | Case manager to review dates of treatment |
| Hospital emergency department | Bills | 3 March | Fax to billing office | No response | Second follow-up due Monday |
| Orthopedic clinic | Records and bills | 5 March | Records vendor | Fee invoice received | Approve and pay the fee |
| Physical therapy | Records and bills | 5 March | Fax | Rejected: authorization incomplete | Paralegal to get a new signed authorization |
| Imaging center | Records and films | Not sent |  | Waiting for provider address | Ask the client |

### The authorization comes first
Every request rides on the client's signed authorization, and providers send requests back when it is incomplete. The federal privacy rule lists the core elements of a valid authorization: a description of the information, who may disclose it, who may receive it, the purpose, an expiration date or event, and the individual's signature and date. An authorization that has expired or is not fully filled out is not valid. Your attorneys decide the form your firm uses and whether a state needs something more. The workflow can check that a signed copy is on file and not past its expiration before a request goes out, and stop if it isn't. How long a provider has to respond and what it can charge depend on the state and the type of request, so the follow-up schedule is one you set.

### A follow-up you can copy
Follow-up to a provider's records department (edit the words in brackets):
```
Subject: Follow-up on records request for [patient name], date of birth [date]

To the records department,

On [date sent] we sent a request for [records / itemized bills] for the patient above, for treatment from [start date] to [end date]. A signed authorization was included. We sent it by [fax / portal / mail] to [number or address].

We have not received the records or a response. Please let us know:
1. Whether you have the request.
2. Whether anything else is needed, including any fee.
3. When we can expect the records.

You can reply to this email or call [name] at [phone].

Thank you,
[name], [firm]
```

### How the workflow runs
1. When a provider is added to a case, a row is created for records and a row for bills, with the provider's request method and contact details.
2. A person prepares and approves each request. The workflow sends it by email where the provider accepts that, or creates a task for the fax, portal or vendor.
3. It logs the date sent and sets the first follow-up date from your schedule.
4. On each follow-up date, it sends the follow-up you approved or puts a call on the case manager's list, and logs the attempt.
5. Letters back from providers, such as a rejection or a fee invoice, are logged against the right row and sent to the person who handles them.
6. When records arrive they are filed under the client and the provider. AI can list the dates of treatment it finds and point out gaps against the dates you asked for, and a person checks that list before anything is marked complete.
7. Each week, every case manager gets one list: requests sent, received, overdue and blocked.

### What stays with you
Which providers to request from, what the request says, whether an authorization is good, and what the records mean for the case. The workflow doesn't review medical records for you, doesn't write a demand and doesn't decide anything about a claim. It keeps the log, follows up and tells you what is still missing. Client records are sensitive, so the build keeps them in the systems your firm already uses and limits who can see them. If you want the start of the file tidier too, see [client intake for small law firms](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/law-firm-client-intake/).

No. A person prepares and approves each request and each follow-up template. The workflow sends what was approved, on the dates you set, and logs it.

## Form E document collection for family solicitors: one checklist, fewer chasing emails
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/form-e-financial-disclosure-document-collection/

Form E document collection means getting a full set of financial papers from a client before the date for exchange. A simple workflow can send each client one checklist built from your own list, give them one place to upload, remind them about what is still missing and show the fee earner where every file stands. A solicitor still reviews every document and decides what goes into the form.

Form E documents arrive in pieces. The client sends three months of statements for one account, a photo of a payslip and a promise to find the pension paperwork. The paralegal writes back, the client sends two more things, and the list of what is still missing lives in someone's head. The date for exchange gets closer. Clients are going through a divorce and paperwork is the last thing they want to do, so they need short, kind, specific reminders. That part is routine, and it can run on its own while the solicitor does the advising.

### Why disclosure takes so long to collect
- The first email lists everything at once, and the client doesn't know where to start
- Statements arrive for part of the period, as screenshots or as dozens of separate files
- Some papers have to be requested from someone else, such as a pension provider or a lender, and the client hasn't asked yet
- Documents come by email, WhatsApp, post and in person, and get saved in different places
- Chasing depends on a paralegal who is also preparing three other files
- Nobody can say in one line what is missing for each client

### A Form E checklist you can copy
The form itself lists the documents to attach, so build your checklist from the current version on GOV.UK. For each bank account listed, it asks for statements covering the last 12 months. The other rows below are what firms commonly ask for; check each against the form and the client's circumstances. Form E1 and Form E2 are separate forms with their own lists.
| Document | Who the client gets it from | What to track |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bank and savings statements, last 12 months, every account | Online banking or the bank | Each account separately, with the first and last date covered |
| Mortgage statement and property valuation | The lender and an estate agent | Requested, received |
| Payslips and the latest P60 | Their employer | Received, and whether the period matches your list |
| Pension valuation | Each pension provider | Date the client requested it, date it arrived |
| Business accounts, if self-employed or a company owner | Their accountant | Requested, received |
| Loan, credit card and other debt statements | Each lender | Each account separately |

We still need:

2. [Item]
3. [Item]

You can upload them here: [upload link]. Photos are fine if they are clear and show the whole page.

If you have asked your pension provider for a valuation, please tell us the date you asked, so we know when to expect it.

We need everything by [date] so that we can prepare your Form E in time. If anything on this list is hard to get, reply to this email or call [name] on [phone] and we will help.

Kind regards,
[name], [firm]
```

### How the workflow runs

2. The client gets one email with the checklist in plain words and one secure upload link. Items they must request from someone else are marked, so they start those first.
3. Each upload is saved in the matter folder under the right item, and the checklist updates.
4. AI can read a statement's account and dates and say which months seem to be missing. A person checks that before the client is asked for anything.
5. Reminders go out on the schedule you choose and list only what is still missing. They stop when the item arrives or when a person pauses them.
6. Any reply from the client goes to the fee earner or paralegal. Nothing is answered automatically.
7. Each week the team gets one list: every disclosure file, what is missing and the date it is needed by.

### What stays with you
The advice, the form and every judgement about what a document shows. The workflow doesn't fill in Form E, doesn't decide what must be disclosed and doesn't talk to the other side. A solicitor approves the checklist, the wording and the timing, and can pause reminders for any client at any time, which matters when a client is struggling. The papers are sensitive, so they stay in the storage your firm already uses, with access limited to the people on the matter. ## Off-hire reminders for plant and tool hire: end or extend, in writing, every time
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plant-hire-off-hire-reminders/

Off-hire reminders work when every hire has an expected end date and someone asks the hirer about it before that date. A simple workflow can message the site contact a day or two before, take a reply to end or extend, send back an off-hire number in writing and put the collection on your list. You still set the rates, the terms and every decision about a dispute.

Most arguments in plant and tool hire start at the end of the hire, not the start. The hirer says they rang to off-hire on Tuesday. Your counter has no note of it. The machine sat on site for another week, the invoice says so, and now there's a credit request. Or the opposite: the hire runs on because nobody asked, and the customer is annoyed when the bill arrives. Asking before the expected end date, and confirming every off-hire in writing with a number, is the same small job on every hire, so it can run on its own.

### Where off-hires go wrong
- The expected end date is on the hire contract, but nobody looks at it until the invoice run
- Off-hires come in by phone to whoever picks up, and the note never reaches the system
- The site contact who booked the hire isn't the person who knows the job has finished
- An off-hire is taken but no number is sent back, so there's no proof for either side
- Collections are booked from a list on the wall, and a machine waits on site for days
- Hire extensions are agreed on the phone and the new date is never recorded

### What the workflow keeps for each hire
One row per item on hire, not per customer. Most hire companies already have the contract details; the workflow only needs the dates and the contacts. Your own terms decide when a hire ends and what is charged. The workflow follows them, it doesn't change them.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Hire number and item | So the reminder and the off-hire number match the contract |
| Site address and site contact | The person who knows when the job is finished, not only the buyer |
| Expected off-hire date | When the first reminder goes out |
| Status: on hire, extended, off-hire requested, off-hired, collected | So the counter, the drivers and accounts see the same thing |
| Off-hire number and time | Proof of when the off-hire was confirmed, sent to the hirer in writing |

### A reminder you can copy
Text or email to the site contact (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], it's [business]. The [item] on hire to [site address] under hire [number] is due off hire on [date].

Reply OFF to end the hire on that date, or EXTEND with a new date. If you'd rather talk to someone, call [phone].

The hire stays live until you get an off-hire number back from us.
```

### How the workflow runs
1. When a hire goes out, the item, site contact and expected off-hire date are logged from your hire contract or booking.
2. A day or two before that date, the site contact gets a message asking them to end or extend the hire.
3. If they reply OFF, the request is logged with the time, and the counter confirms it. The hirer then gets an off-hire number in writing.
4. The confirmed off-hire goes on the drivers' collection list for the depot, with the site address and contact.
5. If they reply EXTEND, the new date is recorded and the next reminder is set from it.
6. If nobody replies, a second message goes out, then the hire goes on a short call list for the counter. The hire is not ended without the customer.
7. Anything that isn't a clear OFF or EXTEND goes straight to a person. If AI drafts an answer, someone at the counter reads and approves it before it is sent.

### What stays with you
Rates, terms, damage and every dispute about dates. The workflow doesn't decide when a hire ended, doesn't credit invoices and doesn't argue with customers. It asks the question on time, keeps a written record and puts the collections in front of your drivers. If you also chase unpaid hire invoices, see [invoice payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/). For trades who hire plant in, [change order approvals](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/change-order-approval-workflow/) covers the paperwork on their side.

A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how off-hires reach you today and where they get lost. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on what you already use (your hire software where it allows a connection, a spreadsheet, email and text), so there's no new system for the counter to learn. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is a fixed $2,000](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it, under the [pay-when-happy agreement](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agreement/). If your hire software already sends off-hire reminders and numbers and you're happy with it, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### Free tools for hire invoices
The free [working days calculator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/working-days-calculator/) counts chargeable working days on a hire, and the [invoice generator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/free-invoice-generator/) makes the hire invoice.

### Does it end hires on its own?
No. A hire ends when the customer asks and your counter confirms it. The workflow asks the question, records the answer and the time, and sends the off-hire number once a person has confirmed it.

Maybe not. If it already reminds hirers before the end date and sends the number in writing, keep it. This is for hire companies where off-hires still arrive by phone and live on paper, or where the software has no reminders.

## Permit and inspection tracking for contractors: every job, every inspection, one list
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/building-permit-inspection-tracking-contractors/

Permit and inspection tracking works when every job has one row per permit and one line per inspection, with a date and a status. A simple workflow can remind your office to check on applications, prompt the crew lead to request each inspection when the work is ready, log the result and tell the customer what's next. Your team still decides when work is ready and talks to the building department.

Permits rarely stop a job because the work is hard. They stop it because nobody noticed the application was still under review, the framing inspection was never requested, or a failed inspection's correction list sat in someone's inbox. Every building department has its own portal, phone line and rules, and every job goes through the same few gates. Keeping the list of where each job stands is the same job every week, so it can run on its own while your crews work.

### Where permits and inspections slip
- Application status lives in a city portal that someone checks when they remember
- The crew finishes rough-in on Friday and the inspection request goes in on Tuesday
- Inspection windows are emailed to the office and never reach the crew or the homeowner
- A correction notice arrives, and nobody owns the re-inspection
- Permit expiry dates are on the permit card, not in any list
- The final inspection passes, but the closed permit never gets to the customer's file

### Check your building department first
There is no single national process. Each local building department (the authority having jurisdiction) sets which work needs a permit, which inspections apply, how they are requested and how long a permit stays valid. Some have online portals and online booking, others take requests by phone. The workflow follows the steps you give it for each department you work with. It doesn't decide what needs a permit, and it shouldn't promise a homeowner a date the department hasn't confirmed.

### A tracker you can copy
One row per inspection, grouped by job. For illustration, on a kitchen remodel:
| Job | Permit | Inspection | Status | Next action | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 12 Oak St kitchen | Building, issued | Rough framing | Passed | None | - |
| 12 Oak St kitchen | Electrical, issued | Rough electrical | Work ready Thursday | Request inspection Thursday | Crew lead |
| 12 Oak St kitchen | Plumbing, issued | Rough plumbing | Failed, correction list received | Fix and request re-inspection | Plumbing sub |
| 12 Oak St kitchen | Building | Insulation | Not ready | Wait for rough inspections | - |
| 40 Elm Ave deck | Building, under review | - | Submitted, no decision | Check portal Monday | Office |

### How the workflow runs
1. When a permit is applied for, the job, permit type, department and application date are logged.
2. While it's under review, the office gets a reminder on the schedule you choose to check the portal or call.
3. Once issued, the inspections you list for that department are added to the job, with the permit expiry date.
4. When the crew lead marks a stage ready, the office gets a prompt to request the inspection, or the request link for departments that book online.
5. The confirmed inspection window goes to the crew lead and a short note goes to the homeowner.

## Uncategorized transactions: one list a month, answers clients can actually give
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/uncategorized-transactions-client-questions/

Asking clients about uncategorized transactions works best as one list per client per month, not one email per transaction. A simple workflow can collect the unclear items after your review, send each client a short list they can answer in a minute or two, remind them, and put the answers back next to each transaction for you to post. You still decide every category.

Every month ends the same way. Twenty transactions in the suspense or uncategorized account, half of them a card payment to a name nobody recognizes. You email the client, they answer three, you email again, and the month can't be closed. Some clients reply in a text, some in the email thread from last quarter, some on a call. The list of questions is different every month, but sending it, chasing it and matching the answers back is the same job, so it can run on its own.

### Why the questions don't get answered
- One email per transaction, so the client sees a pile and answers none
- Questions use account names and bank feed text the client doesn't recognize
- There's no deadline, so the list waits until the client has a free afternoon
- Answers come back by text, email and phone, and someone has to match them to the right line
- Old questions roll into new months and nobody knows which are still open
- Clients aren't asked for the receipt at the same time, so you ask twice

### What a good question list looks like
Short, in the client's words, with the answer options they can pick from. Ask for the receipt in the same line when you need one. For illustration:
| Date | Amount | What the bank shows | Our question | Client answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Oct 3 | $84.20 | SQ *JMS DELI | Client lunch, team meal or personal? | Client lunch with ABC Co |
| Oct 9 | $1,250.00 | ZELLE TO M RIVERA | What was this payment for? Is M Rivera a contractor? | Yes, contractor, tiling job |
| Oct 14 | $39.99 | AMZN MKTP US | What was bought? Please attach the receipt if you have it | Printer ink, receipt attached |
| Oct 22 | $500.00 | TRANSFER FROM 4471 | Is this a loan, your own money or a customer payment? | No reply yet |

### How the workflow runs
1. After you review the month, you mark the transactions you need help with, in your accounting software or a sheet.
2. Each client gets one message with their list and a link to answer: pick an option, type a note or upload a receipt.
3. If they don't answer, a reminder goes out on the schedule you choose, listing only what's still open.
4. Answers come back next to each transaction, so you can post them without searching email threads.
5. Anything unclear, like "ask my wife" or a long explanation, goes to you to read. Nothing is categorized without your approval.
6. Items still open at the next month's review carry forward and are marked as overdue.
7. Every week you get one view: who has open questions, how many, and how long they've waited.

### Software that already asks the client
Some accounting and practice software has its own way to send transaction questions to a client. If your clients use it and reply, keep it. A workflow helps when clients don't log in, when you work across different software for different clients, or when the questions stop after one email. It can send the same list by email or text, chase it and bring the answers back to the place you work. If AI drafts a question in plainer words, you read and approve it before it's sent.

### What stays with you
Every category, every journal and every conversation about whether something is a business expense. The workflow asks, reminds and organizes the answers; it doesn't post to the ledger on its own. For the rest of the monthly records, see [document collection for bookkeepers](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/bookkeeper-document-collection/). If you work in QuickBooks Online, [QuickBooks automation services](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/quickbooks-online-automation-services/) covers the connection side.

Fire extinguisher service reminders work when every site you service has a next-due date and someone contacts the customer before it. - The service record is filled in on site but not sent to the customer for days

One row per site, not per customer. If you already use job or asset software for the extinguishers themselves, the workflow only needs the site, the contact and the dates. The service interval is the one you set and recommend. The workflow follows it, it doesn't decide it.

## Quarterly estimated tax reminders: the right amount, to the right client, before every due date
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/quarterly-estimated-tax-payment-reminders/

Estimated tax payment reminders work when every client who pays estimates has their amounts on one list. A simple workflow can send each client their own amount and how to pay about a week before each federal due date, ask them to confirm once they've paid, and show your team who hasn't. You still calculate the estimates and answer every tax question.

You work out a client's estimates in April, hand over four vouchers or amounts, and hope they remember. By September half of them have lost the letter. Some pay the wrong amount, some pay the state but not the IRS, and some don't pay at all. Then next spring the questions start. Sending each client a short reminder with their own number, before each of the four quarterly dates, is the same job every quarter, so it can run on its own while your team does the actual tax work.

### Where estimated payments get missed
- Amounts are in the return file, but the client only saw them once, in April
- The firm sends one general newsletter reminder, without each client's own amount
- Clients pay federal and forget the state, or the other way round
- Nobody knows who paid until the next return is being prepared
- Mid-year changes, like a big sale or a new job, never reach the preparer
- Reminders go out by hand from one person's inbox, and stop when they're busy

### What the workflow keeps for each client
One row per client who pays estimates. Your team sets the amounts; the workflow only sends them. The federal dates fall in mid-April, mid-June, mid-September and mid-January, and move to the next business day when a date lands on a weekend or holiday. State dates can differ, so they get their own column.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Client and contact preference | Email or text, to the person who actually pays |
| Federal amount per quarter | So the reminder carries their number, not a general note |
| State amount and state due dates | So the state payment isn't forgotten |
| Status: reminded, paid (client confirmed), not paid, question | Your team sees who needs a call |
| Change flag | Clients can say their income changed, so a preparer reviews the amount |

### A reminder you can copy
Email to the client (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], a reminder from [firm]: your [quarter] estimated tax payment is due on [date].

Federal: [amount]. [State]: [amount], due [state date].
You can pay the IRS online at [IRS payment link] and [state] at [state link].

Once you've paid, reply PAID. If your income has changed a lot this year, reply CHANGED and we'll take a look before you pay.
```

### How the workflow runs
1. After the return is done, your team enters each client's estimated amounts for the year, or the workflow reads them from the file you already export.
2. About a week before each due date, each client gets a reminder with their own federal and state amounts and how to pay.
3. Clients reply PAID, and the status is logged with the date. Replies saying CHANGED go to a preparer.
4. Two days before the date, clients who haven't confirmed get a short second reminder.
5. After the date, your team gets a list of clients with no confirmation, to call or note on the file.
6. Every reply that isn't a simple PAID goes to a person. If AI drafts an answer, a preparer reads and approves it before it is sent.

### What stays with you
Every amount, every tax question and every decision about penalties or changes. The workflow doesn't calculate estimates, doesn't move money and doesn't give tax advice. It sends each client their own number on time and tells you who confirmed. ## Retainer replenishment requests: top up the retainer before the work stops
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/law-firm-retainer-replenishment-requests/

A retainer replenishment workflow watches each matter's trust balance against the minimum in the engagement letter. When the balance drops below it, the client gets a clear request with the amount and a payment link, one or two polite follow-ups, and the responsible lawyer gets a list of matters that are still short. A person approves every request and decides what happens to the work. The workflow never touches client money.

Evergreen retainers only work if someone notices when the balance runs low. In a small firm, that someone is usually the lawyer, at month end, after more work has gone in. The request goes out late, the client is surprised, and the firm carries the risk while it waits. Your billing software may already flag low balances. What tends to fall through is the follow-up: who was asked, who paid, and who needs a call from the lawyer.

### Where replenishment goes wrong
- Low balances are spotted at billing time, weeks after they dropped
- Requests are written by hand, so the amount and wording differ from client to client
- Nobody tracks who was asked, so some clients get nothing and some get three emails
- The lawyer only hears about an unpaid request when the matter is already well into the next phase
- Clients ask why they owe more, and the answer sits in a bill they haven't opened
- Hard conversations about pausing work get put off because nobody has the full picture

### What the workflow checks
The minimum balance and the top-up amount come from your engagement letter and your billing software. The workflow reads them. It doesn't set them, and it doesn't decide what the firm can do when a client doesn't pay. That depends on your state's rules and your agreement with the client.
| Step | What happens | Who decides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Balance check | Each matter's trust balance is compared with its minimum, daily or weekly | Rules you set |
| Draft request | A request with the amount, a short reason and a payment link is prepared | Workflow |
| Approval | The responsible lawyer or billing staff approves or edits it | A person |
| Follow-ups | One or two polite reminders if nothing arrives | Schedule you set |
| Still short | The matter goes on the lawyer's list with the full history | The lawyer |

### A request you can copy
Email to a client (edit the words in brackets):
```
Subject: Retainer top-up for [matter name]

Hi [first name],

Under our engagement letter, we keep a minimum of [minimum amount] in trust for your matter. After our latest bill, the balance is [current balance], so we're asking for a deposit of [amount] to bring it back to the agreed level.

You can pay here: [payment link]. Your latest bill is attached if you'd like to see the work it covers.

If you have questions about the amount, reply to this email or call [lawyer name] at [phone].

Thank you,
[firm name]
```

### How the workflow runs
1. On the schedule you choose, the workflow reads each open matter's trust balance and its minimum from your billing software or a report.
2. For every matter below its minimum, it drafts a request with the client's own amounts and your payment link.
3. The responsible lawyer or billing staff reviews the drafts and approves, edits or holds each one. Nothing goes out without that approval.
4. Approved requests are sent and logged. When the deposit shows up in your billing software, the matter is marked as topped up and the reminders stop.
5. If nothing arrives, one or two reminders go out on your schedule, each approved the same way.
6. Matters that are still short go on a weekly list for the lawyer, with every request and reply, ready for a call.

### What stays with you
The engagement letter, the minimum and the top-up amount, trust accounting, applying funds to bills, every legal question and every decision about pausing or withdrawing. The workflow only sends requests you've approved and keeps track of the replies. For the start of the relationship, see [client intake for small law firms](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/law-firm-client-intake/). For overdue bills, see [invoice payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/).

No. It reads balances and sends requests you approve. Deposits, transfers and applying funds to bills stay in your billing software and with your staff.

## Warranty request tracking for home builders: every homeowner issue logged, assigned and closed
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/home-builder-warranty-request-tracking/

Warranty request tracking means every issue a homeowner reports after handover goes into one list through one form, with photos, the plot and the room. A person makes every coverage decision and approves anything AI drafts.

After handover, the homeowner's issues arrive any way they can: a text to the site manager, an email to the office, a call to sales, a message to the trade who fitted the kitchen. Some get fixed twice. Some never get fixed, and the first you hear is an angry review or a call from the warranty provider. Small builders don't need a big warranty system to fix this. ### Where warranty requests get lost

- Homeowners chase for updates because they don't know a job is booked
- Items are fixed but never signed off, so they come back as new complaints
- At the end of the year there's no record of what kept going wrong, plot by plot

### What the request form asks for

5. When the work is done, the homeowner is asked to confirm it's fixed. If they say no, the request reopens. If they don't reply, a second message goes out before it closes.
6. Every Monday, you get a list of open requests by age and trade, and a count of issues by type, so repeat problems show up.

Your request number is [number]. Reply to this message any time if anything changes.

[name], [builder]
```

### What stays with you
What is covered under your warranty and any warranty provider's policy, every judgement about the work, payments to trades, and every conversation with an unhappy homeowner. ## Backflow test reminders: book the retest before the water authority's notice lands

### Why annual backflow work slips away
- Test dates live in old invoices, paper reports or the tester's own notebook

- Test reports sit in a truck waiting to be entered into the water authority's system
- Failed tests need a repair and a retest, and the follow-up gets lost

Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/confirmation-statement-client-reminders/

### Why confirmation statements end up last-minute

- Changes to officers, the registered office or PSCs need their own filings first

- Nobody has one view of which clients replied and which went quiet

### What the workflow keeps for each company

## Court date reminders that reach the client, not just the calendar
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/court-date-reminders-law-firms/

Court date reminders work when every hearing on your calendar also creates messages to the client. A simple workflow takes each date your team enters, texts and emails the client a week before and the day before with the time, courtroom, address and what to bring, asks them to reply YES, and gives your staff a list of clients who haven't confirmed. Your attorneys still set the dates, decide what clients are told and handle every call.

Your calendar knows about the hearing. Your client may not. The court's notice went to an old address, or it's under a pile of mail, or they wrote down the wrong day. Someone on your staff usually calls the night before, if they remember and if the client picks up. The date, the courtroom and the client's phone number are already in your system. A reminder that goes out on its own, and a short list of clients who haven't confirmed, takes that worry off your staff.

### Why clients still miss hearings
- Court notices arrive by mail, weeks ahead, and get lost or forgotten
- Clients change phone numbers and addresses during the case
- Hearings get continued, and the client remembers the old date
- Reminder calls depend on one person having time the day before
- Clients don't know which courtroom, what to wear or what to bring
- Nobody can see, at a glance, which clients have confirmed this week

### What each reminder includes
The reminder only repeats what your firm has already entered and approved. It doesn't give legal advice and it doesn't set dates. Every message template is written and approved by your attorneys before anything goes out.
| In the message | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- |
| Date, time and type of hearing | Your calendar or case management software |
| Courthouse address and courtroom | The entry your staff made for the hearing |
| What to bring and when to arrive | A short note your attorney writes for that hearing type |
| Who to call with a question | The case's assigned paralegal or attorney |
| Reply YES to confirm, or CALL for a call back | So staff only phone the clients who need it |

### A reminder you can copy
Text to a client (your attorney approves the wording first):
```

## Subcontractor pay applications in by the cutoff, complete the first time
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/subcontractor-pay-application-reminders/

Your team still reviews every line, approves percentages and decides what gets paid.

Every month it's the same chase. The owner's draw is due, half the subs haven't sent their pay apps, two of the ones that did forgot the waiver or billed a change order nobody approved, and the project manager is working through texts and emails to work out who's still missing. Your subcontracts already say when pay apps are due and what goes with them. - Unapproved change orders are billed on the same pay app
- Nobody can see, for the whole job, who has billed this month

## Physical therapy prior authorization tracking: renew before the last approved visit
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/physical-therapy-prior-authorization-tracking/

Physical therapy prior authorization tracking means knowing, for every patient on an authorized plan, how many visits were approved, how many are used, and when the authorization ends. A simple workflow updates those numbers from your schedule after each visit, alerts the front desk and the treating therapist a set number of visits or days before either runs out, and keeps a list of renewals requested and still waiting. Your therapists still write the notes and decide on continued care, and your staff still submit every request.

The authorization was approved for a number of visits by a date. The patient is doing well, keeps coming, and nobody notices that today is the last approved visit until the claim comes back. Or the dates run out with visits still left. The numbers are on the approval letter and in the payer portal, but not where the front desk looks when booking. A count that updates itself after every visit, and an alert in good time, means renewals are asked for while there's still room.

### Why authorizations run out unnoticed
- Each payer, and often each plan, has its own rules and portal
- The approval sits in a portal or a PDF, not in the schedule
- Visits used are counted by hand, if at all
- There are two limits, visits and an end date, and either can run out first
- Renewal needs updated notes from the therapist, which takes time
- Requests sent are tracked in someone's inbox, not in one list

### What the tracker keeps for each authorization
One row per authorization, linked to the patient's appointments. Payer rules change often, so your billing team enters the approved visits and dates from each approval. The workflow does the counting and the reminding; it doesn't decide what needs authorization.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Patient, payer and plan | Who to ask and where |
| Authorization number, approved visits, start and end dates | From the approval, entered once |
| Visits used and visits left | Updated from your schedule after each attended visit |
| Alert point: visits or days before the limit | Set per payer, to leave time for the renewal |
| Renewal status: needed, notes ready, requested, approved, denied | So nothing waits in an inbox |

### An alert you can copy
Internal alert to the front desk and therapist (edit the words in brackets):
```
Authorization check for [patient initials], [payer]: [visits left] visits left, ends [end date]. Next booked visit: [date].

[Therapist name]: please update the progress note by [date] if you're asking for more visits.
[Billing name]: renewal request to go to [payer] by [date]. Reply DONE when submitted.
```

### How the workflow runs
1. When an authorization is approved, billing enters the visits and dates once. The tracker links it to the patient's appointments.
2. After each attended visit, visits used and visits left update on their own.
3. At the alert point you set for that payer, the front desk, the therapist and billing get the alert above.
4. When the therapist marks the notes ready, billing gets a task to submit the renewal, and it moves to requested.
5. Each morning, staff see a short list: renewals due, requested and still waiting, and patients booked past their last approved visit.
6. If AI drafts a summary for a renewal, the treating therapist reads and approves it. Nothing goes to a payer without a person submitting it.

### What stays with you
Clinical notes, decisions about continued care, every request to a payer and every conversation with a patient about cost. Patient information should only go into tools your practice is allowed to use for it, which your compliance lead decides; we build on those. ## HOA violation tracking: every notice, photo and cure date in one place
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/hoa-violation-notice-tracking/

HOA violation tracking works when every violation has one record: the lot, the rule, the photos, the notice sent and the cure date. A simple workflow logs each finding from the drive-by, drafts the next notice from your board's approved letters when a cure date passes, files the homeowner's reply with the record, and gives the board a list before each meeting. The manager approves every letter, and the board decides every fine and hearing.

A community manager can drive ten communities in a week. The violations are noted on a phone, a clipboard or a spreadsheet, the letters are typed one at a time, and the follow-up drive is planned from memory. Then a homeowner asks why their neighbor's trailer has been there three months, or disputes a fine because the second notice never went out. The steps your board adopted are already written down. A workflow that keeps every case on those steps protects the manager, the board and the homeowner.

### Where violation follow-up breaks down
- Findings from the drive-by sit in phone photos with no lot number
- Each community has its own rules, letters and enforcement steps
- Cure dates pass without a re-inspection, so the case goes stale
- Homeowners reply by email, phone or the portal, and the reply isn't on the record
- Repeat violations aren't linked, so the second offence starts at step one again
- The board asks for a status list the night before the meeting

### What the workflow keeps for each violation
One row per case, grouped by community. If your HOA software already logs violations, the workflow works around it and only fills the gaps. The steps, letters and any fines come from each community's governing documents and the policy its board adopted. The workflow follows them; it doesn't write them.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Community, lot, owner and mailing address | Letters go to the owner of record, not just the address |
| Rule broken and the wording from the governing documents | Every notice quotes the same rule |
| Photos with date and time | The record shows what was seen and when |
| Notice step, date sent and cure date | When the next re-inspection is due |
| Owner replies and any request for a hearing | Nothing the homeowner said goes missing |
| Status: open, cured, escalated to board, closed | The board sees every open case at a glance |

### A first notice you can adapt
Courtesy notice to a homeowner (edit the words in brackets; your board's approved letter comes first):
```
Dear [owner name],

During a routine inspection of [community] on [date], we noted the following at [address]: [what was seen, e.g. trash bins visible from the street]. This relates to [rule or section] of the community's rules. A photo is attached.

Please correct this by [cure date]. If it's already been fixed, or there's a reason we should know about, just reply to this email and it will be added to the record.

If you'd like to discuss it, reply or call [manager name] at [phone].

Thank you,
[manager name], on behalf of the [community] Board of Directors
```

### How the workflow runs
1. On the drive-by, the manager takes a photo and picks the community, lot and rule on a short phone form.
2. The workflow opens a case and drafts the first notice from the board's approved letter. The manager checks it and sends it.
3. A day after the cure date, the case goes on the next drive-by list for that community.
4. If it's cured, the case closes and the owner gets a short thank-you. If not, the next notice in the board's policy is drafted for the manager to approve.
5. Owner replies, photos and hearing requests are filed with the case. Anything that needs a decision goes to the manager.
6. Before each board meeting, the board gets one list of open and escalated cases. If AI drafts a letter or a summary, a person reads and approves it before it's sent.

### A board report that takes five minutes to read
Boards make faster decisions when the report answers the same questions every month. The workflow can build this table from the open cases, so the manager only adds notes.
| Column | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| Lot and address | Where the violation is |
| Rule | The section of the governing documents it relates to |
| Opened | Date of the first notice |
| Stage | Courtesy notice, second notice, hearing offered, or the step your policy calls it |
| Next date | Cure date or hearing date, whichever comes next |
| Owner response | Replied, asked for a hearing, or no response |
| Decision needed | What the board is asked to decide this month, if anything |

### Keeping enforcement consistent
Owners are more likely to accept a notice when they can see the same rule is applied to everyone. A shared case log helps the manager and board check that.
- Use the board's approved letters for every case, so the wording doesn't depend on who sent it.
- Record each inspection route and date, so similar issues on other lots are noted on the same drive-by.
- Close cases with the date and photo of the fix, so repeat violations can be checked against your policy.
- Keep owner replies and any reasons they give with the case, for the board to weigh.
- Ask your community's attorney to review the letter set and steps once, so they match your governing documents and state law.

### What stays with you and the board
Every finding, every letter that goes out, every fine and every hearing. The workflow doesn't decide what counts as a violation or what the penalty is. Your community's governing documents, state law and the board do. It keeps each case on the steps already agreed and shows what's open. For another property workflow with approval limits, see [landlord repair approval limits](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/landlord-repair-approval-limits/). For UK block management, see [service charge reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/block-management-service-charge-reminders/).

It's built on what you already use (your HOA software where it allows a connection, a phone form, a spreadsheet and email), so there's nothing new to learn. Live in 2-3 days. If your HOA software already handles violations the way your boards want, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### What should an HOA violation log track?
For each case: the lot, the rule, the date and photo of what was seen, every notice sent and when, the cure date, the owner's replies, any hearing request, and the date and photo of the fix. That's enough for the board to see what's open and to keep enforcement consistent.

### Does it decide fines or hearings?
No. The board decides every fine and hearing under its governing documents and state law. The workflow drafts the letters the board approved and keeps the record.

Yes. Each community keeps its own rules, letters and enforcement steps, and every case follows the policy of the community it belongs to.

## LOLER thorough examination reminders: book the visit before the due date
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/loler-thorough-examination-reminders/

LOLER thorough examination reminders work when every report you issue leaves a next due date behind it. A simple workflow keeps one register of items by customer and site, emails the customer a few weeks before the earliest due date with visit dates, books the reply, sends the reports after the visit and follows up any defects. Your competent person still examines the equipment, writes the report and sets the next date.

Your customers have hoists, forklifts, slings and shackles, and each one has its own next examination date. Most of them don't track those dates; they wait for you. If the reminder is late, the visit is rushed or the work goes to whoever rings first. The dates are already on the reports you wrote. A reminder built from them, sent per site rather than per item, keeps customers on time and keeps the work with you.

### Why examination dates slip
- One site can have dozens of items, each on its own interval
- Equipment that lifts people and accessories usually run on shorter intervals than other kit
- Some customers have a written examination scheme with its own dates
- Reports go out, but the next due date isn't put in anyone's diary
- Defects found on the day need repair and a re-examination, and the follow-up gets lost
- New kit arrives between visits and isn't added to the register

### What the workflow keeps for each item
One row per item, grouped by customer and site. If your inspection software already holds the register, the workflow only needs the contacts and the dates. The next due date is the one your competent person puts on the report, from the legal maximum interval or the customer's written scheme. The workflow follows it; it doesn't set it.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Customer, site and the person who books | The reminder reaches someone who can say yes |
| Item, ID or serial number and safe working load | The examiner knows what to expect on site |
| Interval basis: 6 months, 12 months or written scheme | Why the date is what it is |
| Last examination, report number and next due date | When the reminder goes out |
| Defects and the date they must be fixed by | Serious defects get followed up, not filed |
| Status: reminded, booked, examined, report sent | You see what's open at a glance |

### A reminder you can copy
Email to a site contact (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], it's [name] from [company]. The next thorough examinations at [site] are due from [earliest due date]. That covers [number] items, including [examples, e.g. the two pallet trucks and the slings in the loading bay]. The full list is attached.

We can visit on [day 1] or [day 2]. Reply 1 or 2 to book, or reply with a day that works.

If you've bought or hired any new lifting kit since our last visit, reply with what it is and we'll add it to the list.
```

### How the workflow runs
1. Every report you issue updates the register with the item, the result and the next due date your examiner set.
2. A few weeks before the earliest date at each site, the site contact gets one email listing every item due, with visit dates.
3. When they reply, the visit goes in the examiner's diary and the site gets a reminder the day before about access and having the kit ready.
4. If there's no reply, one more message goes out. After that the site lands on a short call list for the office.
5. After the visit, the reports go to the customer and the register gets the new due dates.
6. Defects open a repair quote and a re-examination reminder. Questions go to you. If AI drafts a reply, a person reads and approves it before it's sent.

## PAT testing reminders: rebook the site before the retest date
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pat-testing-reminders/

PAT testing reminders work when every visit leaves a retest date on each site, not just on each label. A simple workflow keeps the asset list by customer and site, emails the customer a few weeks before the earliest retest date with visit dates, books the reply, sends the certificate and asset register after the visit and follows up failed items. The retest interval stays a risk-based decision made by you and the customer.

Offices, shops, schools and landlords all have kettles, laptops, extension leads and power tools with a sticker on them. The sticker shows a date, but nobody at the site looks at it until something fails or an insurer asks. If your reminder doesn't arrive in time, the work goes to whoever leaflets the business park next. The dates are already in your test records. A reminder built from them, sent per site, keeps customers on schedule and keeps the work with you.

### Why PAT retests get missed
- There is no single legal interval, so each customer can be on a different cycle
- Different kinds of equipment at one site may be on different intervals
- The person who booked last time has left, and nobody else knows
- Certificates go out, but the retest date never reaches anyone's diary
- Failed items need repair or replacement, and the follow-up gets lost
- New equipment arrives between visits and isn't on the asset list

### What the workflow keeps for each site
One row per site, linked to the asset list from your testing software or a spreadsheet. The retest interval is set by you and the customer from the type of equipment and where it's used, in line with HSE guidance. The workflow records that decision and follows it; it doesn't set it.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Customer, site and the person who books | The reminder reaches someone who can say yes |
| Number of items and kinds of equipment | You can plan the time on site |
| Agreed retest interval and who agreed it | The date has a reason behind it |
| Last visit, certificate number and next retest date | When the reminder goes out |
| Failed items and what was agreed for each | Repairs and replacements get followed up |
| Status: reminded, booked, tested, certificate sent | You see what's open at a glance |

### A reminder you can copy
Email to a site contact (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], it's [name] from [company]. The next PAT test at [site] is due from [retest date]. Last time we tested [number] items there. Your last certificate is attached.

We can visit on [day 1] or [day 2]. Reply 1 or 2 to book, or reply with a day that works. We can start early or work around opening hours if that helps.

If you've added a lot of new equipment since our last visit, reply with roughly how much so we can plan the time.
```

### How the workflow runs
1. Every visit you finish updates the site with the item count, the certificate and the next retest date you agreed.
2. A few weeks before that date, the site contact gets one email with the last certificate and two visit dates.
3. When they reply, the visit goes in the tester's diary and the site gets a reminder the day before about access and timing.
4. If there's no reply, one more message goes out. After that the site lands on a short call list for the office.
5. After the visit, the certificate and asset register go to the customer and the site gets its new retest date.
6. Failed items open a repair or replacement quote. Questions go to you. If AI drafts a reply, a person reads and approves it before it's sent.

### What stays with you
The testing, the pass or fail on each item and the advice on intervals. The workflow doesn't decide how often equipment is tested or whether it's safe to use; you and the customer do. It reminds customers on time and gets the paperwork to them. ## Appliance repair parts on order: keep customers updated without the calls
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/appliance-repair-parts-on-order-updates/

Parts-on-order updates for an appliance repair business are short messages tied to the job's status. When a technician orders a part, the customer hears what was ordered and roughly when it's expected. When the part arrives, they get a text with return visit times. If the part is late, they hear before they have to call. Your team still diagnoses, quotes and fixes; the workflow keeps the customer informed.

A washing machine that doesn't work is a problem every day it sits there. Most repairs need a second visit for a part, and that gap is where the phone calls start: "Is the part in yet?" Each call pulls someone off the desk to look it up. The answer is usually already in your system or the supplier's email. Turning it into a message to the customer saves the call and makes the wait feel shorter.

### Where the waiting goes wrong
- The customer leaves the first visit unsure what happens next
- Parts arrive at the office, but nobody tells the customer or books the return visit
- Supplier delays only come to light when the customer rings
- Wrong or damaged parts restart the wait with no message
- Parts sit on the shelf because the customer can't be reached
- The office spends its mornings answering "any news?" calls

### The four messages that cover most jobs
| When | What the customer hears |
| --- | --- |
| Part ordered | What was ordered, the expected date, and that you'll text when it arrives |
| Expected date passes | That it's late, what you're doing about it, and a new estimate if you have one |
| Part arrives | Two return visit slots to choose from |
| Day before the visit | The time window and anything they need to do, like clearing access |

### A message you can copy
Text when the part arrives (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], it's [company]. The [part] for your [appliance] has arrived. We can come back on [day 1, time window] or [day 2, time window]. Reply 1 or 2 to book, or reply with a better day.
```

### How the workflow runs
1. The technician marks the job "waiting on parts" in your job software or a shared sheet, with the part and the supplier.
2. The customer gets the "part ordered" message with the expected date.
3. When the part is booked in at the office, the customer gets the "part arrived" text with return visit slots.
4. Their reply puts the visit in the technician's diary and sends a reminder the day before.
5. If the expected date passes with no part, the office gets a nudge to check with the supplier, and the customer gets a short update a person has approved.
6. Questions and complaints go to you. If AI drafts a reply, a person reads and approves it before it's sent.

### What stays with you
The diagnosis, the quote, which part to order and every conversation about cost or warranty. The workflow sends status messages and books return visits; it doesn't promise delivery dates your supplier hasn't given. ## E-file rejection follow-up: tell the client fast and get the fix back in time
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/e-file-rejection-client-follow-up/

E-file rejection follow-up is what a tax preparer does after the IRS rejects a return: read the reject code, fix what you can, and ask the client for what you can't. Summaries of IRS Publication 1345 say that if you can't fix it, you must take reasonable steps to tell the taxpayer within 24 hours that the return wasn't filed and why. A simple workflow puts every reject on one list, drafts the client message for you to approve and reminds you before the perfection period ends.

In peak season, rejects arrive in the acknowledgement list between everything else. Some you fix in a minute. Others need the client: a dependent claimed by someone else, a wrong prior-year AGI, an IP PIN they didn't send. Those are the ones that slip, because the client doesn't know there's a problem and the clock to retransmit and keep the original filing date is short. A workflow can't fix the return, but it can make sure no reject sits unseen.

### Where rejects slip
- Acknowledgements are checked when someone remembers, not every day
- The reject needs something from the client, and the email to them is never sent
- The client replies with half the answer, and the thread goes quiet
- The fix changes the return, and the client needs to authorize the corrected version
- Nobody tracks how many days are left to retransmit
- The client assumes the return was filed because they signed it

### What the workflow keeps for each reject
One row per rejected return, from your tax software's acknowledgement report or the reject emails it sends. How long you have to retransmit depends on the return type, so check the current Publication 1345 and your software's guidance; the workflow uses the date you set.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Client, return type and reject date | You know what was rejected and when |
| Reject code and a short note on the cause | Anyone on the team can pick it up |
| Fix in-house or needs the client | Only the right rejects create a client message |
| Date the client was told | Shows you met the notification step |
| Retransmit-by date | The reminder you can't afford to miss |
| Status: open, waiting on client, retransmitted, accepted | You see what's open at a glance |

### A client message you can copy
Email to the client (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], your [year] federal return was not accepted by the IRS when we sent it on [date], so it has not been filed yet. The reason is [plain-English cause, e.g. the prior-year AGI on file doesn't match].

To fix it we need [what you need, e.g. a photo of last year's return, page 1]. Please reply with it by [date] so we can send the return again in time.

If anything changes on the return, we'll send it to you to approve before we file.
```

### How the workflow runs
1. Each day, new rejects from your software are added to one list with the code and the return type.
2. You or a preparer mark each one: fix in-house, or needs the client.
3. For client rejects, the workflow drafts a plain-English message. A person reads and approves it before it's sent, and the date sent is recorded.
4. If the client hasn't replied, a reminder goes out, and the preparer gets a nudge as the retransmit-by date gets close.
5. If the fix changes the return, the corrected version goes to the client for authorization through your usual signing tool.
6. Once you retransmit, the row waits for the new acknowledgement and closes when it's accepted.

### What stays with you
Reading the reject, deciding the fix, any change to the return and every word that goes to the client about it. The workflow doesn't touch your tax software's data or transmit anything. It keeps the list, drafts the messages for approval and watches the dates. Before you put client data through any automation or AI, read [Section 7216 consent before automation or AI](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/section-7216-consent-before-automation-or-ai/). For getting returns signed in the first place, see [tax return approval chasing](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/tax-return-approval-chasing/).

### How Mike Automations would build this
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how acknowledgements reach you today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on what you already use (your tax software's reports or emails, your practice software, a spreadsheet and email), so there's nothing new to learn. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is a fixed $2,000](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it, under the [pay-when-happy agreement](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agreement/). If your practice software already tracks rejects and your team works from it, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### Free tools for refiling
The free [working days calculator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/working-days-calculator/) counts business days between dates, which helps plan the client follow-up so a rejected return can be fixed and resubmitted in time.

### How long do I have to fix a rejected return?
The IRS gives a short perfection period to correct and retransmit while keeping the original filing date. The length depends on the return type, so check the current Publication 1345 and your software's guidance.

### Do I have to tell the client about every reject?
Summaries of Publication 1345 say that if you can't fix the reject yourself, you must take reasonable steps to tell the taxpayer within 24 hours that the return wasn't filed and why. Many preparers tell clients about every reject anyway.

### Does the workflow send anything to the IRS?
No. It reads reject reports, keeps the list, drafts client messages for approval and reminds you. You correct and retransmit in your tax software.

## Scaffold inspection reminders: never let a scaffold pass seven days unchecked
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/scaffold-inspection-reminders/

Scaffold inspection reminders work when every scaffold on hire has its own row with the date of the last inspection. Under the Work at Height Regulations 2005, a scaffold is inspected before first use, at intervals of no more than 7 days and after anything likely to affect its stability. A simple workflow shows the inspector what's due each morning, sends the signed report to the site contact and flags any scaffold that is close to the limit.

A scaffolding firm with thirty jobs up has thirty clocks running, each started on a different day. The dates live on tags, in a diary and in the inspector's head. Then a week of rain moves the round, one house at the end of a lane is missed, and the site keeps working from a scaffold whose last report is nine days old. The inspection itself takes a competent person and a few minutes. Remembering which scaffold is due today is the part a workflow can carry.

### Why weekly inspections get missed
- Every scaffold went up on a different day, so every seven-day clock is different
- The round is planned by area, not by due date
- Nobody is sure whether the weekly check is yours or the site's under this contract
- High winds or an alteration mean an extra inspection, and nobody tells the inspector
- The report is written on paper and never reaches the site contact
- The job runs past the hire period and falls off the list

### What the workflow keeps for each scaffold
One row per scaffold, started from the handover certificate. Who carries out the weekly inspection depends on your contract with the customer, so the row records it. Check HSE's scaffold guidance for the current rules; the workflow follows the dates and never judges the scaffold.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Site address, customer and site contact | The report reaches someone on site |
| Handover date and certificate | The first inspection and the start of the clock |
| Who inspects weekly: you or the site | No scaffold is left between two firms |
| Last inspection date and inspector | Shows what's due and by when |
| Extra inspections after wind, impact or alterations | The record shows why and when |
| Status: on hire, due, inspected, defect open, struck | You see what's open at a glance |

### A message you can copy
Email to the site contact after an inspection (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], it's [name] from [company]. We inspected the scaffold at [site address] today, [date]. The inspection report is attached. Please keep it with your site records.

[No defects were found. / We found the following and have dealt with it: ...]

The next inspection is due by [date]. If the scaffold is hit, altered or there is bad weather before then, please stop using it and call us on [number] so we can inspect it before work carries on.
```

### How the workflow runs
1. When a scaffold is handed over, a row is created from the handover certificate with the site contact and who inspects weekly.
2. Each morning the inspector gets one list: scaffolds due today and tomorrow, in route order, with any due today at the top.
3. The inspector fills in the report on a phone form. The competent person signs it; the workflow only files it.
4. The report goes to the site contact the same day and the row gets its new due date.
5. If a site reports wind damage, an impact or an alteration, an extra inspection goes on the list and you decide who attends.
6. Any scaffold that reaches day six with no report is flagged to the office. When a scaffold is struck, the row closes.

### What stays with you
Every inspection, every decision that a scaffold is safe to use and every repair. The workflow doesn't inspect anything and can't mark a scaffold as passed without a signed report from your competent person. It keeps the dates, builds the round and gets the paperwork to the site. For other dated inspections, see [LOLER examination reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/loler-thorough-examination-reminders/). For the daily paperwork on a build, see [construction daily site reports](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/construction-daily-site-reports/). If AI drafts a message to a customer, a person reads and approves it before it's sent.

### How Mike Automations would build this
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how handovers and inspections are recorded today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on what you already use (a spreadsheet, a phone form, email and text), so there's nothing new to learn. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is a fixed $2,000](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it, under the [pay-when-happy agreement](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agreement/). If your scaffold software already builds the inspection round and sends the reports, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### Free tools for inspection reminders
The free [appointment reminder generator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/appointment-reminder-generator/) writes the inspection reminders and visit confirmations, and the [invoice generator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/free-invoice-generator/) makes the invoice after each visit.

### How often does a scaffold need inspecting?
Under the Work at Height Regulations 2005, before first use, then at intervals of no more than 7 days, and after anything likely to affect its stability, such as high winds or alterations. Check HSE's guidance for the detail.

### Does the workflow do the inspection?
No. A competent person inspects and signs the report. The workflow shows what's due, files the report, sends it to the site and flags anything close to the limit.

### What if the site does its own weekly checks?
The row records who inspects under the contract. For those scaffolds the workflow can remind the site contact and ask for a copy of their report instead.

## Declined services follow-up: remind customers about the work they put off
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/auto-repair-declined-services-follow-up/

Declined services follow-up means going back to customers about recommended work they said no to, at the time the work should be done. A simple workflow takes each declined line from the repair order, keeps it on one list with the advisor's note and a follow-up date, sends one plain text or email when that date comes, and books the reply. Safety items go to a person to call instead.

The inspection found worn rear brake pads and a seeping water pump. The customer approved the oil change and said "not today" to the rest. The advisor wrote it on the repair order, the car left, and that was the last anyone thought about it. Three months later the customer has the brakes done somewhere else, or doesn't, and comes back on a tow truck. The recommendation was honest and the customer meant to deal with it. Nobody reminded them.

### Why declined work is never followed up
- The declined lines sit on a closed repair order nobody opens again
- Advisors are busy with today's cars, not last quarter's
- Nobody wrote down why the customer said no: price, time, or a second opinion
- A reminder a week later feels pushy; one when the work is due gets forgotten
- Safety items and "keep an eye on it" items get the same treatment
- The customer changed their number and the text never arrives

### What the workflow keeps for each declined item
One row per declined line, from your shop management system's report or export. The advisor sets the follow-up date when the car leaves, based on the part and how the customer drives. The workflow follows that date; it doesn't decide when work is needed.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |

| Urgency: safety, soon, or monitor | Safety items go to a person to call |
| Follow-up date set by the advisor | The reminder arrives when the work is due |
| Status: waiting, reminded, booked, done elsewhere, closed | You see what's open at a glance |

5. If there's no reply, one more message goes out later. After that the row waits for the customer's next visit.
6. When the customer books anything, the advisor sees their open declined items before the car arrives.

### What stays with you
The inspection, the recommendation, the price and every conversation about safety. The workflow doesn't diagnose anything or decide what a car needs. Text only customers who agreed to get texts from you, and honor every opt-out. For keeping customers informed while the car is with you, see [body shop repair updates](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/body-shop-repair-updates/). For jobs waiting on a part, see [parts-on-order updates](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/appliance-repair-parts-on-order-updates/). If AI drafts a reply, a person reads and approves it before it's sent.

## Certified payroll reminders: every subcontractor, every week, on one list
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/certified-payroll-report-reminders-subcontractors/

Certified payroll report reminders work when every subcontractor on a prevailing-wage job has a row for every week they were on site. On Davis-Bacon work, certified payrolls are due weekly, within seven days after the regular payment date, each with a signed Statement of Compliance. A simple workflow reminds each sub, logs what arrives, chases what's missing and shows the gaps before the next pay application goes in.

On a prevailing-wage job, the general contractor answers for every tier's paperwork. Six subs means six reports a week, and a week when a sub wasn't on site still needs an answer. The reports arrive by email, by upload and sometimes on paper in the trailer. Nobody notices the missing week until the agency holds a payment, and then someone spends two days asking a drywall sub for a report from March.

### Why certified payrolls go missing
- Each sub has its own pay week and pay date, so each report is due on a different day
- Nobody tells the office which subs were on site that week
- A sub with no work that week sends nothing, and nobody knows if that's a gap
- The report arrives without a signed Statement of Compliance
- Lower-tier subs send reports to the sub above them, and they stop there
- Missing weeks are found at pay application time, months later

### What the workflow keeps for each sub and week
One row per subcontractor per week, for each job with prevailing-wage rules. Federal jobs, state jobs and local jobs can have different forms and deadlines, so the row follows what the contract says. The workflow tracks whether a report arrived. It never judges whether the wages on it are right.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Job, subcontractor, tier and payroll contact | The reminder reaches the person who runs their payroll |
| Week ending and the sub's regular pay date | The due date is counted from it |
| On site that week: yes, no or not known | A no-work week is answered, not guessed |
| Report received, with signed statement: yes or no | An unsigned report isn't finished |
| Reviewed by, and sent to the agency on | Shows the report didn't stop on your desk |
| Status: due, received, sent back, complete, missing | You see what's open at a glance |

[We can't include your work in the next pay application until the reports are up to date.] Questions? Call me at [number].
```

1. When a sub starts on a prevailing-wage job, they're added once with their payroll contact, pay week and pay date.
2. Each week a row opens for every active sub. Their payroll contact gets one reminder with an upload link, a day or two ahead of the due date.
3. The sub uploads the report or marks the week as no work. The row records the time it arrived.
4. Your payroll or compliance person reviews each report, as they do now, and marks it complete or sends it back with a note.
5. Anything past its due date gets one more reminder. After that the project manager gets it on a call list.
6. Before each pay application, the project manager gets one page per job: every sub, every week, and what's still missing.

### What stays with you
Reviewing every report, checking wage rates and classifications, and every decision to hold a sub's payment. The workflow doesn't read wage determinations and can't tell you a report is correct. ## F-gas leak check reminders: every system's next check on one list
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/f-gas-leak-check-reminders/

F-gas leak check reminders work when every system you look after has its own row with its charge, its check interval and the date of the last check. Equipment holding F gas equivalent to 5 tonnes of CO2 or more needs leak checks at least every 12, 6 or 3 months, depending on its size. A simple workflow shows what's due, offers the customer a visit, and sends the record after your certified engineer has done the check.

A small air conditioning firm looks after hundreds of systems across shops, offices and restaurants. Some need a leak check once a year, some twice, a few every three months.
