Then a facilities manager asks for the leak check records for an audit, and you find one rooftop unit hasn't been checked since the summer before last.

### Why leak checks get missed
- Each system has its own interval, set by the type and amount of refrigerant
- The charge and gas type were never written down in one place
- The customer thinks the annual service and the leak check are the same visit
- A leak was repaired, and nobody booked the check that follows a repair
- The record stays on the engineer's job sheet and never reaches the customer
- Customers with no service contract are only seen when something breaks

### What the workflow keeps for each system
One row per system, not per customer. The interval is entered by your certified engineer from the equipment's charge. Intervals can be longer where a leak detection system is fitted, and some sealed equipment is treated differently, so check gov.uk's guidance on checking F gas equipment for leaks. The workflow follows the dates and never judges the equipment.
| Field | Why it matters |

| Refrigerant, charge and CO2 equivalent | The check interval comes from it |

| Last check: date, engineer and result | The record the customer has to keep |
| Repairs and the check that follows them | A repaired leak isn't left unchecked |

## New hire paperwork: every form in before the first week is over
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/new-hire-paperwork-collection-small-business/

New hire paperwork works when every hire has one row with a checklist: the forms you need, what's arrived and the dates that matter. Section 1 of Form I-9 is due no later than the first day of work, and the employer completes Section 2 within three business days of that day. A simple workflow sends the forms once an offer is accepted, reminds the hire about only what's missing, and shows the manager which I-9 is still open.

A small business hires a few people a year, or a few people a month in the busy season. Each time, someone has to remember the same pile of forms: the I-9, the W-4, the state forms, direct deposit, the handbook sign-off. The new hire starts Monday, the owner is on a job, and the paperwork is a folder on a desk. By Thursday payroll is asking for a W-4 that nobody has, and the I-9 is still blank.

### Why new hire paperwork slips
- The list of forms lives in one person's head, and that person is busy on the hire's first day
- Forms go out as email attachments and come back as phone photos, or not at all
- The hire forgets to bring identity documents on day one
- Nobody is watching the three business days for Section 2 of the I-9
- Payroll finds out about the hire when the first timesheet arrives
- Seasonal hires start in a group, and one missing form hides among ten complete sets

### What goes on each hire's checklist
You decide the list once, with your payroll provider or accountant, and the workflow follows it for every hire. Your state may add its own forms, so the checklist is yours, not a fixed template. For the I-9 rules and the list of acceptable documents, see the USCIS page for Form I-9.
| Item | Who completes it | What the row tracks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Form I-9, Section 1 | The new hire | Done by the first day of work |
| Form I-9, Section 2 | You, after examining the hire's documents | Done within three business days of the first day |
| Form W-4 and your state's withholding form | The new hire | Received, and passed to payroll |
| Direct deposit details | The new hire | Entered in your payroll system, not kept in email |
| Handbook and policy sign-off | The new hire | Signed and filed |
| Emergency contact and uniform or tool sizes | The new hire | Received |

### A message you can copy
Email to the new hire once the offer is accepted (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], welcome to [company]. Your first day is [date], [time], at [place]. Ask for [name] when you arrive.

Before then, please fill in your new hire forms here: [link]. It takes about [time]. You can do it on your phone.

On your first day, bring original documents for your Form I-9. The list of documents you can choose from is on the last page of the form: [link]. We need to see the originals, not photos.

Any questions, reply here or call [number].
```

### How the workflow runs
1. When you mark an offer as accepted, the hire gets a row with your checklist and their start date.
2. The hire gets an email or text you've approved, with one link to the forms and a note about what to bring on day one.
3. Each form that arrives is ticked off on the row. A reminder goes out two days before the start date, about only what's still missing.
4. On the first day, the manager gets a short list: who starts today, whose Section 1 is done and whose documents need to be examined.
5. A person examines the documents and completes Section 2. The workflow only records the date it was done.
6. Any I-9 still open on the second business day goes to the owner. Completed forms go to payroll before the first pay run.

### A new hire paperwork timeline
The I-9 dates come from USCIS. The other timings are suggestions to fit your own process.
| When | What happens | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Offer accepted | Checklist row created with the start date, welcome message with the forms link | Workflow, message approved by you |
| Two business days before the start | Reminder about anything still missing, plus what to bring on day one | Workflow |
| First day of work | Form I-9 Section 1 completed by the employee, by this day at the latest | New hire |
| Within three business days of the first day | Documents examined and Form I-9 Section 2 completed | A person at your business |
| Before the first pay run | Form W-4, your state's forms and direct deposit details are in payroll | Payroll, checked against the row |
| First week | Handbook acknowledgement and any policy sign-offs collected | Workflow reminds, manager confirms |

## Security deposit returns: every move-out's deadline on one list
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/security-deposit-return-deadline-tracking/

Security deposit return tracking works when every move-out has one row with the move-out date, the deadline your state sets, and the steps still open: forwarding address, inspection, vendor invoices, itemized statement and payment. Each state sets its own deadline, so the number of days is entered per property. A simple workflow counts down each row, chases the missing pieces, and shows the manager which statements are due this week.

A small property management company handles a handful of move-outs in a quiet month and dozens at the end of summer. Each one starts a clock. The inspection has to happen, the cleaner's invoice has to arrive, the owner has to agree the deductions, and the statement and the check have to go to an address the tenant may not have given yet. In a busy month, one move-out sits in an inbox until the deadline has already passed.

### Why deposit deadlines get missed
- The clock starts at move-out, but nobody writes the deadline down that day
- The tenant left without giving a forwarding address
- The statement waits on a vendor invoice that hasn't arrived
- The owner hasn't answered the email about deductions
- Properties in two states have two different deadlines, and both are kept from memory
- August brings thirty move-outs in two weeks

### What each move-out row holds
One row per move-out. The deadline comes from your state's law and the lease, and you or your attorney enter the number of days for each property once. Some states also set rules about receipts, interest or how the statement is delivered. The workflow follows what you entered and never works out the law for you.
| Field | Why it matters |

| Move-out inspection: date, photos and notes | The evidence behind each deduction |
| Vendor invoices or estimates | Each deduction has a figure and a document |
| Owner's approval of the deductions | The decision is on file |
| Statement sent and payment made: dates | Proof it went out on time |

Amount returned: [amount], sent by [method] on [date]

[Company name], [date]

## Corporation Tax payment reminders: every client told what to pay, and by when
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/corporation-tax-payment-reminders-for-clients/

Corporation Tax payment reminders work when each client company has its own row: the accounting period end, the payment date, the amount once you've agreed it and the payment reference. For companies with taxable profits up to £1.5 million, the payment is due 9 months and 1 day after the period ends, which is before the return is due. A simple workflow emails each director ahead of the date and lists who hasn't confirmed they've paid.

Self Assessment has one payment date that every client half remembers. Corporation Tax doesn't. Each company pays on its own date, set by its year end, and that date falls before the return has to be filed. So a practice with sixty limited company clients has sixty payment dates spread across the year. The director hears the figure once, in a long email with the accounts attached, and then nothing. A few months later a letter about interest arrives, and they ring you.

### Why Corporation Tax payments get missed
- Every company has a different date, so there's no busy season to prompt anyone
- The payment is due before the return, so "we haven't filed yet" feels like "nothing is due yet"
- The figure went out once, inside the accounts email, months before the date
- The payment reference changes with each accounting period, and clients reuse last year's
- The accounts aren't final close to the date, so nobody tells the client anything
- Nobody at the practice has a list of who has paid

### What each client row keeps
One row per company and accounting period. The payment date is worked out from the period end, and your team enters the amount and the reference. The rule here is for companies with taxable profits up to £1.5 million. Larger companies normally pay in instalments, and they need their own schedule from you. To work out the dates for a whole client list at once, use the free [company filing deadline calculator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/company-deadlines/).
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |

| Accounting period end | Sets the payment date |
| Payment date: 9 months and 1 day after the period end | Sets every reminder |
| Amount: agreed, estimated or nothing to pay | The client sees a figure you've approved |
| Payment reference for this period | The payment lands against the right period |
| Status: not told, told, confirmed paid, no reply | You see who is open at a glance |

[Your name]
[Practice name]

6. Three working days before the date, anyone still open goes on your call list with their phone number.

## Preliminary notice deadline tracking: every new job, before the clock runs out
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/preliminary-notice-deadline-tracking-subcontractors/

Preliminary notice deadline tracking works when every new job opens a row on the day it's awarded: the first day on site, the state, the deadline your office enters for that state and the names the notice has to reach. Many states require this notice early in a job to keep lien rights, and the rules differ from state to state. A simple workflow chases the missing job details, counts down the days and files proof of sending.

The notice itself is a short form. The hard part is everything around it. A crew starts on a new job on Monday. The office hears about it on Thursday, from a timesheet. Nobody has the owner's name, the lender or the legal address, and the general contractor's project manager doesn't answer email. The deadline started running on the first day of work, and three weeks later it has passed. Nobody notices until an invoice goes unpaid months later, and by then the lien right may be gone.

### Why preliminary notices go out late
- The clock starts when work or deliveries start, not when the office hears about the job
- The notice needs names the subcontractor doesn't have: owner, lender, sometimes the surety
- Each state has its own deadline, its own name for the notice and its own delivery rules
- Small jobs get skipped because "we never have trouble with this GC"
- Proof of mailing sits in someone's truck or inbox
- Nobody has one list of open jobs with the days left on each

### What each job row keeps
One row per job. The deadline comes from your state's rules, and it can depend on your role, the type of project and whether other notices were filed on the job. So your office or your attorney enters it, once per state and job type, and the workflow follows it. It never assumes a number of days.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Job, address and state | Which rules apply |
| First day of work or first delivery | The date most deadlines count from |
| Notice deadline, entered by your office | Sets every reminder |
| Owner, general contractor, lender and anyone else the notice must reach | The notice can't go without them |
| How it was sent, the date and the receipt or tracking number | Proof if it's ever questioned |
| Status: details missing, ready, sent, proof filed, not required | You see what's open at a glance |

### A message you can copy

```

3. The legal address or parcel number of the property
4. The surety's name, if the job is bonded

A reply to this email is fine. We start on [date], so we'd be grateful to have it by [date].

[Your name]
[Company]
```

4. Missing details are chased every two working days. Only what's still missing is asked for.
5. When the row is complete, the office gets one page with everything the notice needs. A person prepares, checks and sends it.
6. The receipt or tracking number is filed on the row. Any job inside five days of its deadline with nothing sent goes to the owner of the business each morning.

### What stays with you
Deciding whether a notice is required, what it must say, who must receive it and how it has to be delivered. Those are legal questions, and the answers differ by state, so they belong with you and your attorney. The workflow doesn't prepare a legal document, doesn't send one on its own and can't tell you a notice was valid or on time. It keeps the dates, the details and the proof in one place. For the payment side of the same jobs, see [lien waiver tracking](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/lien-waiver-tracking-subcontractors/) and [pay application reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/subcontractor-pay-application-reminders/). ## Retention release reminders: the money you've already earned, asked for on time
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/retention-release-reminders-subcontractors/

Retention release reminders work when every finished job keeps a row: the amount held, the two release dates from the subcontract and who to ask. Retention is commonly released in two parts, the first around practical completion and the rest at the end of the defects period, which can be a year or more later. A simple workflow reminds your office before each date, sends the request you've approved and chases it until it's paid.

Retention is easy to forget because it comes due long after the job has left your head. The work finished in spring. The last part of the retention falls due the following year, when the crew is on other sites, the contracts manager who ran the job has moved on and the main contractor has no reason to remind you. A subcontractor with thirty jobs a year can have a large sum spread across old jobs, and no list that says which of it can be asked for today.

### Why retention goes unclaimed
- The second release date is a year or more after the work finished
- The date depends on completion paperwork that the subcontractor never received
- Each subcontract has its own percentages, dates and conditions
- The accounts system shows the invoice as part paid, not as retention with a date
- Nobody is asked for it, so nobody pays it
- Defects are raised late, and nobody recorded that they were fixed

### What each job row keeps
One row per job. The amounts and dates come from the subcontract and from the completion paperwork, and your office enters them. Subcontracts differ, so the workflow follows what yours says and never assumes a percentage or a period. If a date isn't known yet, the row says so and asks for it.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Job, main contractor and who to ask | Where the request goes |
| Total retention held | What you're owed across the job |
| First release: date or event, and amount | Usually tied to completion |
| Second release: date and amount | Usually the end of the defects period |
| Completion certificate or email, and any defects raised and closed | The answers to the usual objections |
| Status: held, due soon, requested, paid, in dispute | You see what's open at a glance |

### A message you can copy

Our works were completed on [date]. [All defects notified to us were closed on [date]. / No defects have been notified to us.]

Our application is attached. Could you confirm it's been received and when it will be paid?

Thanks,
[Your name]
[Company]
[Phone]
```

### How the workflow runs
1. When a job finishes, the contracts manager fills in a short form: the retention held, the release dates and who to ask. The completion paperwork is filed on the row.
2. If the completion date isn't confirmed, the main contractor is asked for it, and asked again every two weeks until it's on file.
3. On the first of each month the office gets a list of every release falling due in the next 60 days, with the amounts.
4. A person checks the row and approves the request. It goes out with the application attached.
5. No reply after seven days sends a short follow-up, then puts the job on the call list.
6. When the payment is matched in your accounts, the row moves to paid. A defect raised late opens a task for the contracts manager, with a date.

### What stays with you
Reading the subcontract, deciding what is due and when, answering defects and deciding what to do when a main contractor won't pay. The workflow doesn't interpret a contract, and it isn't legal advice. If a release is disputed, the row holds the dates and the paperwork your adviser will ask for. If AI drafts a message, a person reads and approves it before it's sent.

## IRS notice tracking: every client letter on one list, with its response date
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/irs-notice-tracking-tax-practices/

IRS notice tracking works when every letter a client forwards becomes one row: the client, the notice number, the date on the notice, the response date printed on it and who owns it. Response periods differ by notice type, so the preparer enters the date from the letter itself. A simple workflow collects the letters, reminds the owner before the date, asks the client for anything missing and keeps proof of what was sent.

Client notices arrive the worst possible way: a photo in a text, a scan attached to an email about something else, an envelope dropped at the front desk. Each one has its own response date, and some come with a matching state letter. In a small practice the notices live in three inboxes and one person's memory. Nobody notices a letter has been forgotten until a second, sharper letter arrives.

### Why notices slip
- Clients send letters by text, email, upload or in person
- The response date is on page one, and nobody copies it anywhere
- The letter sits with whoever happened to receive it
- A state notice on the same issue is tracked separately, or not at all
- Documents needed from the client take longer than expected
- Proof of the response is in a sent folder, not on the client file

### What each notice row keeps
One row per notice. A person reads the letter and fills in the dates; the workflow never guesses a deadline. If the response date can't be read, the row says so and stays at the top of the list until someone checks.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Client and tax year | Which return the letter is about |
| Notice number and date on the notice | What kind of letter it is |
| Response date and any payment date, from the letter | Kept separately, since they can differ |
| Matching state notice, if any | So both are answered |
| Owner and documents needed from the client | Who acts and what they're waiting for |
| Status and proof of response | Open, waiting on client, sent, closed |

### A message you can copy
Email to a client after their notice is logged (edit the words in brackets):
```
Subject: Your IRS letter dated [date]: next steps

Hi [first name],

Thanks for sending the IRS letter dated [date]. We've logged it and [preparer name] is looking after it.

To respond, we need:
- [document 1]
- [document 2]

Please upload them here: [secure upload link]. We'd like them by [date] so we can reply before the date on the letter.

Please don't pay or reply to the IRS yourself until we've spoken. If you get another letter about this, send it to us straight away.

Thanks,
[Your name]
[Firm]
```

### How the workflow runs
1. Clients send letters to one address or upload link. Each upload opens a row and files the letter on the client's record.
2. A preparer reads the notice and enters the notice number, the dates and what's needed. Until then the row is flagged as unread.
3. The client gets the approved message with the list of documents and a secure upload link.
4. Missing documents are chased every few days, and the owner is told when the client hasn't replied.
5. Each morning the team sees every open notice sorted by response date, with the ones in the next 14 days at the top.
6. When the response is sent, the proof is filed on the row and a follow-up date is set to check for the IRS reply.

### What stays with you
Reading each notice, deciding whether to agree, pay or dispute, preparing the response and every conversation about tax. The workflow tracks dates and documents; it isn't tax advice. Using client tax information in any tool needs the right care, so see [Section 7216 consent before automation or AI](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/section-7216-consent-before-automation-or-ai/). For returns that bounce back from e-file, see [e-file rejection follow-up](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/e-file-rejection-client-follow-up/). ## Bid invitation tracking: every invitation to bid, one list, no missed due dates
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/bid-invitation-tracking-subcontractors/

Bid invitation tracking works when every invitation to bid becomes one row: the project, the general contractor, the due date, the job walk, the estimator and a bid or no-bid decision. A simple workflow pulls invitations out of email into that list, updates the row when an addendum moves the date, reminds the estimator before each deadline and follows up with the GC after you submit.

A busy subcontractor can get invitations to bid from a dozen general contractors in a week, through email, bid boards and phone calls. Some are worth pricing and most aren't. The ones that matter get buried under the ones that don't, an addendum moves a due date without anyone noticing, and a bid that went out two weeks ago never gets a follow-up call. The estimator is good at pricing work, not at reading forty invitation emails a week.

### Why bids get missed
- Invitations come from many GCs, each in its own format
- A due date changes by addendum and the spreadsheet isn't updated
- Nobody decides bid or no-bid, so invitations just sit
- Job walks and pre-bid meetings aren't in the diary
- Two estimators price the same project for different GCs without knowing
- Nobody asks the GC what happened after the bid went in

### What each bid row keeps
One row per project per general contractor. The workflow fills in what it can read from the invitation, and the estimator checks it. Anything it can't read, like a due time, is left blank and flagged rather than guessed.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Project, location and general contractor | The same project can come from several GCs |
| Bid due date and time, and any addenda | The date you actually work to |
| Job walk or pre-bid meeting | Goes straight into the diary |
| Bid or no-bid, with a reason | So the list only holds work you're pricing |
| Estimator and status | Pricing, submitted, follow-up, won, lost |
| Bid amount and follow-up date | What was sent and when to ask |

### A message you can copy

```
Subject: [Project name]: our [trade] bid submitted [date]

Hi [first name],

We submitted our [trade] bid for [project name] on [date]. Our number was [amount], based on [drawings / addenda up to number X].

Have you had a chance to level the bids yet? If you need anything clarified or a scope question answered, I can turn it around today.

If the job has been awarded, I'd be grateful to know the outcome either way so we can keep our records straight.

Thanks,
[Your name]
[Company]
[Phone]
```

### How the workflow runs
1. Invitations sent to your bids address open a row with the project, the GC and the dates the workflow could read. The estimator checks each new row.
2. Each morning the estimator gets the new invitations to mark bid or no-bid. No-bid rows get a short, polite reply to the GC if you want one.
3. Job walks and due dates go into the shared calendar. When an addendum changes a date, the row and the calendar are updated and the estimator is told.
4. Three days and one day before each due date, the estimator gets a reminder with anything still missing, like supplier quotes.
5. When the bid is marked submitted, a follow-up is scheduled. The approved email goes out after a set number of days with no reply, then the row goes on the call list.
6. Won and lost results are recorded, so you can see which GCs actually award you work.

Deciding what to bid, the takeoff and pricing, scope questions and every conversation with the GC. The workflow keeps the list and the dates; it doesn't price anything. | Faults found and quote status | So repairs don't stall |

## K-1 tracking for tax preparers: know which returns are waiting on which K-1
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/k1-tracking-tax-preparers/

K-1 tracking works when every expected Schedule K-1 has its own row: the client, the partnership, S corporation or trust that issues it, whether it arrived last year and when, and whether it's in this year. A simple workflow builds the list from last year's returns, asks clients to forward each K-1 as it arrives, files what comes in and shows you, well before the deadline, which returns are still waiting so you can decide on an extension early.

A return with three K-1s can't be finished until the last one lands, and the client often doesn't know which ones they're due. K-1s from partnerships and investment funds tend to arrive late, and later still when the issuer extends its own return. In most practices the list of what's outstanding lives in the preparer's head or a note on the client file, so the gaps show up in April.

### Why K-1s fall through
- Nobody listed which K-1s each client should expect
- The client gets the K-1 by email or on a portal and forgets to forward it
- A new investment this year means a K-1 nobody knew about
- An issuer extends, and the client isn't told
- Returns sit at "waiting on K-1" with no date to follow up
- Extension decisions are made in the last week

### What each K-1 row keeps
One row per client per issuer. The workflow fills the list from last year's returns and the client's answers; your staff check it. If a date isn't known, the row says so.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Client and return | Which return is blocked |
| Issuer name and type | Partnership, S corporation, trust or estate |
| When it arrived last year | A guide to when to start asking |
| Status: expected, received or not needed | One clear answer per row |
| Issuer's expected date, if the client knows it | So late K-1s are planned for |
| Extension flag and who decided | Kept with the return, not in someone's head |

### A message you can copy

- [issuer 1]
- [issuer 2]

These usually come by email or through the investment's online portal. When one arrives, please forward it or upload it here: [upload link].

If you've sold an investment, or have a new one this year, just reply and let us know.

Thanks,
[Your name]
[Practice name]
```

### How the workflow runs
1. Before the season starts, the list of expected K-1s is built from each client's prior-year return and checked by your staff.
2. Your organizer or first email asks the client to confirm the list and add any new investments.

4. Clients with K-1s still missing get the approved email on a set schedule, naming each issuer.
5. Each week you get a short list of returns still waiting, with any expected dates the client gave.
6. Before your cut-off date, returns still waiting are flagged for an extension decision. You decide.

### What stays with you
Reading every K-1, preparing the return and deciding whether to file an extension. The workflow keeps the list and sends the reminders; it doesn't give tax advice. ## Statute of limitations tracking: no matter without a checked date
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/statute-of-limitations-tracking-law-firms/

Statute of limitations tracking works when every open matter has a limitation date that an attorney set and a second person checked, kept on one list apart from the everyday calendar. A simple workflow refuses to leave a new matter without a date, sends warnings to more than one person as the date gets closer, and stops only when someone records that the case was filed or the date no longer applies.

A missed limitation date can't be fixed later. Most small firms know this, and still the date often lives in one attorney's calendar, typed once at intake, with nobody checking it again. When that attorney is out, a matter changes hands, or a new fact moves the date, the reminder can be wrong or missing. The legal judgment is the attorney's. The tracking around it is clerical, and it's where gaps appear.

### Where limitation dates go wrong
- A new matter is opened and nobody enters a date
- The date is entered once and never checked by a second person
- Reminders go only to one attorney's calendar
- A matter moves to another attorney and the reminders don't follow
- New facts change the date, but the old date stays on file
- Nobody records when the date stops applying, so the list fills with noise

### What each matter row keeps
One row per potential claim. The attorney sets the date and the reason for it; the workflow never calculates or suggests a limitation period. A row without a checked date is shown as a problem until it has one.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Matter, client and responsible attorney | Someone owns the date |
| Limitation date and the note on how it was set | The reasoning is on file, not in someone's head |
| Set by, checked by, and when | Every date has a second pair of eyes |
| Warning dates | Chosen by the firm, sent to more than one person |
| Status: open, filed, resolved or not pursued | Warnings stop only when someone records why |

### How the workflow runs
1. When a new matter is opened, the workflow adds a row and asks the responsible attorney for the limitation date and a short note.
2. Until the date is entered, the matter shows on a daily "no date" list for the attorney and the office manager.
3. Once a date is entered, a second person you name is asked to check it and mark it checked.
4. At the warning points your firm chooses, the attorney, the backup and the office manager each get a reminder.
5. If a matter changes attorney, the warnings move with it, and the new attorney is asked to confirm the date.
6. Every Monday the partners get one list: dates in the next 90 days, dates not yet checked and matters with no date.

### What stays with you
Every legal decision: what the limitation period is, when it started, whether anything pauses it, and when to file. ### Why lease dates get missed
- Dates live in the lease PDF, a side letter and a calendar, not in one place
- A reminder says "break due" but not the clause, the notice window or who acts
- The reminder goes to someone who has left or changed portfolio
- A deed of variation changed a date and the record was never updated
- The client is asked for a decision too late to take advice
- Nobody sees the next six months of events across every property

### What each lease event row keeps
One row per event per lease. Your team enters every date from the signed lease and any variations, and a second person checks it. Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/certificate-of-insurance-requests-insurance-agencies/

Certificate of insurance requests run smoothly when every request arrives through one short form that asks for the holder, the job and any special wording up front. COI requests arrive by email, text and phone, often at the end of the day and usually missing something: the holder's address, the project or whether they need additional insured wording. Each one means a reply, a wait and another look at the policy. Requests that ask for wording the policy doesn't support need a careful answer, not a quick one. Most of the work around a certificate is the same every time, so it can run on its own while your account managers keep every coverage decision.

### Where certificate requests get stuck
- Requests come in by email, text, phone and the client portal
- The holder's name or address is missing, so someone has to ask
- Additional insured or waiver wording is requested without the contract
- The account manager isn't sure the policy has the endorsement asked for
- Certificates aren't reissued to holders when the policy renews
- Nobody can see which requests are still waiting, and on whom

### What the intake form asks
One form for clients and the holders who request certificates directly. It goes on your website and in your email signature. Anything you need to check against the policy is asked for up front, so the account manager doesn't have to write back.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Insured client and policy type | Matched to the right account |
| Certificate holder name and address | The certificate is right the first time |
| Project or job description | Some holders need it on the certificate |
| Special wording requested | Additional insured, primary, waiver: flagged for a person |
| Contract or requirements page | The account manager can check what's needed |
| Needed by | Urgent requests go to the top |

### A message you can copy
Reply when a request is missing details (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], thanks for your certificate request for [client name].

To get it right the first time, we need:
- [missing item 1]
- [missing item 2]

You can reply to this email or add them here: [form link]. If the holder asked for special wording, please attach the contract or their insurance requirements so we can check it against the policy.

We'll send the certificate as soon as it has been checked.

[Your name], [agency], [phone]
```

### How the workflow runs
1. A request arrives through the form or by email. The workflow logs it on one list with the client, the holder and the date needed.
2. If anything is missing, the requester gets the message above. No reply gets a reminder the next morning.
3. Complete requests are matched to the client's policies. Where your agency management system allows it, a draft certificate is prepared from the policy details already on file.
4. Any request for special wording, or for coverage the policy may not have, goes to the account manager with the contract attached. The workflow never adds wording on its own.
5. The account manager checks and approves the certificate. The workflow emails it to the holder, copies the client and logs it on the account.
6. Before each renewal, the account manager gets a list of holders on that policy so new certificates go out once the renewal is bound.

### What stays with you

## Interview confirmations for recruitment agencies: both sides confirmed, feedback the same day
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/interview-confirmations-recruitment-agencies/

Interview confirmations work when every interview has one row: the candidate, the client, the time, the place or link, and who has confirmed. A simple workflow sends both sides the details, reminds them the day before, flags a candidate who hasn't confirmed so the consultant can call, and asks the candidate and the hiring manager for feedback straight after.

An interview takes days to arrange and minutes to lose. The candidate didn't see the address, the hiring manager moved the time and nobody told the candidate, or the feedback arrives a week later when the candidate has accepted somewhere else. Consultants spend their afternoons on confirmation calls and feedback chasing instead of talking to new candidates. The steps are the same for every interview, so most of the messages can go out on their own while consultants keep the conversations that matter.

### Where interviews go wrong
- The candidate gets the time but not the address, parking or video link
- The client moves the interview and the candidate hears too late
- Nobody notices that the candidate never confirmed
- The candidate has no easy way to say they're running late or can't make it
- Feedback from the hiring manager takes days to arrive
- The consultant doesn't hear how the candidate felt about the role

### What each interview row keeps
One row per interview, in your recruitment software or a shared sheet. The consultant books the interview as now; the workflow takes it from there.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Candidate, role and client | The right messages go to the right people |
| Date, time and stage | First interview, second interview or trial shift |
| Address or video link, and who to ask for | The candidate arrives at the right place |
| Candidate confirmed / client confirmed | Gaps show up before the day |
| Feedback from both sides | The consultant can act the same day |

Where: [address / video link]. Ask for [contact name] at reception.

```

### How the workflow runs
1. When the consultant books an interview, the candidate gets the details by email and text, and the hiring manager gets a calendar invite with the candidate's CV.

4. If the client changes the time, the consultant updates the row and the candidate gets the new details at once.

- Damaged materials found on the visit never become a quote for remedial work
- Nobody sees which clients are about to go overdue

## Dental lab case tracking: every case back before the patient sits down
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/dental-lab-case-tracking/

- The case is due back the day before the appointment, so there's no time to react
- Nobody checks which cases are still out until the morning of the fit
- The lab's dispatch email lands in one person's inbox, and they're off that day
- A case comes back with a query or a remake, and the appointment isn't moved
- The patient takes a day off work and arrives for a crown that isn't there
- Several labs, several ways of sending updates, and no single list

### What each case row keeps

## Patient referral tracking: closing the loop on every referral
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/patient-referral-tracking-medical-practices/

Patient referral tracking works when every referral has one row with one owner: the patient, the specialist, the date sent, whether the patient is scheduled, whether they were seen and whether the consult note came back. A simple workflow flags referrals that stall at any step, reminds the owner to follow up, and asks the specialist's office for the note, so no referral quietly disappears.

A referral can fail in three places: the specialist never receives it, the patient never books, or the patient is seen and the note never comes back. Guidance from IHI and CMS says the same thing: log every referral and track it to the end. Your EHR may already have a referral screen. The gap is usually that nobody owns the follow-up when a referral sits still.

### Where referrals get lost
- The referral is faxed or sent, but nobody confirms the specialist received it
- The patient gets the specialist's number and never calls
- The specialist's office can't reach the patient and closes the referral
- Prior authorization is still pending, so the visit can't be scheduled
- The patient is seen, but the consult note never reaches the referring provider
- Nobody is named as owner, so everyone assumes someone else is following up

### What each referral row keeps
One row per referral, with one owner. If your EHR already tracks referrals, the workflow works from a report or export instead of a second list. Which referrals are urgent, and how long each step may take, is decided by your clinicians.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Patient, specialist and reason | Everyone follows up on the same referral |
| Urgency set by the provider | Urgent referrals are checked sooner |
| Date sent and received | You know the specialist has it |
| Scheduled and seen dates | Stalled referrals show up |
| Consult note received | The loop is only closed when the note is back |
| Owner | One person follows up |

### A message you can copy
Request to a specialist's office for a consult note (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [specialist office],

We referred [patient name, date of birth] to [specialist] on [date] for [reason]. Our records show the patient was seen on [date].

Could you send the consult note to [provider name] at [fax or secure email]?

Thank you, [name], [practice], [phone]
```

### How the workflow runs
1. When a provider orders a referral, it's added to the list with an owner and the urgency they set.
2. If the specialist hasn't confirmed receipt after the days you choose, the owner gets a reminder.
3. If the patient isn't scheduled in time, the owner gets a task to call the patient or the specialist.
4. After the visit date, if no consult note has arrived, the request above goes to the specialist's office, approved by the owner.
5. Every week the practice manager sees one short list: open referrals by step and by owner.

### What stays with you
Every clinical decision: who to refer, how urgent it is and what to do with the consult note. Calls to patients stay with your staff. The workflow only keeps the list, sends reminders and drafts requests. It runs in tools your practice already uses for patient information, and stores only what the referral list needs. ## P11D client reminders: benefits information in before June
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/p11d-benefits-information-chasing-accountants/

P11D client reminders work when every company client gets the same short questionnaire in April, a reminder until they answer, and a list for you of who still hasn't. GOV.UK sets 6 July for filing P11D and P11D(b) and 22 July for paying Class 1A National Insurance electronically (19 July by cheque), so the questions need to go out long before June.

P11D season is rarely hard because of the tax. It's hard because the information sits with clients: the company car's list price, who had private medical cover, the loan to the director, the gym membership the company paid for. Ask in April and half of them answer. The rest reply in the last week of June. A simple workflow sends the questions early, chases the gaps and shows you who is holding things up.

### Where P11D season goes wrong
- The benefits questions go out late, or only to the clients you remember
- Clients answer "same as last year" and nobody checks what changed
- Car details, private use and dates arrive in five separate emails
- Nobody can see which companies still haven't replied
- Clients don't know they also need to pay Class 1A, or by when
- Payrolled benefits are forgotten on the P11D(b)

### The dates that drive it
GOV.UK lists the deadlines in its expenses and benefits guidance for employers. Check the page each year before you set your own dates.
| Deadline (per GOV.UK) | What's due |
| --- | --- |
| 6 July | P11D for each employee with benefits, and P11D(b) for the company |
| 22 July | Class 1A National Insurance paid electronically |
| 19 July | Class 1A National Insurance paid by cheque |

### Mandatory payrolling is coming
GOV.UK says payrolling of benefits in kind becomes mandatory in phases, starting from 6 April 2027 with company cars, vans and their fuel, and most other benefits following later. Until then, and for anything not payrolled, P11D and P11D(b) are still needed. The same questionnaire is worth keeping: payroll will need the benefit details too, just earlier. Check HMRC's current guidance for which benefits are in each phase.

### A message you can copy

Please fill in this short form by [date]: [link]

It asks about company cars and vans, medical cover, loans to directors or staff, and anything else the company paid for personally. If nothing changed from last year, there's a box for that, but please check the car details.

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### How the workflow runs
1. In April, every company client on your list gets the questionnaire with a link to a short form.
2. Answers land in one sheet, one row per company, with last year's benefits shown next to this year's.
3. Clients who haven't answered get a reminder each week, and after the date you set they move to your call list.
4. When you've filed, the director gets an email with the Class 1A amount and date you've entered.
5. Every Friday you get a short list: companies not answered, answers to check, and returns not yet filed.

### What stays with you
Deciding what's taxable, the values on every form, and filing with HMRC. The workflow only sends questions and reminders, collects answers and keeps the list; it never calculates the tax. If AI drafts a message, a person reads and approves it before it's sent. For the rest of the year, see [Corporation Tax payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/corporation-tax-payment-reminders-for-clients/) and [confirmation statement reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/confirmation-statement-client-reminders/).

| Apply and wait | Application date, chase dates, approval logged before the install is booked |
| Supply issue (e.g. looped) | Request to the DNO, customer updates until it's resolved |

- Councils ask for updated documents during the licence and the request gets lost

## VAT threshold monitoring: spot clients nearing £90,000 before it's late
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/vat-registration-threshold-monitoring-clients/

VAT threshold monitoring works when every client who isn't VAT registered has one row with their monthly taxable turnover, and a sum of the last 12 months is checked every month. GOV.UK sets the threshold at £90,000 over a rolling 12 months, with 30 days from the end of the month it's passed to register. A simple workflow collects the monthly figure, flags clients getting close, and puts them on your list for a conversation.

The VAT threshold isn't a tax-year test: it's any rolling 12 months. A growing sole trader can pass it in July and only find out at year end, by which time the registration is late and VAT is owed on months of sales they never charged it on. Most practices check when they do the accounts. A monthly check of the clients who are close gives you months of warning instead.

### Where it goes wrong
- Turnover is only looked at once a year, when the accounts are prepared
- The client thinks the threshold is per tax year
- Bank feeds show money in, but nobody adds up the last 12 months
- A big one-off contract pushes turnover over in a single month
- The client doesn't tell you about a new income stream
- Registration is discussed, then nobody follows up

### How the monthly check works
Each row holds the client's taxable turnover month by month, from their bookkeeping software or a figure they send you. What counts as taxable turnover is your judgement. The workflow only adds up the last 12 months and compares it with the levels you set, for example a warning at £75,000 and an alert at £85,000.
| Rolling 12 months (example levels) | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Below your warning level | Nothing: checked again next month |
| Above your warning level | Client gets a heads-up, you get a note |
| Above your alert level | On your call list this week |
| Over £90,000 | Urgent task with the month it was passed |

### A message you can copy

```

Book a time here: [link]
[your name]
```

### How the workflow runs
1. Each month the workflow pulls last month's turnover from the bookkeeping software, or asks the client for it.
2. It adds up the last 12 months for every non-registered client.
3. Clients above your warning level get the heads-up email, and you see them on a list.
4. Clients above your alert level go on your call list with their monthly figures.
5. Every month you get a short list: who's close, who's over, and who hasn't sent a figure.

### What stays with you
What counts as taxable turnover, whether and when a client registers, which scheme suits them, and the registration itself. The workflow adds up numbers and sends reminders; it doesn't give advice. If AI drafts a message, a person reads and approves it before it's sent. - The client has moved, changed members or a registered agent, and nobody updates the filing
- Approval to file and pay the fee sits in an unanswered email
- Confirmation of filing isn't saved, so nobody can prove it was done
- The client gets a scary third-party "compliance" letter and calls in a panic

## CAQH re-attestation reminders: every provider, every cycle, on one list
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/caqh-re-attestation-reminders-medical-practices/

A CAQH reminder workflow keeps one list of your providers with their last attestation date and the expiry dates of the documents on their profile. Ahead of each re-attestation date it reminds the provider or your credentialing person, then checks it was done. Expiring licenses, DEA registrations and malpractice certificates are flagged early. A person always logs in and attests; the workflow only keeps the dates and the reminders.

CAQH ProView asks each provider to re-attest every 120 days, even when nothing on the profile has changed. In a small practice with several providers, those dates drift apart, and CAQH's own emails land in busy inboxes. When an attestation lapses, payers can't pull current data, and a credentialing or recredentialing file can stall at the worst moment. Keeping the dates on one list, with a reminder that goes to a named person, is a small, repeatable job.

### Where attestations slip
- Each provider's re-attestation date is different, and nobody holds them all in one place
- CAQH reminder emails go to the provider's own inbox, not to the office manager
- A license, DEA registration or malpractice certificate expires and the profile still shows the old one
- A new provider joins and their profile setup is half finished when payer applications go out
- A provider leaves and their profile and payer links are never updated
- Some payers ask for directory details to be confirmed on their own schedule, separate from CAQH

### What the list keeps for each provider
One row per provider. Your credentialing person probably keeps some of this already in a spreadsheet; the workflow makes the dates do the work. It doesn't log in to CAQH or attest for anyone.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Provider, NPI and CAQH ID | So every reminder points to the right profile |
| Last attestation date | The next due date is worked out from it |
| Who attests: the provider or a delegate | So the reminder goes to the person who will do it |
| License, DEA and malpractice expiry dates | So new documents are uploaded before the old ones expire |
| Payers and their own confirmation rules | Some payers check directory details on a different cycle |

### How the workflow runs
1. Your credentialing person adds each provider with their last attestation date and document expiry dates.
2. A few weeks before the next due date, the provider or delegate gets an email or text with a link to log in and attest.
3. When they reply DONE, or the new date is entered, the next due date is set from it.
4. If nothing happens, a second reminder goes out, then the provider goes on a short list for the office manager.
5. Before a license, DEA registration or malpractice certificate expires, the provider is asked for the new document so it can be uploaded.
6. Every Monday the office gets one list: attestations due soon, overdue, and documents about to expire.
7. Anything unusual, like a payer letter or a question about the profile, goes straight to a person. If AI drafts a reply, someone reads and approves it before it is sent.

### What stays with you
Logging in, checking the profile and attesting, which only the provider or an authorized delegate should do. Payer applications, contracts and every credentialing decision stay with your team. The workflow keeps dates, sends reminders and shows who is behind. In England, for residential buildings over 11 metres, the Fire Safety (England) Regulations 2022 guidance asks for communal fire doors to be checked at least every three months, and for best endeavours to check flat entrance doors at least every twelve months. The hard part isn't the check. It's the diary across many buildings, the letters asking residents for access, the record of who didn't answer, and making sure a fault found in March isn't still open in June.

### Where fire door checks slip

- A fault is found, a quote is asked for, and nobody follows it up
- Inspection reports sit in an inbox instead of the building's file
- A new building joins the portfolio and its first check is never booked

### What the list keeps
One row per building, and one per flat entrance door where you need it. Your existing spreadsheet or block management software may already hold the buildings; the workflow adds the dates and the follow-up. It doesn't judge whether a door is safe.

## Driver qualification file tracking: every expiry date on one list
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/driver-qualification-file-expiry-tracking/

A driver qualification file tracking workflow keeps one row per driver with the dates that expire or repeat, such as the medical card, the license and the annual motor vehicle record review. It reminds the driver and the office before each date, asks for the new document, files it, and shows what is missing. Your safety manager makes every qualification decision.

A small fleet rarely fails on the big things. It fails on a medical card that ran out last month, or an annual motor vehicle record review nobody dated. Under 49 CFR Part 391, a motor carrier keeps a qualification file for each driver, gets and reviews the driver's motor vehicle record at least once every 12 months, and keeps a current medical examiner's certificate on record. The rules are known. The dates are the problem: they are different for every driver, and they usually live in a folder nobody opens until an audit.

### Where driver files slip
- Each driver's medical card ends on a different date, and some are issued for less than two years
- The annual motor vehicle record is pulled, but the review note with a name and date is missing
- A license is renewed and nobody asks the driver for the new copy
- A new driver starts before the whole file is in
- The dates are in a spreadsheet that one person updates when they have time
- A driver leaves and nobody knows how long the file has to be kept

### What the list keeps
One row per driver. Your spreadsheet may already have most of it; the workflow adds the reminders and the follow-up. It does not decide whether a driver is qualified.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |

| Medical card expiry date | The reminder starts well before it, with time to book an exam |
| License expiry date | So a renewed copy is asked for and filed |
| Last motor vehicle record and review date | So the next one is pulled and reviewed inside 12 months |
| Missing items for new hires | So a file is complete before it is needed |
| Status: current, due soon, overdue | One weekly list for the safety manager |

### How the workflow runs
1. Each driver goes on the list with the dates from the documents already in the file.
2. Some weeks before a medical card or license expires, the driver gets a text or email asking them to renew and send the new copy.
3. If nothing arrives, the driver is reminded again and the office is told, with time left to act.
4. When the new document comes in, it is filed in the driver's folder and a person checks it and updates the date.
5. Before the 12-month mark, the office is reminded to pull the motor vehicle record and to record who reviewed it and when.
6. Every week the safety manager gets one list: due soon, overdue and missing.
7. Anything unclear goes to a person. If AI reads a document or drafts a message, someone checks and approves it before it is used or sent.

### What stays with you
Pulling the motor vehicle record, reviewing it, deciding whether a driver can drive, drug and alcohol testing, and everything you say to an auditor. The workflow keeps the dates and asks for documents. It is not compliance advice: the full list of what belongs in a file is in 49 CFR Part 391, and your own safety consultant or insurer may ask for more. Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/lev-testing-reminders/

Local exhaust ventilation (LEV) takes dust, fume and vapour away from the people working next to it. HSE says an LEV system should have a thorough examination and test at least once every 14 months, and more often for some processes, and that the record is kept for at least 5 years. Fourteen months is an awkward interval: it doesn't fall on the same month each year, so a note in the diary drifts. A testing company with a few hundred systems across its customers, or a workshop with several booths and arms, needs a list that counts for it.

### Where LEV tests slip
- The due date is on last year's report, in a folder nobody opens

- The customer's contact has left and the reminder goes to an old email address
- A system that needs a shorter interval is treated like the rest
- The report lists repairs, and nobody asks whether they were done
- A new booth or arm is installed and never added to the list

7. If AI reads a report or drafts a message, a person checks it before it is sent.

## Law firm conflict check workflow: no file opens before the check is cleared
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/law-firm-conflict-check-workflow/

A conflict check workflow collects every name on a new matter at intake, sends them to the person who searches your records and to each lawyer, records who cleared the check and when, and holds the file until that is done. It asks for the check again when a new party joins the matter. A lawyer always decides whether a conflict exists and what to do about it.

Every firm knows a conflict check comes before a new matter. In a small firm it often depends on memory: someone searches the practice software for the client's name, nobody asks the partner who handled a related matter years ago, and the result is never written down. The search itself takes minutes. What goes wrong is around it: names collected halfway, a consultation booked before anyone looked, and no record that the check happened.

### Where conflict checks go wrong
- Intake asks for the client's name and not the other side, related companies or family members
- The consultation is booked, and advice given, before anyone checks
- One person searches the software, and lawyers who would recognize a name never see it
- A name is spelled differently from the old record, so the search finds nothing
- The check is done and nobody records who cleared it or when
- A new party joins the matter months later and the check is not run again

### What is collected for every new matter
The intake form asks for the same things every time, so the search doesn't depend on who took the call.
| Asked at intake | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Client's full name and any former names | Old records may be under another name |
| Business names, owners and related companies | A conflict can sit with a company, not a person |
| Opposing and other parties | The other side may be a current or former client |
| Opposing counsel, if known | Some firms check this too |
| Type of matter and a one-line description | So a lawyer can spot a related matter |
| Who referred the client | A referral can point to a connection |

### How the workflow runs
1. A new enquiry gets a short intake form, or staff fill it in on the phone. The form won't submit without the other parties' names.
2. The names go to the person who runs the search in your practice software or your own records, with a task and a time limit.
3. The same names go to every lawyer in a short email: do you know any of these people or companies? Each lawyer replies clear or flags a name.

## TM44 inspection reminders: every building booked before its five-year date
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/tm44-air-conditioning-inspection-reminders/

GOV.UK's guide to air conditioning inspections says that systems with an effective rated output of more than 12kW must be inspected by an energy assessor, and that the inspections must be no more than five years apart. The guide covers England and Wales. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own rules. Five years is long enough for everything around the date to change: the person who booked the last inspection has moved on, the building has a new managing agent, and the report is in an inbox nobody can open. An assessor or contractor with a few hundred buildings can't hold those dates in their head.

### Where TM44 inspections slip
- The due date is on a report from five years ago, and the contact on it has left
- The building changed owner or managing agent and nobody passed the report on
- New units were added, so a building that was under 12kW is now over it and isn't on any list
- The assessor arrives and there is no asset list, no maintenance records and no roof access
- The report recommends changes, and nobody looks at them again
- A customer with twenty sites has twenty different dates

### What the list keeps
One row per building. If you already keep a spreadsheet or use job software, the workflow reads from it and adds the reminders and the follow-up.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |

| Total rated output and number of units | So a building that grows past 12kW gets a date |
| Last inspection date and report reference | So the next date is counted, not remembered |
| Next inspection due | So the visit is offered months before the date, not after |
| Site contact and a second contact | So the message still lands after five years of staff changes |
| Pre-visit information received | Asset list, maintenance records, access |
| Report sent and recommendations | So each recommendation gets a reply |

### How the workflow runs

3. A reply books the visit and puts it in the diary. No reply gets a second message, then a message to the second contact, then a place on a short call list.
4. Once the visit is booked, the site gets one form asking for what the assessor needs: the asset list, maintenance records, and who gives access to plant rooms and the roof.
5. The day before, the site contact gets a reminder with the time and what is still missing.
6. After the visit, the report is sent to the customer and filed against the building, and the next date is set.
7. Each recommendation in the report becomes a line. The customer is asked about it once, a few weeks later, and you can offer a quote.
8. Once a year, each customer is asked whether units were added or removed, so the list stays right.
9. If AI reads a report or drafts a message, a person checks it before it is sent.

## Workers' comp premium audit: the documents collected before the auditor asks
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/workers-comp-premium-audit-document-collection/

A premium audit workflow keeps one checklist per policy with the records the insurer's auditor usually asks for: payroll reports, quarterly payroll tax reports, payments to subcontractors and each subcontractor's certificate of insurance. It asks for each item ahead of the audit, reminds about what is missing and shows what is still open. A person reviews everything before it goes to the auditor.

A workers' compensation premium is first set on estimated payroll. After the policy period, the insurer audits the real numbers and the premium is adjusted. Insurers' own guides say the auditor will typically ask for payroll records, quarterly payroll tax reports, payments to subcontractors and the subcontractors' certificates of insurance. They also say that where a certificate is missing, the payments to that subcontractor may be treated as payroll and charged for. So the expensive problem is usually a missing piece of paper, and it is found in the week of the audit, when the subcontractor from last spring no longer answers the phone.

### Where the audit goes wrong
- The audit letter arrives and nobody starts until the week it is due
- A subcontractor worked for two months and no certificate was ever collected
- A certificate is on file, but it expired halfway through the job
- Payroll is in one total, so office staff and field staff can't be shown separately
- The bookkeeper has the payroll reports, the office has the certificates, and the owner has the letter
- The agency hears about the audit after the bill, when the client is upset

### What the checklist keeps
One checklist per policy and one row per subcontractor. The list below is what insurers typically ask for. Your insurer's audit letter is the real list, and the workflow follows it.
| Item | Who has it |
| --- | --- |
| Payroll reports for the policy period, by employee | Bookkeeper or payroll provider |
| Quarterly payroll tax reports | Bookkeeper or payroll provider |
| Overtime shown separately, where your records allow | Payroll provider |
| Payments to each subcontractor | Bookkeeper |
| Each subcontractor's certificate, with dates that cover the work | The subcontractor or their agent |
| Description of what each employee does | Owner or office manager |

### How the workflow runs
1. Each policy goes on the list with its period end date and the people who hold each record.
2. During the year, every new subcontractor is added when the first payment is made, and is asked for a certificate the same day.
3. A certificate's expiry date goes on the list. Before it runs out, the subcontractor is asked for the new one.
4. A few weeks before the policy period ends, each person gets one message with only the items they hold and a link to upload them.
5. Missing items get a reminder a week later. After that they show on a short list for a phone call.
6. Subcontractors with payments and no certificate for the dates worked are shown at the top, so they are chased first.
7. When the audit letter arrives, the checklist is compared with it and anything extra is requested.
8. A person reviews the pack and sends it to the auditor. Nothing goes to the insurer automatically.
9. If AI reads a certificate or drafts a message, a person checks it before it is sent.

### For insurance agencies
An agency can run the same checklist for every commercial client with a workers' comp policy: one row per policy, sorted by period end date. Clients are reminded before the period ends, and the account manager sees who has sent nothing. The agency doesn't need to hold payroll data to do this. The workflow can track that each item was sent to the auditor without the agency storing it. For certificates your own clients ask you for, see [certificate of insurance requests](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/certificate-of-insurance-requests-insurance-agencies/).

### What stays with you
How employees are classified, what counts as payroll, any dispute about the audit result, and every conversation with the insurer. Rules differ by state and by insurer, and this page is not insurance or legal advice. The workflow only collects, reminds and shows what is missing. Contractors who want the certificates tracked all year, not only at audit time, can use [subcontractor COI tracking](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/subcontractor-coi-tracking/).

If your agency system or accounting software already collects these records and chases certificates, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### What documents does a workers' comp premium audit need?
Insurers typically ask for payroll records for the policy period, quarterly payroll tax reports, payments to subcontractors and each subcontractor's certificate of insurance. Your insurer's audit letter gives the exact list.

Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/retirement-plan-census-data-collection-tpa/

Your staff review the data, run the testing and prepare the Form 5500.

A third-party administrator can't start a plan's year-end work without the sponsor's census: who was employed, dates of birth and hire, hours, pay and contributions. The same request goes to every sponsor in January, and the replies arrive over months, in different formats, with columns missing. Meanwhile the filing date doesn't move. The IRS says the Form 5500 is generally due on the last day of the seventh month after the plan year ends, which is July 31 for a calendar-year plan, unless an extension is requested first. Most of the delay is not the testing. It's waiting for the file and asking the same questions again.

### Where census collection slips
- The request goes to a contact who left the company last summer

- Terminated employees are left off the file, with their termination dates
- The questionnaire comes back with the ownership and related-company questions blank
- Follow-up questions go out by email and the answers are spread across three threads
- Nobody can say how many plans are still waiting, so the partner asks every week

| Status | Requested, partly received, complete, in review |

4. If something is missing, the sponsor gets a short list of exactly what to fix. A person on your team sees the message before it goes.
5. Follow-up questions from your administrator go out from the same place, and the answers are saved against the plan.
6. Each Monday the team gets one list: plans complete, plans partly received, plans with nothing, sorted by plan year end.
7. When a plan is complete, the administrator is told it's ready for review.
8. If AI reads a file or drafts a message, a person checks it before it is sent.

### Keeping the data safe
A census holds dates of birth, pay and sometimes Social Security numbers. It should not travel as an email attachment. The workflow sends sponsors a link to your secure upload folder or portal and never puts census data in the body of a message. Reminders say only that a file is missing. Who can open the folder stays under your control, and your own security policy decides where the data is stored.

### What stays with you
Reviewing the census, the compliance testing, the contribution calculations, the Form 5500 and every piece of advice to the sponsor. ## Forklift operator evaluation reminders: every operator evaluated before the three-year date
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/forklift-operator-evaluation-reminders/

A forklift evaluation reminder workflow keeps one row per operator with the date of their last evaluation and the truck types they are cleared for. It tells the supervisor and the trainer a few weeks before the next evaluation is due, books it, and files the signed record. A qualified trainer does the evaluation and decides whether the operator passes.

OSHA's powered industrial truck standard, 29 CFR 1910.178(l), says an evaluation of each operator's performance must be done at least once every three years. Refresher training is a separate thing: it's needed after events such as unsafe operation, an accident or near miss, a move to a different type of truck, or a change in the workplace. Each operator has their own date, counted from their own last evaluation. With thirty operators hired in different months, on three shifts and two sites, the dates are spread across the whole calendar, and the list is often a spreadsheet one person updates when they remember.

### Where operator evaluations slip
- The dates live in a spreadsheet that only the safety manager opens
- An operator moves to another site or shift and their row doesn't move with them
- A temp arrives from a staffing firm with a wallet card, and nobody records who evaluated them on your trucks
- An operator starts using a reach truck and the record only covers a sit-down counterbalance truck
- A near miss happens and the refresher training is agreed in a meeting, then forgotten
- The evaluation was done, but the signed form is in a binder at the other building

### What the list keeps
One row per operator. If you already keep a training matrix in a spreadsheet or in HR software, the workflow reads from it and adds the reminders and the filing.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |

| Truck types they are cleared for | So a move to a different truck shows as a gap |
| Initial training date and trainer | The start of the record |
| Last evaluation date and evaluator | So the next date is counted, not remembered |
| Next evaluation due | So it is booked weeks before, not found afterwards |
| Open refresher training and the reason | So training agreed after an incident is done and recorded |
| Signed record on file | So the paper can be found on the day someone asks for it |

### How the workflow runs
1. Every operator goes on the list with their last evaluation date. Operators with no record on file are marked "no date" and go to the top.
2. A few weeks before an evaluation is due, the supervisor and the trainer get an email with the operator's name, the due date and the truck types.
3. The trainer picks a time and the operator and supervisor get a calendar invite. Operators due in the same month are grouped so the trainer comes once.
4. A week before the due date, anything still not booked goes on a short list for the safety manager.
5. After the evaluation, the trainer fills in one short form on a phone: operator, date, truck type, result and their name. The signed record is saved against the operator.
6. The next date is set for three years on, or sooner if your own policy is shorter.
7. When a supervisor reports unsafe operation, an accident or a near miss on a form, a refresher training line opens for that operator and stays open until the trainer closes it.
8. When an operator is assigned a new truck type, the list shows them as not yet cleared for it.
9. If AI reads a form or drafts a message, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with you
The training, the evaluation, the decision on whether someone may operate a truck, and what to do after an incident. The workflow reminds, books and files. ## PSSR examination reminders: every pressure system examined before its date
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pssr-written-scheme-examination-reminders/

A PSSR reminder workflow keeps one row per pressure system with the interval from its written scheme of examination and the date of the last examination. It contacts the customer a few weeks before the next one is due, books the visit, checks the system can be made ready, and files the report. A competent person does the examination and writes the report.

HSE's guidance on the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000 says a written scheme of examination must be in place before a pressure system is used, and that a competent person must examine the system within the intervals the scheme sets. There is no single interval for every system: the scheme for a small air receiver in a garage and the scheme for a steam boiler in a laundry give different dates, and one scheme can give different intervals for different parts. A compressor service company with a few hundred customers has hundreds of dates, each read from a different document.

### Where PSSR examinations slip
- The due date is on the last report, and the report is in a file in the customer's workshop
- The customer thinks the annual service and the examination are the same visit
- A receiver was replaced or a second compressor added, and the written scheme was never updated
- The examiner arrives and the system is running, so nothing can be opened up
- One site has an air receiver, an autoclave and a steam boiler, each with its own interval
- The report lists repairs to do before a date, and nobody follows them up

### What the list keeps

| Last examination date and report reference | So the next date is counted from a record |
| Next examination due | So the visit is offered weeks before the date |
| Repairs or changes the report asked for, with dates | So each one gets an answer |

### How the workflow runs

4. When the visit is booked, the customer gets one message about what the examiner needs: when the system can be shut down and isolated, and who gives access.
5. The day before, the site contact gets a reminder with the time.
6. After the visit, the report is sent to the customer, filed against the system, and the next date is set from the scheme.
7. Each repair or change the report asks for becomes a line with its date. The customer is asked about it before that date, and you can offer a quote.
8. When a job sheet shows a part was replaced or added, the row is flagged "scheme may need review" for the competent person.
9. If AI reads a report or drafts a message, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with you
The written scheme, the examination, the report, and the decision on whether a system needs a scheme at all. The workflow reminds, books and files. ### How often does a pressure system need a PSSR examination?
There is no single interval. HSE's guidance says a competent person examines the system within the intervals set in its written scheme of examination. The workflow uses the interval from each system's own scheme.
