Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/bankruptcy-client-document-collection/

A bankruptcy document collection workflow sends each client one checklist of what their case needs, records what has arrived, and reminds them about what is still missing. It shows the attorney which documents have a date attached, such as pay stubs and the credit counseling certificate. It doesn't review the documents or decide when to file: the attorney does.

A consumer bankruptcy case runs on the client's paperwork. Bankruptcy court websites list the same core items: a certificate showing the client took credit counseling from an approved agency within 180 days before filing, pay stubs received in the 60 days before filing, and the most recent federal tax return or a transcript, which goes to the trustee no later than 7 days before the meeting of creditors. Local rules and each trustee add their own lists. The client is under stress, often has no scanner, and sends photos in pieces over several weeks. Meanwhile some of what they sent goes out of date.

### Where bankruptcy document collection gets stuck
- The client gets a three-page list at the first meeting and sends a third of it
- Documents arrive as phone photos by text, email and in person, and nobody has one view of what's missing
- Filing slips by a few weeks, so the pay stubs on file no longer cover the 60 days before filing
- The credit counseling certificate was done early and is close to 180 days old
- A spouse's income documents are needed and nobody asked the spouse
- The trustee's own document request arrives after filing and sits in one paralegal's inbox
- The debtor education course after filing is forgotten until the court sends a notice

### What the checklist keeps
One checklist per client, built from the list your firm already uses for that chapter and district. The workflow doesn't decide what is needed. It asks for what your list says and keeps the dates in view.
| Item | What the workflow watches |
| --- | --- |
| Credit counseling certificate | The date on it, so the attorney sees when it is close to 180 days old |
| Pay stubs or other proof of income | Whether they still cover the 60 days before the planned filing date |
| Most recent federal tax return or transcript | Received, and sent to the trustee at least 7 days before the meeting of creditors |
| Bank statements | Which accounts and months are still missing |
| ID and proof of Social Security number | Received before the meeting of creditors |
| Anything your trustee or local rules add | Listed per district, with the trustee's own due date |
| Debtor education certificate | Asked for after filing, until it's on file |

### How the workflow runs
1. When a client signs your fee agreement, they get one message with their checklist and a link to upload from a phone. Each item has a plain description and an example.
2. Each upload is saved to the client's folder and ticked off. Photos of several pages are kept together under the item.
3. Every few days the client gets a short message listing only what is still missing. After the third message with no reply, the client goes on a call list for a paralegal.
4. The attorney or paralegal sets a planned filing date. The list then shows which pay stubs and statements will be too old by that date and asks the client for the newer ones.
5. The date on the credit counseling certificate is recorded. If the planned filing date gets close to 180 days after it, the attorney sees a warning.
6. After filing, the meeting of creditors date goes on the list. The tax return and the trustee's requested documents show as due before it, and a paralegal sends them after the attorney's review.
7. The client gets a reminder about the debtor education course until the certificate is on file.
8. Each Monday the firm gets one list of every open case and what it is waiting for.
9. If AI reads a document or drafts a message, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with the attorney
Legal advice, reviewing every document, the petition and schedules, deciding when to file, and everything sent to the court or the trustee. The workflow asks, reminds and files, and a person sends anything that leaves the firm. Deadlines differ by district and by trustee, so the dates in the workflow are the ones your firm enters. Client documents stay in the storage you already use, with access limited to your staff. For the first contact with a new client, see [law firm client intake](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/law-firm-client-intake/). Firms that also do immigration work can use the same approach for [immigration document checklists](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/immigration-law-firm-document-checklists/).

Bankruptcy court websites list a credit counseling certificate, pay stubs from the 60 days before filing, the most recent federal tax return or a transcript, and ID. Trustees and local rules add more, such as bank statements. The workflow uses your firm's own list.

## RMD reminders for financial advisors: every client's distribution confirmed before the deadline
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/rmd-reminders-financial-advisors/

An RMD reminder workflow keeps one row per client account that has a required minimum distribution this year. It shows which ones are already set up, reminds the client and the advisor about the ones that aren't, and gives the team a short list of what is still open as December 31 gets close. The advisor and the custodian work out the amount; the workflow keeps the list and sends the reminders.

The IRS says the first required minimum distribution from a traditional IRA is due by April 1 of the year after the year the owner turns 73, and each later one is due by December 31. A client who waits until April 1 for the first one has two distributions in the same year. A missed amount can face a 25% excise tax, reduced to 10% if it is corrected within two years. Most firms know all this. What goes wrong is the list: clients who turn 73 this year, accounts held at another custodian, a spouse's account nobody mentioned, and a December when the whole team is busy.

### Where RMDs get missed
- The list is last year's spreadsheet, and the clients who turn 73 this year are not on it
- A client has an old IRA at another custodian that your reports don't show
- A client chose to delay their first distribution to April 1, and nobody set the second one for December
- The client says "I'll call you about it" in September and doesn't
- A distribution was requested but the paperwork came back unsigned
- An inherited account follows different rules and sits on the same list with no note
- Nobody checks in January that every distribution on the list was paid

### What the list keeps
One row per account. If your CRM or portfolio software already holds dates of birth and account types, the workflow reads the list from an export and adds the reminders.
| Field | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Client, advisor and account | So the reminder goes to the person who knows the client |
| Account type and custodian | So accounts held elsewhere are on the list too |
| Date of birth and first-RMD year | So clients reaching the age this year are added in January, not found in December |
| Deadline for this year (April 1 or December 31) | So a delayed first distribution is not treated like the others |
| Amount, as worked out by the advisor or custodian | So the client sees the figure your team has checked |
| Status: not started, client asked, form sent, scheduled, paid | So the open ones are easy to see |
| Notes: withholding choice, charity gift, inherited account | So the special cases are not handled from memory |

### How the workflow runs
1. In January, the list is built from your client export: every account with a distribution due this year, including clients who reach the age during the year.
2. The advisor checks the list and fills in or confirms each amount. The workflow does not calculate RMDs.
3. Accounts with an automatic distribution already set up at the custodian are marked "scheduled" and only get a check that the payment arrived.
4. In early fall, each remaining client gets a short email from their advisor's address: the account, the deadline and how to tell you what they want to do. The advisor approves the wording once, and approves any message that is not the standard one.
5. Clients who don't reply get a reminder two weeks later, then a task for the advisor to call them.
6. Clients with a first distribution due by April 1 get their own reminder early in the year, and a second row for December 31.
7. From mid-November, the team gets one list each Monday of everything not yet scheduled or paid.
8. In January, the list is checked against the custodian's records and anything unpaid goes straight to the advisor.
9. If AI drafts a message or reads a form, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with you
The amount, the advice, the timing, the withholding choice and every conversation with the client. The workflow reminds and keeps the list. It is not tax or investment advice. Rules differ for employer plans, where some people can wait until they retire, and for inherited accounts, and the starting age is set to rise to 75 for people born in 1960 or later, so check the current IRS guidance for each client. Your firm's compliance rules on client emails apply to these messages as they do to any others. If you also chase clients for tax payments, see [quarterly estimated tax payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/quarterly-estimated-tax-payment-reminders/). For review meetings and their paperwork, see [client review paperwork for financial advisers](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/financial-adviser-client-review-paperwork/).

If your CRM already builds this list and reminds clients, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### When is a required minimum distribution due?
The IRS says the first one from a traditional IRA is due by April 1 of the year after the year the owner turns 73, and each later one by December 31. Employer plans and inherited accounts can follow different rules, so check each account.

## Construction closeout documents: collecting them from every subcontractor
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/construction-closeout-document-collection-subcontractors/

A closeout document workflow gives each subcontractor a list of what their subcontract asks for: usually O&M manuals, warranties, as-built drawings, test reports and a final lien waiver. It starts asking before the job ends, reminds each sub about what is still missing, files what arrives in the job folder, and shows the project manager one list of who still owes what.

The building is finished and the owner wants the closeout package before releasing final payment. A typical package has the punch list sign-off, the certificate of substantial completion, final inspection reports, as-built drawings, operation and maintenance manuals, warranties, lien waivers and commissioning records. A large part of it has to come from the subs, and by then the subs have moved to their next job. So a project manager spends weeks emailing fifteen companies for PDFs, and the final payment waits for the last one.

### Where closeout stalls
- Nobody asks for closeout documents until the last week, when the sub's crew has already left
- Each sub gets the same general email, with no list of what their own contract asks for
- A warranty letter arrives with no start date, or names the wrong project
- An O&M manual comes as forty separate attachments across six emails
- The as-builts are a marked-up set in a truck, and nobody has scanned them
- The project manager moves to the next job and the list lives in their inbox
- The owner's team finds the gaps, and the package goes back and forth

### What each sub is asked for
The contract documents decide the real list. This is a typical one, and the workflow uses the list you set per trade.
| Document | What gets checked when it arrives |
| --- | --- |
| O&M manuals | They cover the equipment that was installed, in one file per system |
| Warranties | Project name, start date, length and a signature |
| As-built drawings | Every sheet for that trade is there and marked up |
| Test, balancing and commissioning reports | Signed and dated, for the right equipment |
| Attic stock and spare parts receipt | Signed by the person who received them |
| Owner training sign-in sheet | Date, system and who attended |
| Final lien waiver | The right form, the right amount and a signature |

### How the workflow runs
1. When the subcontract is signed, the sub's closeout list is set from a template for their trade and adjusted for the job.
2. A few weeks before substantial completion, each sub gets an email with their own list and one upload link per item. The date is the one you choose.
3. Each file that arrives is named, saved in the job's closeout folder and ticked off the list.
4. Simple gaps are caught on arrival: a warranty with no start date, or a waiver that isn't signed. The sub gets a note saying what to fix. The project manager decides whether a document is acceptable.
5. Subs with open items get a reminder each week that lists only what is still missing.
6. After two reminders with no reply, the project manager gets a task to call, with the sub's contact and the open items.
7. The project manager sees one list per job: every sub, every item, received or missing.
8. When a sub's list is complete, the project manager is told, so the final payment step isn't held up by a document that already came in.
9. When every list is complete, the folder is ready for the package to the owner or architect.
10. If AI reads a document or drafts a message, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with you
Whether a document is good enough, what the contract requires, when to release final payment and every hard conversation with a sub. The workflow asks, reminds and files. It is not legal advice: payment terms, retainage and lien waiver forms depend on your contracts and your state. For waivers on every draw, see [lien waiver tracking](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/lien-waiver-tracking-subcontractors/). For documents during the job, see [RFI and submittal tracking](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/construction-rfi-and-submittal-tracking/). ### What are closeout documents in construction?

## Tachograph calibration reminders: every vehicle booked in before the two-year date
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/tachograph-calibration-reminders/

A tachograph calibration reminder workflow keeps one row per vehicle with the date on its last calibration certificate. A few weeks before the two-year date, it tells the operator, offers booking slots and records the new date once the work is done. An approved tachograph centre does the calibration and issues the certificate.

GOV.UK guidance for goods vehicle operators says digital and smart tachographs must be recalibrated every 2 years, and analogue tachographs inspected every 2 years and recalibrated every 6 years. The date is on the plaque in the cab and on the certificate, and each vehicle has its own. An operator with twelve lorries bought in different months has twelve dates, and they don't line up with the MOT or the safety inspections. A tachograph centre has the dates for hundreds of customers' vehicles in old job sheets, and most customers only ring when a driver notices the plaque.

### Where calibration dates slip
- The date is on a plaque in the cab and nobody in the office has it written down
- The operator tracks the MOT and safety inspections, and assumes the calibration comes with them
- A vehicle is bought second-hand and the last certificate isn't with the paperwork
- The tyres are changed for a different size, or the unit is repaired, and nobody books the recalibration that follows
- A vehicle gets a new registration number and the tachograph still holds the old one
- The centre did the last calibration but has no list of what is due next month

### When a recalibration is due
These are the points in the GOV.UK operator guidance. The workflow tracks the dates and asks about the events; your approved centre decides what the vehicle needs.
| Tachograph or event | What the guidance says |
| --- | --- |
| Digital or smart tachograph | Recalibrated every 2 years |
| Analogue tachograph | Inspected every 2 years and recalibrated every 6 years |
| After any repair to the tachograph | Recalibrated |
| The vehicle's registration number changes | Recalibrated |
| The clock (UTC) is out by more than 20 minutes | Recalibrated |
| Tyre circumference or the characteristic coefficient changes | Recalibrated |

### How the workflow runs for a tachograph centre
1. Every vehicle you have calibrated goes on one list: operator, registration, tachograph type, certificate date and next due date. Past jobs are loaded from your job sheets or your software's export.
2. Six weeks before a due date, the operator gets an email or a text with the registration, the date and two or three booking slots.
3. The operator picks a slot and it goes in the workshop diary. Vehicles from the same operator due in the same month are offered together.
4. No reply after a week brings one reminder. After that, the vehicle goes on a short call list for your front desk.
5. The day before the visit, the operator gets a reminder with what to bring, such as the vehicle's previous certificate.
6. After the calibration, your technician marks the job done and the next due date is set on the list.
7. If the operator says the vehicle was sold, the row is closed so they stop getting reminders about it.
8. If AI drafts a message, a person checks it before it is sent.

### If you run the fleet
The same list works from the operator's side. Each vehicle has a row with its calibration date next to its MOT and safety inspection dates, and the transport manager gets a reminder six weeks before, with the centre's phone number. When a tyre size change or a tachograph repair is recorded on a short form, the row is flagged so someone asks the centre whether a recalibration is needed. For the other dates, see [HGV safety inspection and MOT reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/hgv-safety-inspection-and-mot-reminders/).

### What stays with you
The calibration, the certificate, the plaque and every decision about whether a vehicle is fit to use. Only a vehicle manufacturer or an approved tachograph centre can do the work. The workflow reminds and books. It is not legal advice, and it follows the GOV.UK guidance for Great Britain, so check the current guidance for your own vehicles. Garages that also remind car customers can see [MOT reminders for garages](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/garage-mot-reminders/).

## I-9 reverification reminders: every expiry date seen weeks before it arrives
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/i-9-reverification-reminders/

An I-9 reverification reminder workflow keeps one row per employee whose work authorization has an end date. Weeks before that date, it reminds the employee to bring a current document and gives HR a task to complete Supplement B. A person in HR examines the document and signs the form.

USCIS guidance says that when an employee's temporary employment authorization expires, the employer must reverify it no later than the expiry date, and record it on Supplement B of Form I-9. The date was written on the form on the day the person was hired, and the form went into a folder. In a small business nobody opens that folder again. A staffing agency has the same problem across hundreds of workers placed with different clients. The date arrives on an ordinary Tuesday, and the first person to notice is often the employee.

### Where reverification dates get missed
- The expiry date is on a paper I-9 in a folder and on no list or calendar
- The person who did the hiring paperwork has left, and nobody took over the dates
- The employee has renewed their document and nobody asked to see the new one
- Someone asks a U.S. citizen or a green card holder for new documents by mistake, because every row on the list looked the same
- An employee has a renewal pending and nobody checks whether an automatic extension applies
- A staffing agency tracks the dates per client and misses a worker who moved between clients

### Who goes on the list, and who doesn't
These are points from the USCIS Handbook for Employers (M-274). The workflow only tracks rows that HR has marked as needing reverification. If a case is unclear, ask your employment attorney before anyone contacts the employee.
| Situation | What the USCIS guidance says |
| --- | --- |
| Temporary employment authorization with an end date | Reverify no later than the date it expires, on Supplement B |
| U.S. citizens and noncitizen nationals | Do not reverify |
| Lawful permanent resident who showed a Permanent Resident Card (Form I-551) | Do not reverify |
| Temporary I-551 stamp or notation | Reverify no later than when it expires |
| List B identity documents, such as a driver's license | Not reverified when they expire |
| A renewal was filed on time | An automatic extension may apply. Check the current USCIS rules |

### How the workflow runs
1. Every employee whose I-9 has a work authorization end date goes on one list: name, the date, the document type and who in HR owns the row. HR marks the rows once from the existing forms.
2. New hires with an end date are added from your [new hire checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/new-hire-paperwork-collection-small-business/), so the list stays complete.
3. Ninety days before the date, the employee gets a short, neutral email: their work authorization on file ends on this date, and they will need to show a current document before then. They choose which acceptable document to show.
4. The message never asks for a specific document. You approve the wording once, with your attorney if you have one.
5. Sixty and thirty days before, the employee gets a reminder, and HR gets a task with the date.
6. If the employee says a renewal is pending, the row is flagged for HR to check whether an extension applies. The workflow doesn't decide that.
7. HR examines the document, completes Supplement B and enters the new end date, or marks the row as having no further date.
8. Two weeks before the date, any row still open goes to the owner or HR lead as a short list.
9. If AI drafts a message, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with you
Examining the document, completing and signing Supplement B, deciding who needs reverification and every decision about someone's employment. The workflow holds dates and sends reminders. It doesn't store copies of documents unless you already keep them, and it doesn't replace E-Verify or your payroll system. It is not legal advice. The rules change, so check the current USCIS guidance or ask an employment attorney. Staffing agencies that also chase other worker documents can see [candidate compliance document chasing](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/candidate-compliance-document-chasing/).

A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how many employees have an end date and where those dates live today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on what you already use (a spreadsheet, email and your calendar). Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is a fixed $2,000](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it, under the [pay-when-happy agreement](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agreement/). If your HR or payroll software already sends these alerts and someone acts on them, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### When does an I-9 need reverification?
USCIS guidance says that when an employee's temporary employment authorization expires, the employer reverifies it no later than the expiry date and records it on Supplement B of Form I-9. Some employees with a renewal filed on time may have an automatic extension.

### Do we reverify U.S. citizens or green card holders?
USCIS says employers should not reverify U.S. citizens, noncitizen nationals, or lawful permanent residents who presented a Permanent Resident Card. That is why HR marks the rows first, and only marked rows get reminders.

### Does the workflow complete Supplement B?
No. A person in HR examines the document and completes and signs the form. The workflow keeps the dates, reminds the employee and HR, and records the new date afterwards.

## Dry riser testing reminders: the six-monthly check and the annual test, booked before they're due
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/dry-riser-testing-reminders/

A dry riser testing reminder workflow keeps one row per riser with the dates of its last visual check and last pressure test. Weeks before either is due, it tells the building's contact, offers visit dates and records the result afterwards. A competent engineer does the test and writes the certificate.

Fire protection firms describe the same routine under BS 9990: a visual inspection of each dry riser every six months and a full pressure test once a year. So every building has two dates a year, and a tall block can have several risers. For the firm, the dates sit in last year's job sheets. For the managing agent, they sit in a certificate in a shared folder. The six-monthly check is the one that slips, because it is a short visit that nobody put in the diary.

### Where riser dates slip
- The annual test is in the diary but the six-monthly visual check isn't
- A building changes managing agent and the new one doesn't know when the last test was
- The engineer needs the inlet cabinet key and roof access, and the visit is wasted when nobody is there
- A check finds a missing cap or a damaged valve, the repair is quoted, and the retest is never booked
- One block has three risers tested on different dates after past repairs
- The firm did last year's test and has no list of what is due next month

### What the list holds for each riser
One row per riser, not per building. The firm's engineer decides what each visit covers and whether the riser passes.
| On the row | Why it's there |
| --- | --- |
| Building, riser location and inlet location | The engineer finds it without a phone call |
| Date of the last visual check | Sets the next six-monthly date |
| Date of the last pressure test and certificate | Sets the next annual date |
| Site contact, key holder and access notes | The visit isn't wasted |
| Open defects and quotes | A repair and its retest don't get lost |
| Who gets the certificate | Managing agent, landlord or the responsible person |

### How the workflow runs for a fire protection firm
1. Every riser you look after goes on one list with its two dates. Past jobs are loaded from your job sheets or your software's export.
2. Six weeks before a check or a test is due, the building's contact gets an email with the address, what is due and two or three visit dates.
3. The contact picks a date and confirms access: who holds the keys and who meets the engineer. The visit goes in the engineers' diary.
4. Risers in the same building, or buildings on the same street, are offered on the same day.
5. No reply after a week brings one reminder. After that, the building goes on a short call list for your office.
6. The day before, the contact gets a reminder with the time and the access you need.
7. After the visit, your engineer records the result. A pass sets the next date. A defect opens a line for the quote and the retest, so it stays visible until it's closed.
8. The certificate or report is emailed to the person named on the row and filed against the building.
9. If AI drafts a message, a person checks it before it is sent.

### If you manage the building
The same list works from the managing agent's side. Each riser has a row next to the building's other fire safety dates, and the property manager gets a reminder six weeks before, with the contractor's details. When the contractor's report arrives, it is filed and any defect becomes a task with an owner. ## Trademark renewal reminders: every filing window opened with the client's answer in hand
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/trademark-renewal-reminders-law-firms/

A trademark renewal reminder workflow keeps one row per registration with its registration date and the filing windows that follow from it. When a window opens, it asks the client whether the mark is still in use and for a specimen, reminds them, and gives the attorney a dated task. The attorney decides what to file and files it.

The USPTO says a registration owner must file a Section 8 declaration between the fifth and sixth years after registration, and a combined Sections 8 and 9 filing between the ninth and tenth years and every ten years after that. So the first deadline comes five years after the work was finished, when the client has changed their email address, their logo and sometimes their company name. A small firm without docketing software keeps these dates in a spreadsheet or a calendar. The filing itself is quick. Getting an answer and a specimen from the client is what takes the year.

### Where maintenance deadlines get missed
- The registration was six years ago and the date lives in a calendar that one person owned
- The client's contact has left and the reminder email bounces
- The client replies "yes, renew it" and never sends a specimen showing the mark in use
- The mark is used on some of the registered goods and not others, and nobody asks until the last week
- The firm assumes the client is watching the date, and the client assumes the firm is
- A registration came from another firm and its dates were never added to the list

### The windows the list tracks
These are the points on the USPTO's post-registration timeline for registrations other than Madrid Protocol ones, which follow a different timeline. The dates on each row are calculated from the registration date, and your attorney confirms them.
| Filing | When the USPTO says it is due |
| --- | --- |
| Section 8 declaration of use | Between the fifth and sixth years after registration |
| Combined Sections 8 and 9 (declaration and renewal) | Between the ninth and tenth years after registration |
| Later renewals | Every ten years after that, in the year before each ten-year date |
| Grace period | Six months after each deadline, for an additional fee |
| Nothing filed by the end of the grace period | The registration is canceled |

### How the workflow runs
1. Every registration the firm looks after goes on one list: client, mark, registration number, registration date, classes and the client's contact. The next window's opening and closing dates are calculated on the row.
2. Three months before a window opens, the responsible attorney gets a note, and the client's contact details are checked with a short "is this still the right person?" email.
3. When the window opens, the client gets an email in plain words: the registration needs a filing in the next year to stay alive, here are the goods and services it covers, and three questions to answer.
4. The questions go on a short form: is the mark still in use on each item, has the owner's name or address changed, and can they upload a current example of the mark in use.
5. No reply brings a reminder every month. After the third, the attorney gets a call task.
6. The answers and the uploads are filed in the client's folder and the row shows what is still missing.
7. The attorney reviews the answers, decides what to file and files it. The workflow never files anything with the USPTO.
8. Six months before the window closes, any row without a filing goes on a weekly list to the attorney, and stays there through the grace period.
9. After the filing, the attorney marks it done and the next window is set on the row.
10. If AI drafts a message, the attorney checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with the attorney
Whether the mark is in use, whether a specimen is acceptable, what to delete from the registration, whether to claim excusable nonuse, the filing and every piece of advice to the client. The workflow holds the dates, asks the questions and collects the answers. It isn't legal advice and it isn't docketing software: if your malpractice carrier expects a particular docketing system, keep using it. ## UCC continuation reminders: every filing's six-month window on one list
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ucc-continuation-filing-reminders/

A UCC continuation reminder workflow keeps one row per financing statement with its filing date and lapse date. When the six-month window before the lapse date opens, it asks whether the loan is still outstanding, gives the responsible person a dated task and repeats it weekly until someone records the continuation or marks the filing as no longer needed. A person files the continuation.

Under UCC 9-515, a filed financing statement is effective for five years, and a continuation statement can be filed only in the six months before that period ends. File too early and it doesn't count. File too late and the filing has lapsed. So the date that matters arrives four and a half years after the loan closed, when the person who made the filing may have left and the loan may have been renewed, sold or paid off. Large lenders use a filing service for this. A small lender, an equipment dealer that finances its own sales or a two-attorney firm usually has a spreadsheet and a calendar entry that one person owns.

### Where continuations get missed
- The lapse date sits in the calendar of someone who has left
- The loan was renewed or amended, and everyone assumed the amendment moved the date
- A reminder fired a year early, was dismissed, and never came back
- The filing was made in more than one state and only one is on the list
- The debtor changed its name or moved, and nobody asked whether the filing still matches
- The loan was paid off, the filing was never terminated, and the list is full of rows nobody trusts

### The dates the list tracks
These follow UCC 9-515 as most states have enacted it. State versions differ in places and some kinds of filing have a different period, so your attorney or the person responsible confirms the lapse date on each row.
| Point on the row | What UCC 9-515 says |
| --- | --- |
| Filing date | The financing statement is effective for five years from this date |
| Window opens | Six months before the five-year period ends |
| Window closes (lapse date) | The end of the five-year period |
| Continuation filed in the window | Adds five years, counted from the original lapse date |
| Amendment filed | Does not move the lapse date |

### How the workflow runs
1. Every financing statement goes on one list: debtor, secured party, state, file number, filing date, the loan it secures and who is responsible. The window's opening date and the lapse date are calculated on the row.
2. The responsible person confirms the dates once. Rows for filings with a different period get their dates entered by hand.
3. Sixty days before a window opens, the loan officer or attorney gets a short question: is this loan still outstanding, and has the debtor's name or address changed?
4. If the loan is paid off, the row goes on a separate list of filings to terminate. If it is outstanding, the row waits for the window.
5. On the day the window opens, the responsible person gets a dated task with the file number, the state and the lapse date.
6. The task repeats every week. With 60 days left, a second person is copied in. With 30 days left, it goes to the owner or managing attorney too.
7. A person prepares and files the continuation, or instructs the filing service. The workflow never files anything.
8. The filer records the continuation's file number and date. The row shows the new lapse date, counted from the old one, and the next window.
9. Once a month, the list goes to the owner: windows open now, windows opening in the next quarter and rows with missing dates.
10. If AI drafts a message to a borrower or a client, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with your people
Whether a continuation should be filed, whether the debtor's name on the filing is still right, the filing itself and any advice to a client. The workflow holds the dates and keeps asking until someone answers. It isn't legal advice and it doesn't replace a filing service or docketing software: if your insurer or your lender agreements expect a particular system, keep using it. For other dated matters, see [commercial lease critical dates tracking](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/commercial-lease-critical-dates-tracking/) and [trademark renewal reminders for small law firms](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/trademark-renewal-reminders-law-firms/).

A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how many filings you hold and where the dates live today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on what you already use (a spreadsheet, email and a calendar). Live in 2-3 days. If a filing service already tracks every lapse date for you and reminds the right person, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### When can a UCC continuation statement be filed?
Under UCC 9-515, only within the six months before the financing statement's five-year period ends. A continuation filed before that window opens or after the lapse date is not effective. State versions differ in places, so confirm the dates for your state.

### Does the workflow file the continuation?
No. A person prepares and files it, or instructs your filing service. The workflow keeps the dates, opens the task on the first day of the window and repeats it until the filing is recorded.

### Does amending a UCC-1 extend it?
No. Under UCC 9-515 only a continuation statement filed in the window extends the filing. An amendment doesn't move the lapse date, which is why the list keeps the original date on the row.

## Pallet racking inspection reminders: every site booked before its date
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pallet-racking-inspection-reminders/

A racking inspection reminder workflow keeps one row per site with the date of its last expert inspection and the next one. Weeks before the date it emails the site's contact with visit dates, books the reply into the inspectors' diary and reminds the site the day before. After the visit it sends the report, sets the next date and keeps any damage that needs repair on a follow-up list.

HSE's warehousing guidance, HSG76, is widely described by inspection bodies as calling for an expert racking inspection by a technically competent person at least once a year, alongside regular in-house checks by someone the warehouse has nominated. For a racking inspection firm that means every customer comes round again in about twelve months. The inspection is the skilled part. The part that slips is remembering which site is due, reaching the right person there, agreeing a day when the aisles can be walked, and going back to see whether the damaged upright in the report was ever replaced.

### Where repeat inspections get lost
- Due dates live in last year's reports, and nobody reads them until a customer rings
- The warehouse manager who booked last year has moved on and the email bounces
- A customer with four sites has four dates, and only the head office one is in the diary
- The site wants a quiet day, proposes one by phone, and it never reaches the inspector
- The report listed items to unload and repair, and nobody asked whether it was done
- New bays were added in the summer and the firm hears about it at the next visit

### What the list holds for each site
One row per site, not per customer, because sites fall due on different dates. The interval on each row is set by your inspector: guidance describes twelve months as the longest gap, and a site with heavy truck traffic or a history of damage may be seen sooner.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Site address and access notes | So the visit is booked for a day the aisles can be walked |
| Site contact and a second contact | So a reminder still lands when one person has left |
| Last inspection date and inspector | The next date is counted from it |
| Interval set by your inspector | Twelve months at most in the guidance, shorter where the inspector says so |
| Open items from the last report | So repairs are followed up before the next visit, not at it |

### How the workflow runs

2. Eight weeks before the date, the site contact gets an email in plain words: the annual racking inspection is due, here are three dates, and has the racking changed since last time?
3. The reply books the visit into the inspectors' diary. A changed layout is flagged so the office can check the time allowed.
4. No reply brings a reminder after a week and another a week later, to the second contact too. After that, the site goes on a call list for the office.
5. The day before the visit, the site gets a reminder with the inspector's name and the arrival time.
6. Your inspector carries out the inspection and writes the report. The workflow never judges racking.
7. The office marks the visit done. The report goes to the site contact and the next date is set on the row.
8. Items the inspector marked for repair go on a follow-up list. The site is asked at two and four weeks whether the work is done, and the answer is recorded on the row.
9. Once a month, the owner gets the list: sites due in the next quarter, sites not yet booked and repairs still open.
10. If AI drafts a message to a site, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with your inspector
The inspection, the damage classification, the report, the interval and any advice about unloading a bay. The workflow books the visit and keeps asking about repairs. It doesn't replace the warehouse's own regular checks, which stay with the person the site has nominated. HSG76 is guidance, so this page doesn't tell a warehouse what the law requires of it: your inspector does that. ## DEA registration and license renewal tracking: every provider's dates on one list
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/dea-registration-and-license-renewal-tracking/

A renewal tracking workflow keeps one row per provider per credential: DEA registration, state license, state controlled substance registration and anything else with an expiry date. It reminds the provider and the office manager well before each date, repeats until the provider confirms the renewal, and asks for the new certificate so the next date goes on the row.

A practitioner's DEA registration is renewed every three years, and the DEA sends its renewal notice to the email address on the registration. A state license runs on its own cycle, set by the state board. So a practice with six providers has a dozen or more dates, on different cycles, and the official reminders go to each provider's personal inbox, sometimes at an address from a previous job. The office manager usually finds out when a pharmacy calls or a payer asks for a current copy. Each renewal takes the provider a few minutes. Knowing that it is due is the part nobody owns.

### Where renewals get missed
- The DEA's notice goes to an old email address and the practice never sees it
- A three-year cycle is long enough that nobody remembers when the last renewal was
- The provider renewed online and nobody at the practice got the new certificate
- A provider works in two states and only one license is on the list
- A new hire's dates were collected for credentialing and never copied to the practice's own list
- The office manager who kept the spreadsheet left, and the calendar reminders left with them

### What the list holds for each provider
One row per credential, not per provider, because each one expires on its own date. Only the DEA cycle is the same everywhere. Every other date is entered from the certificate, because state boards set their own cycles and requirements.
| Credential | Where the date comes from |
| --- | --- |
| DEA registration | The expiry date on the certificate. Practitioner registrations are renewed every three years |
| State professional license | The state board's record. Cycles vary by state and profession |
| State controlled substance registration | The state's certificate, where the state has one |
| Continuing education needed for renewal | Entered by the provider, as the board sets it |
| Board certification and other dated items | Entered from the certificate |

4. Reminders repeat at 60 days, then every week from 30 days. The practice's lead clinician is copied in from 30 days.
5. The provider renews. The workflow never signs in to the DEA or a state board, and never holds a provider's login.
6. The provider replies "done" or uploads the new certificate. The office manager checks it and enters the new expiry date.
7. A row without a new certificate stays open, even after a "done" reply, until the document is in the folder.
8. When the new certificate arrives, the office manager gets a short list of who else needs a copy, such as payers, the hospital or the practice's pharmacy accounts. A person sends them.
9. Once a month, the office manager gets the list: dates in the next 90 days, rows still open and rows with no certificate on file.
10. If AI drafts a message, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with the provider and the practice
The renewal application, every statement on it, the fee, continuing education and any decision about what a provider may do while a renewal is pending. The DEA has changed its policy on late renewals more than once, so the workflow doesn't plan around a grace period: check the DEA Diversion Control Division's site for the current rules. ## OSHA bloodborne pathogens training reminders for dental and medical offices
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/osha-bloodborne-pathogens-training-reminders-dental-offices/

An OSHA training reminder workflow keeps one row per employee with the date of their last bloodborne pathogens training. It reminds the office manager and the employee before a year has passed, adds every new hire to the list on their first day, and keeps the row open until the training record, with the date, the trainer and the attendee's job title, is in the folder.

OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030, calls for training when an employee with occupational exposure is first assigned and at least annually after that, and for training records to be kept for three years. In a dental office that usually means one all-staff session a year and a binder. The session is not the hard part. The hard part is the hygienist who was on leave that day, the assistant hired in March who has not been trained yet, and the sign-in sheet that never made it into the binder.

### Where annual training slips
- The yearly session is booked from memory, and this year it lands thirteen months after the last one
- Two people were out that day, and nobody arranged a make-up session
- A new hire starts seeing patients before anyone checks whether they have been trained
- The sign-in sheet exists, but it doesn't show the trainer or what was covered
- Part-time and temporary staff are not on the list at all
- The office manager who ran it left, and the binder went quiet

### What the list holds for each employee
One row per employee, because people fall due on different dates once anyone misses the group session or joins mid-year. Who counts as having occupational exposure is decided by the practice, not by the list.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Name and job title | The training record names both |
| Start date | So a new hire is flagged for training at the start, not at the next group session |
| Last training date | The next date is counted from it |
| Trainer and session summary | They belong in the record alongside the date |
| Where the record is filed | So it can be found in the three years it has to be kept |

### How the workflow runs
1. Every employee the practice has marked as exposed goes on one list with their last training date. The next date is calculated on the row.
2. Sixty days before the earliest date, the office manager gets a message: these people fall due in this window, time to book the session.
3. Once the session is booked, each person on the list gets the date and a reminder the day before.
4. After the session, the office manager marks who attended and uploads the sign-in sheet, the trainer's name and qualifications and a summary of what was covered.
5. Anyone who missed it stays open. They and the office manager are reminded weekly until a make-up session is recorded.
6. A new hire added to the staff list gets a row on their first day, and the office manager is asked when their initial training is booked.
7. Each record is filed in one folder by year and kept on the list for three years from the training date.
8. Once a month, the dentist or practice owner gets a short list: who is due in the next 60 days and who is still open.
9. If AI drafts a reminder, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with the practice
Who has occupational exposure, what the training covers, who delivers it and the exposure control plan itself. The workflow keeps dates and records. It doesn't deliver training and it is not a compliance review: this page covers one standard, and your state may run its own OSHA plan with its own rules. ## HOA architectural review request tracking: every request answered before its deadline
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/hoa-architectural-review-request-tracking/

An architectural review tracking workflow logs each owner's request with the date it was received and the response deadline from that community's governing documents. It checks the application is complete, sends it to the committee, reminds members as the deadline nears and drafts the decision letter for the manager to send. Each board gets one list of open requests before its meeting.

An owner wants a fence, a new roof color or solar panels, and sends in an architectural request. Many governing documents give the committee a set number of days to answer in writing, and some say what happens if it doesn't: in certain communities a request that gets no answer in time is treated as approved. For a management company with twenty communities, that is twenty different periods, committees of volunteers who answer email when they can, and a stream of requests arriving by email, by mail and through the portal. The decision is the committee's. Getting it made, and sent, inside the period is the manager's problem.

### Where architectural requests go wrong
- A request arrives by email to one manager and sits there while they are on vacation
- Nobody wrote down the day it was received, so nobody knows when the period ends
- The application is missing the plot plan, and the owner is told three weeks later
- Committee members reply to different email threads and nobody counts the votes
- The committee decided at a meeting, but the letter to the owner was never sent
- The owner starts work, and the file doesn't show whether it was ever approved

### What the log holds for each request
One row per request. The response period on the row comes from that community's governing documents and is entered by the manager, who reads the documents. The workflow counts days. It doesn't interpret anything.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Community, lot and owner | So the request reaches the right committee |
| Date received and how it arrived | The deadline is counted from the date your documents say |
| What is missing, if anything | So the owner is asked for it in the first days, not the last |
| Response period for that community | Entered by the manager from the governing documents |
| Each member's vote and the decision | So the letter matches what the committee decided |
| Date the decision letter was sent | The answer to the question owners ask later |

### How the workflow runs
1. Every request, however it arrives, is logged from one form: community, lot, what the owner wants to do, and the documents they sent.
2. The row sets the response deadline from the received date and that community's period.
3. The manager checks the application against the community's checklist. If something is missing, the owner gets a message that day listing it.
4. A complete application goes to the committee members in one email with the documents and a simple way to answer: approve, approve with conditions, deny, or discuss at a meeting.
5. Members who haven't answered are reminded weekly. In the last ten days the reminders go daily and the manager is copied.
6. When the committee has decided, the workflow drafts the decision letter from the board's approved wording, with any conditions listed.
7. The manager reads the letter, edits it and sends it. The date sent is recorded on the row.
8. Before each board meeting, the board gets one list: requests open, days left on each, and decisions made since the last meeting.
9. If AI drafts a letter or a summary of a request, the manager reads it before anything is sent.

### What stays with the committee and the manager
Every decision and every condition belongs to the committee. Reading the governing documents, deciding when an application counts as complete and deciding what a missed deadline means belong to the manager and the association's attorney. The workflow keeps dates, sends reminders and drafts letters. ## Fire damper testing reminders: every building booked, every failed damper followed up
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/fire-damper-testing-reminders/

A fire damper testing reminder workflow keeps one row per building with the date of its last test and the next one. Weeks before the date it emails the building's contact with visit dates and asks about access, books the reply into the engineers' diary and reminds the site the day before. After the visit it sends the report, sets the next date and keeps every failed or unreached damper on a follow-up list until the customer answers the quote.

BS 9999 is a code of practice, not a regulation, and testing firms widely read it as expecting fire dampers to be tested by a competent person at least once a year, and more often in places such as hospitals. For a firm that tests dampers, that makes every building a repeat visit. The drop test is the skilled part. The part that slips is the office work around it: knowing which building is due, reaching the person who looks after it now, getting above the ceilings, and going back to the dampers that failed or could not be reached last time.

### Where repeat damper tests get lost
- Due dates sit in last year's reports, and nobody opens them until the customer's fire risk assessor asks
- The facilities manager has changed and the reminder goes to an inbox nobody reads
- The engineer arrives and the ceiling voids are locked, the ward is in use or the plant has to stay running
- Last year's report listed dampers that could not be reached, and nobody arranged access hatches before this visit
- Failed dampers were quoted for repair, the quote went out with the report, and nobody asked about it again
- A building was refitted, dampers were added or moved, and the firm finds out on the day

### What the list holds for each building
One row per building, with a link to its damper register (the numbered list of dampers and where they are). The register is your engineers' record. The row is what the office needs to book the next visit well.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Building address and type | A hospital or care home may be on a shorter interval than an office |
| Site contact and a second contact | So a reminder still lands when the facilities manager changes |
| Last test date and interval | The next date is counted from them. Your firm sets the interval with the customer |
| Access notes | Out-of-hours working, permits, escorts and which areas need notice |
| Dampers failed or not reached last time | So the visit plan and the quote start from them, not from memory |
| Open remedial quote | So it is followed up before the next test, not at it |

### How the workflow runs
1. Every building you test goes on one list with its last test date, the interval and its contacts. The next date is calculated on the row.
2. Eight weeks before the date, the site contact gets an email in plain words: the fire damper test is due, here are three dates, and has the building or its ventilation changed since last time?
3. The same email asks the access questions: can the work be done in the day, is a permit or an escort needed, and which areas need notice.
4. If dampers could not be reached last time, the email lists them and asks whether access hatches have been fitted.
5. The reply books the visit into the engineers' diary. A refit or a change of use is flagged so the office can check the time allowed.
6. No reply brings a reminder after a week and another a week later, to the second contact too. After that, the building goes on a call list for the office.
7. The day before the visit, the site gets a reminder with the engineers' names and the arrival time.
8. Your engineers test the dampers and write the report. The workflow never judges a damper.
9. The office marks the visit done. The report goes to the site contact, the next date is set and the failed and unreached dampers are copied onto the row.
10. If the report led to a remedial quote, the contact is asked about it at two and four weeks, and the answer is recorded.
11. Once a month, the owner gets the list: buildings due in the next quarter, buildings not yet booked and quotes still open.
12. If AI drafts a message to a customer, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with your engineers
The test, the result for each damper, the report, the interval and any advice about what a failed damper means for the building. The workflow books the visit and keeps asking about the quote. This page doesn't tell a building owner what the law or their fire risk assessment requires: that is for the responsible person and their assessor. For other test rounds on the same buildings, see [fire door inspection reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/fire-door-inspection-reminders/) and [dry riser testing reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/dry-riser-testing-reminders/).

Live in 2-3 days. If your job management software already books repeat tests and follows up quotes, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### How often are fire dampers tested?
Testing firms widely read BS 9999 as expecting a test by a competent person at least once a year, and more often in buildings such as hospitals. BS 9999 is a code of practice. Your firm and the building's responsible person set the interval for each building.

### Does the workflow do any of the testing?
No. Your engineers test the dampers and write the report. The workflow keeps the dates, books the visit, asks about access, sends the report and follows up the quote.

## Charity annual return reminders: every charity client filed inside its 10 months
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/charity-annual-return-reminders-accountants/

A charity annual return reminder workflow keeps one row per charity client with its financial year end and the filing deadline 10 months later. It asks the treasurer for the records soon after the year end, reminds until they arrive, asks for the date of the trustees' meeting that will approve the accounts, and shows the accountant which charities are close to the deadline with something still missing.

A charity registered in England and Wales sends its annual return to the Charity Commission within 10 months of the end of its financial year. A charity with a 31 December year end has until 31 October. Ten months sounds generous, and that is the problem. The treasurer is a volunteer, the trustees meet a few times a year, and the records arrive in month eight. For a practice with a few dozen charity clients on different year ends, the work is rarely the return itself. It is knowing where each charity is, and asking early enough.

### Where charity filings run late
- The treasurer changed at the AGM and the new one doesn't know the practice is waiting for anything
- Records are asked for once, by email, and nobody notices there was no answer
- The accounts are ready, but the next trustees' meeting is after the deadline
- Nobody is sure who has access to the charity's Charity Commission account this year
- Trustees joined or left, and the details on the register were never updated
- Each charity has a different year end, so there is no one busy season to remind everyone

### What the list holds for each charity
One row per charity. The deadline is calculated from the year end, so nobody counts months by hand.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Financial year end | The 10-month deadline is counted from it |
| Treasurer and a second trustee | So a request still lands when the treasurer changes |
| What you do for them | Accounts, independent examination, the return itself, or only some of these |
| Records received | Bank statements, the cash book, grant letters, Gift Aid claims: ticked as each arrives |
| Trustees' meeting date | The accounts and the trustees' annual report must be approved before filing |
| Who files, and filed date | So it is clear whether the practice or a trustee presses the button |

### How the workflow runs
1. Every charity client goes on one list with its year end and contacts. The deadline appears on the row.
2. Two weeks after the year end, the treasurer gets an email in plain words with the list of records you need and the date you need them by.
3. As items arrive, the practice ticks them off. The next reminder lists only what is still missing.
4. No reply brings a reminder after two weeks and another two weeks later, copied to the second trustee. After that, the charity goes on a call list.
5. The same email asks when the trustees will next meet. If the meeting is after the deadline, the accountant is told at once, while there is still time to ask for an earlier one.
6. Your accountant prepares the accounts and carries out the examination. The workflow has no part in either.
7. When the accounts are ready, the trustees get them with a request to approve and sign, and a reminder a few days before the meeting.
8. Before filing, the charity is asked to confirm its trustees and contact details are up to date, and who will sign in to file.
9. The practice records the filed date. The row moves to next year.
10. Every Monday, the partner gets one list: charities inside three months of the deadline, and what each is waiting for.
11. If AI drafts a message to a trustee, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with the accountant and the trustees
The accounts, the independent examination or audit, the answers on the return and the decision to file all stay with people. The trustees are responsible for their charity's filing. The workflow only keeps the dates and does the asking. This page covers charities registered in England and Wales. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own regulators and their own deadlines, and a row for one of those charities would carry that deadline instead. If your practice software already tracks charity deadlines and chases records, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### When is a charity's annual return due?
For charities registered in England and Wales, within 10 months of the end of the financial year. A 31 December year end means 31 October. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own regulators and deadlines.

## Trust funding follow-up: every signed trust tracked until the assets are in it
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/trust-funding-follow-up-estate-planning-attorneys/

A trust funding follow-up workflow opens a checklist on the day a client signs a trust: one row for each asset the attorney listed, with who moves it and what proof closes it. It sends the client plain instructions for their part, reminds them asset by asset until a new statement or a recorded deed comes back, and shows the attorney which signed trusts are still unfunded.

A living trust only covers the assets that are moved into it. Estate planning attorneys know this, and say it at the signing. Then the client goes home with a binder, the bank wants its own form, the brokerage wants a certificate of trust, and the letter of instructions sits in the binder. The firm finds out years later, when the family calls. The legal work was done well. What was missing was somebody asking, a month after signing and again a month after that, whether each account has been retitled.

### Where funding stalls after the signing
- The client leaves with funding instructions and nobody at the firm is assigned to ask about them again
- The firm records the deed, but the bank and brokerage accounts are left to the client, and nothing confirms they were done
- Each bank asks for different paperwork, and the client gives up after the first branch visit
- The attorney wanted beneficiary forms changed on some accounts, and the client was never sure which ones
- A paralegal keeps the status in their head, and it leaves with them
- The client buys a house or opens an account a year later, and it never goes near the trust

### What the funding checklist holds
One checklist per trust, with one row per asset. The attorney decides how each asset is handled. The row records that decision, so a reminder never has to make one.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| The asset, in the client's words | "Checking account at the credit union", so the reminder is clear to them |
| How the attorney wants it handled | Retitle, change the beneficiary form, assign, or leave outside the trust |
| Who does it | The firm (a deed, an assignment) or the client (a bank visit, a form) |
| What the institution usually asks for | So the client takes the right papers the first time |
| Proof that closes the row | A recorded deed, a new statement in the trust's name, a confirmation letter |
| Status and date | Not started, in progress, proof received, or client declined |

### How the workflow runs
1. When the trust is signed, the paralegal opens the checklist from the asset list the attorney already approved.
2. The client gets one email with their part only: each account, what to ask the institution for, and what to send back when it is done.
3. The firm's own rows (the deed, the assignment of business interests) appear on the paralegal's task list with dates.
4. The client uploads or emails proof. A person at the firm looks at it and marks the row.
5. Two weeks later, the client gets a reminder that lists only the rows still open. Finished ones are not mentioned again.
6. Reminders repeat monthly for as long as the attorney has set. They are short and say what is left.
7. If the client replies with a question about how an asset should be handled, it goes to the attorney. The workflow never answers it.
8. When every row is closed, the attorney reviews the checklist and the firm sends the closing letter.
9. If the client stops answering or decides to leave an asset out, the attorney sees it and decides what the file needs: a call, or a letter that records the choice.
10. Once a month, the attorney gets one list: trusts signed, rows still open, and how long each has been waiting.
11. If AI drafts a message to a client, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with the attorney
Every decision about an asset: whether it is retitled, handled by a beneficiary form or left alone, and what a retirement account or a property in another state needs. The engagement letter decides how far the firm's duty to follow up goes, and your state's rules decide what the firm may send to a former client. The workflow asks, records and reports. It gives no legal advice and this page doesn't either. For other deadlines and documents in a small firm, see [bankruptcy client document collection](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/bankruptcy-client-document-collection/). Advisors who work with the same clients may know [RMD reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/rmd-reminders-financial-advisors/).

If your practice management software already runs a funding checklist with client reminders, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### What does funding a trust mean?
Moving assets into the trust so it controls them: recording a deed, retitling accounts or changing beneficiary forms, as the attorney directs. A trust generally covers only the assets that were moved into it.

## Fire risk assessment review reminders: every premises reviewed on the date you set
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/fire-risk-assessment-review-reminders/

A fire risk assessment review reminder workflow keeps one row per premises with the date of the last assessment and the review date the assessor set. Weeks before that date it emails the client with visit dates and asks what has changed in the building, books the reply into the assessor's diary and reminds the site the day before. Between visits it asks the client about the open actions from the last report and records each answer.

In England and Wales, the Fire Safety Order says a fire risk assessment must be reviewed regularly to keep it up to date, and again when there is reason to think it is no longer valid or the premises have changed. It sets no fixed interval. Many assessors recommend a review about once a year, and sooner for higher-risk buildings, and they write that date in the report. Then the report is filed. A year later nobody at the client remembers the date, and the assessor's own list is a folder of PDFs. The assessment is the skilled part. The part that slips is knowing who is due, reaching the right person and finding out what happened to last year's actions.

### Where reviews get lost
- The review date is on page two of a report, and nobody looks at it again
- The person who ordered the assessment has left, and the reminder goes to an old inbox
- The client changed the layout, the use of a floor or the number of staff, and did not think to say
- Last year's action plan had twelve items, and nobody knows which were done
- A managing agent has forty blocks with different dates and asks for them all in one week
- The assessor arrives and the plant room, the roof space or a flat is locked

### What the list holds for each premises
One row per premises, with a link to the last report. The report is the assessor's record. The row is what the office needs to book the next review well.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Address and type of premises | A care home or a block of flats may be on a shorter review date than a small office |
| Client contact and a second contact | So a reminder still lands when the first person has moved on |
| Date of the last assessment and the review date | The assessor sets the review date. The workflow only counts back from it |
| Open actions from the last report | So the client can be asked about them before the visit, not at it |
| Access notes | Keys, escorts, areas that need notice and the best days to visit |
| Changes the client has reported | A refit or a change of use is flagged to the assessor straight away |

### How the workflow runs
1. Every premises you assess goes on one list with the date of the last assessment, the review date from the report and its contacts.
2. Eight weeks before the review date, the client gets an email in plain words: the review of your fire risk assessment is due, here are three dates for the visit.
3. The same email asks a short set of questions: has the layout changed, has the use of any area changed, have there been building works, a fire or a false alarm problem since last time?
4. It also lists the open actions from the last report and asks which are done.
5. The reply books the visit into the assessor's diary. Answers about changes go to the assessor before the visit, so the time allowed can be checked.
6. No reply brings a reminder after a week and another a week later, to the second contact too. After that, the premises goes on a call list for the office.
7. The day before the visit, the site gets a reminder with the assessor's name, the arrival time and the areas that need to be open.
8. The assessor carries out the review and writes the report. The workflow never judges a risk.
9. The office marks the visit done. The report goes to the client, the new review date is copied onto the row and the new actions replace the old list.
10. Three months after the report, the client is asked about the open actions again, and each answer is recorded with its date.
11. If a client writes at any time to say the building has changed, the message goes to the assessor the same day.
12. Once a month, the owner gets the list: reviews due in the next quarter, premises not yet booked and clients who have not answered.
13. If AI drafts a message to a client, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with the assessor
The assessment, every finding, the priority of each action and the review date. The workflow asks the client what they have done. It does not check that an action was done properly, and it does not tell a client what the law requires of them: that is the assessor's advice to the responsible person. For test and service rounds on the same buildings, see [fire door inspection reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/fire-door-inspection-reminders/) and [fire alarm service reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/fire-alarm-service-reminders/).

If your assessment software already books reviews and follows up actions, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### How often should a fire risk assessment be reviewed?
The Fire Safety Order sets no fixed interval. It says the assessment must be reviewed regularly to keep it up to date, and when there is reason to think it is no longer valid or things have changed. A review about once a year is common practice. The assessor and the responsible person set the date for each premises.

## DOT annual inspection reminders: every customer truck and trailer booked before its date
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/dot-annual-inspection-reminders-truck-repair-shops/

A DOT annual inspection reminder workflow keeps one row per truck and trailer with the date of its last periodic inspection. About six weeks before the 12 months are up, it texts and emails the fleet's contact with bay times, books the reply into the shop calendar and reminds them the day before. After the inspection it sends the report, sets the next date and keeps asking about any repair estimate that is still open.

FMCSA rules say every commercial motor vehicle, including each unit of a combination, must pass a periodic inspection at least once every 12 months. For a shop that does these inspections, every truck and trailer you have ever stickered is a repeat job with a known date. Most small fleets and owner-operators don't track that date well. They remember when a driver notices the sticker, or at a roadside stop. The inspection is the skilled part. The part that slips is the office work: knowing which units are due, reaching the person who schedules them and getting the truck into a bay while it is still in date.

### Where repeat inspections get lost
- The due date is on a sticker and a paper report, and nobody at the shop has a list
- Trailers are forgotten because they sit in a yard and nobody drives them to the shop
- A fleet has eight units due across the year and wants them done in two visits, not eight
- The customer bought two more trucks, and the shop finds out when one is already out of date
- An inspection found defects, the estimate went out, and nobody asked about it again
- The owner-operator is on the road for three weeks and can't answer a phone call in shop hours

### What the list holds for each unit
One row per truck or trailer, grouped by customer. Your inspection reports stay where they are today. The row is what the front desk needs to book the next one.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Customer, contact and a second contact | So the message reaches whoever schedules the trucks now |
| Unit number, type and plate | The customer knows the truck by its unit number, not by your invoice |
| Last inspection date | The next date is counted from it |
| Where the unit is usually parked | A yard trailer may need a mobile visit or a driver to bring it in |
| Open repair estimate | So it is followed up before the next inspection, not at it |
| Other units for the same customer due soon | So one visit can cover several |

3. If the same customer has other units due in the next two months, the message lists them and offers to do them together.
4. The message also asks one question: have you added or sold any trucks or trailers since last time?
5. The reply books the bay time into the shop calendar. New units are added to the list for the front desk to confirm.
6. No reply brings a reminder after a week and another a week later, to the second contact too. After that, the unit goes on a call list.
7. The day before, the customer gets a reminder with the drop-off time and what to bring.
8. Your qualified inspector does the inspection and signs the report. The workflow never decides whether a unit passes.
9. The front desk marks the job done. The report is sent to the customer, the next date is set and any defects are noted on the row.
10. If the inspection led to a repair estimate, the customer is asked about it after three days and again after ten, and the answer is recorded.
11. Two weeks before a date with no booking, the unit is flagged in red on the owner's list.
12. Once a month, the owner gets the list: units due in the next quarter, units not yet booked and estimates still open.
13. If AI drafts a message to a customer, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with the shop and the carrier
The inspection, every pass and fail, the report and the repair work stay with your inspector. Keeping each vehicle in date is the motor carrier's job, and the reminder doesn't move that to the shop: it is a service to your customers, and the messages say so.
