## HUD annual recertification reminders: every notice on time, every household's file complete
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/hud-annual-recertification-reminders-property-managers/

An annual recertification reminder workflow keeps one row per household with its recertification anniversary date. It prepares each reminder notice on the day your program calls for it, puts it in front of the site manager to approve and serve, books the tenant's interview, lists the documents still missing and asks for them until the file is complete. Staff verify income and do every calculation. The workflow only keeps the dates and the checklist.

In HUD-assisted housing, each household is recertified every year, and the notices leading up to it run on a calendar. HUD's sample reminder notices in Handbook 4350.3 are dated at least 120, 90 and 60 days before the anniversary date. With 30 units, a site manager can keep that in a binder. With 200 units and anniversaries in every month, a notice goes out late, an interview is missed, or a file sits for weeks waiting for one pay stub. The income work is the skilled part. The part that slips is the calendar and the follow-up.

### Where recertifications slip
- The anniversary dates are in the software, but nobody pulls the list until the month is half gone
- The first notice went out on time and the second was forgotten
- A tenant came to the interview without half the documents, and nobody asked again
- A verification request went to an employer and no one noticed it never came back
- The site manager was out for two weeks and the notices for that month waited
- The regional manager learns about late files at the next review, not while there is time to fix them

### What the list holds for each household
One row per household, filled from a report out of your property software. The tenant file stays in your software and your folders. The row holds dates and a checklist, not income figures.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Unit, head of household and how they prefer to be contacted | So interview reminders go by letter, email or text as the tenant chose |
| Recertification anniversary date | Every notice date is counted back from it |
| Notice dates and the day each was served | So a missed notice shows up the same week |
| Interview date | So it can be reminded and rebooked |
| Checklist of documents and verifications | Each one is marked asked, received or still waiting |
| Who is handling the file | So a colleague can pick it up when someone is out |

### How the workflow runs

3. The site manager checks the notice, signs it and serves it the way your program requires. They mark the date served on the row.
4. If a notice is not marked as served within two working days, the site manager is reminded and the regional manager sees it on their list.
5. The tenant is offered interview times. A reminder goes out two days before and on the morning of the interview.
6. A missed interview is flagged the same day so it can be rebooked.
7. After the interview, staff tick what was received. The tenant gets a short list of what is still missing and a date to bring it by.
8. Missing documents are asked for again after a week. Verification requests sent to employers or agencies are flagged if nothing has come back in two weeks.
9. Staff verify income, do the calculation and complete the certification in your software. The workflow takes no part in that.
10. Every Monday, each site manager gets their list: notices due this week, interviews booked and files still waiting.
11. The regional manager gets one page: households inside 60 days with an incomplete file.
12. If AI drafts a message to a tenant, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with your staff
Serving the notices, verifying income, every calculation, every decision about a household and anything to do with ending assistance. Notice dates and wording come from your program's current rules and your own templates, and your compliance staff set them in the workflow. This page is not compliance advice. Tenant documents go straight to your own folders and are not passed through AI. If your property software already prepares each notice on time and follows up missing documents, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

## Trust Registration Service annual declaration reminders: every client trust checked before 31 January
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/trust-registration-service-annual-declaration-reminders/

A Trust Registration Service reminder workflow keeps one row per client trust with its lead trustee, whether it is taxable and when the register was last confirmed. In the autumn it asks each lead trustee a short set of questions about what has changed, reminds until they answer and gives the practice a list of trusts ready to declare. A person at the practice signs in, makes any changes and makes the declaration.

GOV.UK guidance says a taxable trust must be declared up to date on the trust register every year by 31 January, and that changes must be reported within 90 days. For a practice that looks after trusts, the declaration itself takes minutes. The slow part is finding out whether anything has changed. A trustee has retired, a beneficiary has moved abroad, an address is out of date, and nobody told the practice. The question goes out in January with the tax return, the answer comes back late, and the declaration is made in a rush. The skilled work is knowing what has to be reported. The part that slips is asking every trust in time and keeping track of who has answered.

### Where trust declarations slip
- The list of trusts lives in the tax return software, and it only shows trusts with a return this year
- The lead trustee is elderly, and the person who really deals with the paperwork is a son or daughter
- A trustee died or retired in the summer, and the practice hears about it in January
- A beneficiary changed their name or moved abroad, and nobody thought it mattered
- The agent authorisation for the trust has lapsed, and nobody notices until someone tries to sign in
- Non-taxable trusts have no January deadline, so their changes are never asked about at all

### What the list holds for each trust
One row per trust. The trust deed, the tax return and your working papers stay where they are today. The row is what the team needs to ask the right person and know what is still open.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Trust name and your reference | So the trustee recognises which trust the message is about |
| Lead trustee and a second contact | So the question reaches the person who actually answers |
| Taxable or non-taxable | A taxable trust has the 31 January declaration; both kinds have changes to report |
| Date the register was last confirmed | So nobody has to sign in to find out |
| Agent authorisation in place | A lapsed authorisation is found in October, not in January |
| Changes reported and the date they happened | The 90 days run from the change, not from when you were told |
| Who at the practice makes the declaration | So every trust has a named person |

### How the workflow runs
1. Every client trust goes on one list with its lead trustee, a second contact and whether it is taxable.
2. In October, each lead trustee gets a short email with a form. It asks about trustees, beneficiaries, names, addresses and countries of residence, in plain words, with a "nothing has changed" button.
3. The form shows the names the practice holds today, so the trustee corrects a list. They don't have to write one from memory.
4. No reply brings a reminder after two weeks and another two weeks later, to the second contact too. After that, the trust goes on a call list.
5. An answer that reports a change goes to the person named on the row, with the date of the change. A change older than 60 days is marked urgent.
6. Your adviser decides what has to be reported. The workflow never decides whether a change matters.
7. Because part-finished updates can't be saved on the register, the workflow checks that every detail needed is on the row before the trust is marked "ready".
8. A person at the practice signs in, makes the changes and makes the declaration. Changes that need a letter to HMRC are listed separately for that person.
9. They mark the row done with the date. The trustee gets a short confirmation.
10. From 1 December, the partner gets a weekly list: trusts not yet answered, trusts with changes waiting and trusts ready to declare.
11. During the year, a trustee can use the same form to report a change when it happens. Non-taxable trusts get the same question once a year.
12. If AI drafts a message to a trustee, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with the practice
Deciding whether a trust is taxable, what has to be reported, and everything entered on the register stay with your adviser. The workflow doesn't sign in to HMRC and doesn't make a declaration. This page doesn't cover which trusts have to register or penalties: check the current GOV.UK guidance for those. For the trust's tax return records, see [Self Assessment document chasing](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/self-assessment-document-chasing/), and for the similar yearly check on companies, see [confirmation statement reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/confirmation-statement-client-reminders/).

If your practice software already asks trustees about changes and tracks the declarations, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### When is the Trust Registration Service annual declaration due?
GOV.UK guidance says a taxable trust must be declared up to date every year by 31 January. Changes to the trust's details must be reported within 90 days. Check the current GOV.UK guidance for your clients' trusts.

## Form 990 deadline reminders: every nonprofit client's records, review and filing on one list
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/form-990-deadline-reminders-nonprofit-accountants/

A Form 990 reminder workflow keeps one row per nonprofit client with its fiscal year end, the due date counted from it and any extension. When the year closes it asks the treasurer or director for the records, reminds until they arrive and asks when the board will review the return. Two weeks before the due date it tells the preparer which clients are not ready, so a person can decide about an extension.

The IRS says Form 990-series returns are due on the 15th day of the fifth month after the organization's fiscal year ends. For a firm with nonprofit clients, that means due dates spread across the year: May for calendar-year clients, November for a June year end, and others in between. The contact is often a volunteer treasurer who changes every couple of years. The board meets a few times a year and wants to see the return before it is filed. The return is the skilled part. The part that slips is the office work: knowing whose year has just closed, asking the right person and fitting the review into a board calendar.

### Where nonprofit returns run late
- The firm's calendar is built around April, and a June or September year end is easy to miss
- The treasurer changed in the spring, and the records request goes to someone who has left
- The records arrive in pieces: bank statements now, the donor list later, board minutes never
- The board wants to review the return, and its next meeting is after the due date
- An extension was filed, and the new date lives in one preparer's head
- A very small client files the e-Postcard itself, forgets, and nobody notices for two years

### What the list holds for each client
One row per organization. Your tax software and working papers stay where they are today. The row is what the team needs to ask on time and see what is waiting.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Organization, treasurer and a second contact | Volunteers change, so every row has two people |
| Fiscal year end | The due date is counted from it |
| Which return the preparer expects to file | Your preparer sets it; an e-Postcard can't be extended |
| Due date, and the extended date if one was filed | One place for both, with the confirmation |
| Records still missing | Reminders ask only for what is open |
| Next board meeting date | So a review that falls too late is seen months ahead |
| Who files, the firm or the client | Clients who file their own e-Postcard still get a reminder and a check |

### How the workflow runs
1. Every nonprofit client goes on one list with its fiscal year end. The due date is calculated on the row and your preparer confirms it.
2. In the week after the year closes, the treasurer gets an email with a checklist of the records you need and a link to upload them.
3. The same message asks two questions: has the treasurer or any officer changed, and when is the next board meeting?
4. Each item that arrives is filed in the client's folder and ticked off. Reminders after two and four weeks list only what is still missing, and go to the second contact too.
5. If the board meeting falls after the due date, the row is flagged for the preparer straight away.
6. Your preparer prepares the return. The workflow never decides which form applies or what goes on it.
7. The draft goes to the client for review with a plain cover note. The contact is reminded a week before the board meeting and the day after it.
8. Two weeks before the due date, the preparer gets a list of clients that are not ready. A person decides whether to file an extension and files it.
9. When an extension is filed, the preparer adds the new date and the confirmation to the row. The reminders move to the new date.
10. A person at the firm files the return and adds the acceptance to the row. The client gets a copy and the date of next year's request.
11. Clients who file their own e-Postcard get a reminder a month before the date and are asked to send the confirmation. No confirmation puts them on the partner's list.
12. Once a month, the partner gets the list: returns due in the next 90 days, records still missing and extensions running.
13. If AI drafts a message to a client, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with the firm
Which return applies, everything on it, the decision to extend and the filing itself stay with your preparer. The IRS says an organization that doesn't file for three consecutive years loses its exempt status automatically, so the monthly list also shows any client with a year that has no filing recorded. This page doesn't cover state charity registrations, penalties or filing thresholds. For funder deadlines, see [grant reporting deadline reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/grant-reporting-deadline-reminders/), and for state filings, see [state annual report reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/state-annual-report-reminders-llc-clients/).

A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how many nonprofit clients you have and where their dates live today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on what you already use (a spreadsheet, email and shared folders, or your practice software). Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is a fixed $2,000](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it, under the [pay-when-happy agreement](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agreement/). If your practice software already requests records by fiscal year end and tracks board review, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### When is Form 990 due?
The IRS says Form 990-series returns are due on the 15th day of the fifth month after the organization's fiscal year ends. For a calendar-year organization that is May 15. Your preparer confirms the date on each client's row.

### Can the due date be extended?
IRS instructions say Form 8868, filed by the original due date, gives an automatic 6-month extension. The e-Postcard (Form 990-N) can't be extended. A person at your firm decides and files; the workflow only records the new date.

## IFTA and Form 2290 filing reminders: every trucking client's records in before the due date
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ifta-and-form-2290-filing-reminders-trucking-clients/

An IFTA and Form 2290 reminder workflow keeps one row per trucking client with its trucks, its filings and their due dates. When a quarter closes it texts and emails the client for mileage and fuel records, reminds for what is missing and tells your preparer who is ready. Before Form 2290 season it asks each client to confirm their truck list. A person at your firm prepares and files every return.

State IFTA offices list the same four due dates: quarterly returns are due on the last day of the month after each quarter, so April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31. IRS instructions say Form 2290 is due by the last day of the month after the month a vehicle is first used on a public highway, which is August 31 for trucks used in July. For a bookkeeper or permit service with trucking clients, the return is rarely the hard part. The hard part is the records. The owner-operator is on the road, the fuel receipts are in the cab, and the mileage report comes on the 29th. Then every client is late in the same week.

### Where trucking filings run late
- The client drives all day and answers email once a week, so the request has to go by text
- Fuel receipts arrive as phone photos, a few at a time, with some months missing
- The mileage report from the ELD or the trip sheets comes without the state breakdown
- A client bought a truck in October, and nobody at your firm knew a Form 2290 was due for it
- A client sold a truck, and it is still on the list you file from
- All the quarterly work lands in the last week of the month because nobody asked earlier

### What the list holds for each client
One row per client, with its trucks listed under it. Your tax and bookkeeping software stay where they are today. The row is what the team needs to ask early and see who is ready.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Client, cell phone and email | Drivers answer a text before an email |
| Trucks, with the month each was first used | A truck added mid-year has its own Form 2290 date |
| Which filings you do for this client | Some clients file their own IFTA and only want the 2290 |
| Where mileage comes from | An ELD report, a fuel card report or trip sheets need different requests |
| Records received for the quarter | Reminders ask only for what is open |
| Due date and the confirmation after filing | So anyone can answer the client's question |
| Other renewals, with dates you enter | Permits and registrations your firm handles sit on the same list |

### How the workflow runs
1. Every trucking client goes on one list with its trucks and the filings you do for it. Your preparer sets the due dates, and the list moves a weekend date to the next business day.
2. On the first working day after a quarter closes, each IFTA client gets a text and an email asking for miles by state and fuel receipts, with a link to upload photos or reports.
3. The message also asks one question: have you added or sold a truck since last quarter?
4. Each file that arrives goes into the client's folder for the quarter and is ticked off the row.
5. Reminders after one and two weeks list only what is still missing. After that, the client goes on a call list.
6. A reported new truck goes to your preparer the same day, with the month it was first used, so a Form 2290 for it isn't missed.
7. Your preparer prepares the return. The workflow never calculates miles, fuel or tax.
8. The client gets the amount due to approve, with one reminder. A person at your firm files, and adds the confirmation to the row.
9. In June, every client gets their truck list and is asked to confirm it for the new Form 2290 period. Changes go to your preparer.
10. When a Form 2290 is filed, the stamped Schedule 1 is saved to the client's folder and sent to the client.
11. Ten days before any due date, your preparer gets a list of clients whose records are still missing.
12. Once a month, the owner gets the list: filings due in the next 60 days, clients not ready and renewals coming up.
13. If AI drafts a message to a client, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with your firm
Every calculation, every return, the filing and any advice stay with your preparer. The workflow doesn't sign in to a state portal or to the IRS. This page gives no tax rates or penalties, and it names no dates for UCR, IRP or state permits: those go on the list as dates your firm enters. For the driver side of a fleet's paperwork, see [driver qualification file expiry tracking](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/driver-qualification-file-expiry-tracking/), and for clients in other trades, see [sales tax filing reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/sales-tax-filing-reminders-bookkeepers/).

### When are IFTA quarterly returns due?
State IFTA offices list the last day of the month after each quarter: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31. A date on a weekend or holiday moves to the next business day. Your preparer confirms the dates on the list.

## 60-day CGT property returns: hear about the sale early and track every return on one list
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/cgt-60-day-property-return-tracking-accountants/

A 60-day return workflow asks your property-owning clients a few times a year whether a sale is planned. When one is, it opens a row with the expected completion date, asks for the purchase and sale papers, and reminds until they arrive. On completion it counts 60 days and shows your adviser each week which returns are waiting, so nobody learns about a sale in January.

GOV.UK says Capital Gains Tax on UK residential property has to be reported and paid within 60 days of completion. The return itself is skilled work and it stays with your adviser. The trouble is the timing. Clients think of tax as a January job, so the firm often hears about a sale months after it completed. Then the purchase papers from years ago have to be found, the client has to set up an HMRC account and authorise the firm, and most of the 60 days is already gone. The fix is office work: asking early, asking for the right papers and keeping the dates in one place.

### Where the 60 days go
- The client mentions the sale in passing, months after completion
- The solicitor's completion statement is in the client's inbox and nobody asked for it
- The purchase costs and improvement invoices are in a box in the loft
- The client has no Capital Gains Tax on UK property account, or has not authorised the firm
- The property is jointly owned and each owner needs their own figures
- The completion date moved and the firm is working from the old one

### What the list holds for each sale
One row per owner per property. Your tax software and working papers stay where they are today. The row is what the team needs to ask on time and see what is waiting.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Client, property and each owner | Joint owners are tracked separately |
| Expected completion date, then the actual one | The 60 days are counted from completion, and the date often moves |
| Solicitor's name and contact | So the completion statement can be asked for with the client's consent |
| Papers still missing | Reminders ask only for what is open |
| HMRC account set up and firm authorised, yes or no | This step can take days, so it starts early |
| Adviser's decision: return needed or not | A person decides; the row records it |
| Date the return was submitted and paid | The row closes only when both are on it |

### How the workflow runs
1. Clients with a rental property, second home or inherited property are tagged on your client list.
2. A few times a year they get a short message: are you planning to sell or give away a property in the next few months? One tap answers it.
3. The same question sits on your Self Assessment records checklist and your new client form.
4. A yes opens a row and sends the client a checklist: purchase completion statement, costs of buying, improvement invoices and the solicitor's details.
5. The client is asked for the expected completion date, and asked again a week before it in case it has moved.
6. The client gets plain steps for setting up their HMRC account and authorising the firm. A reminder goes out until they confirm it is done.
7. Each paper that arrives is filed in the client's folder and ticked off. Reminders list only what is still missing.
8. On completion, the client confirms the date and sends the sale completion statement. The row now shows the 60-day date.
9. Your adviser decides whether a return is needed and prepares it. The workflow never calculates a gain or decides on a relief.
10. The client gets the figures to approve and the amount to pay. A person at the firm submits the return.
11. Every week the adviser gets the list: sales completing soon, returns open and how many days are left on each.
12. With 20 days left and papers still missing, the row goes to the partner.
13. If AI drafts a message to a client, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with the firm
Whether a return is needed, the calculation, any relief or estimate and the submission all stay with your adviser. This page doesn't cover rates, reliefs, penalties or the rules for non-residents. HMRC's guidance for agents explains how a client authorises you on their account. ## 1031 exchange deadline tracking: every 45-day and 180-day date on one list
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/1031-exchange-deadline-tracking/

A 1031 deadline workflow opens one row per exchange on the day the first property closes. It counts the 45-day and 180-day dates, shows them to a person to confirm, and reminds the client, their agent and their CPA as each date gets closer. Each morning the exchange officer sees which files have a date coming and what is still missing.

An IRS fact sheet on like-kind exchanges gives two time limits. The client has 45 days from the sale of the old property to identify replacement property in writing. The replacement property must then be received by the earlier of 180 days after the sale or the due date, with extensions, of that year's tax return. These are calendar days, so weekends and holidays count. A missed date can't be fixed afterwards. The legal and tax work in an exchange is skilled, and it stays with your people. What slips is the office work: several exchanges running at once, each with its own two dates, and clients who think they have more time than they do.

### Where exchange dates slip
- The dates are worked out once, written in the file and not looked at again
- The client believes day 45 is a target and sends the identification a day late
- The identification arrives as a text message with no signature
- The replacement purchase is set to close in the last week, and the lender is running behind
- The sale closed late in the year, and nobody told the client's CPA about the tax return date
- The officer handling the file is out, and the dates live in their calendar

### What the list holds for each exchange
One row per exchange. Your exchange documents, escrow records and accounting stay where they are today. The row is what the team needs to see every date and who has been told.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Client, their agent, their CPA and their attorney | Each gets the reminders that concern them |
| Closing date of the property sold | Both periods are counted from it |
| Day 45 and day 180, confirmed by a named person | The workflow counts; a person confirms |
| Tax return due date for that year | The client's CPA confirms it, because it can come before day 180 |
| Identification received: date, signed, yes or no | So an unsigned or late one is seen at once |
| Replacement property and its planned closing date | A closing planned for the last days is flagged early |
| Who was told what, and when | A record of every reminder sent |

### How the workflow runs
1. When the sale closes, a person adds the closing date to the row, or it is read from your closing confirmation email.
2. The workflow counts day 45 and day 180 and shows both to the exchange officer, who confirms them.
3. The client, their agent and their CPA get one message with both dates in plain words and what has to happen by each.
4. The CPA is asked one question: does the tax return due date for this year come before day 180?
5. The client is reminded at day 15, day 30, day 38 and day 42, each time with the identification form attached.
6. When the identification arrives, a person checks that it is in writing and signed, and marks it on the row.
7. With no identification by day 43, the officer gets the file to call the client that day.
8. After identification, the client and agent are asked for the planned closing date of the replacement property.
9. A planned closing in the last ten days before the deadline is flagged for the officer.
10. The agent is asked for a short status every two weeks: contract signed, loan approved, closing booked.
11. Each morning the officer gets the list: dates in the next 14 days and what each file still needs.
12. When the exchange closes, the client and CPA get the closing dates in one message for the tax return.
13. If AI drafts a message to a client, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with your people
Whether an exchange qualifies, what counts as a valid identification, the exchange documents, the funds and every piece of tax or legal advice stay with your team and the client's advisers. The workflow counts dates and reminds. It doesn't decide anything. This page doesn't cover how many properties can be identified, reverse or improvement exchanges, or state rules. The IRS says the exchange is reported on Form 8824 with the tax return, and the client's CPA handles that. For other dates that can't move, see [commercial lease critical dates tracking](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/commercial-lease-critical-dates-tracking/) and [statute of limitations tracking](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/statute-of-limitations-tracking-law-firms/).

Live in 2-3 days. If your exchange software already reminds clients and their advisers on these dates, you don't need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### What are the 45-day and 180-day deadlines?
An IRS fact sheet says the client has 45 days from the sale to identify replacement property in writing, and must receive it by the earlier of 180 days after the sale or the due date, with extensions, of that year's tax return. The client's tax adviser confirms the dates for each exchange.

### Do weekends and holidays count?

## First aid certificate renewal reminders: every learner's expiry date, and a booking before it runs out
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/first-aid-certificate-renewal-reminders-training-providers/

A renewal reminder workflow keeps one row per learner with the course, the employer and the certificate's expiry date. Months before the date it tells the employer which of their people are due and gives them a link to book. It reminds until they book or say no, and offers the yearly refresher in between. Each week you see who is due and who hasn't answered.

HSE says first aid at work certificates last for three years, and that first-aiders need a requalification course before the certificate expires. It also strongly recommends refresher training every year in between. For a training provider, that means every learner you certify is a likely booking three years later, and a possible one each year. Most providers lose that booking for a simple reason: three years is a long time, the person who booked the course has moved on, and the employer only notices when a certificate has already run out. The training is your skill. Keeping the dates and asking on time is office work.

### Where renewals are lost
- Certificates are issued and the expiry dates sit in a folder of PDFs
- The office manager who booked the course left two years ago
- The employer remembers a month after expiry and books whoever answers first
- Six learners from one company expire in different months, and each needs a separate conversation
- A learner changed jobs, and the new employer has never heard of you
- The yearly refresher is recommended on the course and never mentioned again

### What the list holds for each learner
One row per learner per certificate. Your course records and certificates stay where they are today. The row is what you need to ask on time and see who has answered.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Learner, course and certificate expiry date | The reminders are counted back from the date |
| Employer and the person who books training | Reminders go to whoever books, grouped by company |
| A second contact at the employer | People move on over three years |
| Learner's own email, with their consent | So a learner who changed jobs can still hear from you |
| Refresher offered and booked, by year | The yearly refresher is tracked separately |
| Answer: booked, later, no longer employed, no thanks | A no stops the reminders for that learner |

### How the workflow runs
1. After each course, the learners go on the list from your register, with the expiry dates from the certificates.
2. The booking contact gets a short message with the dates in plain words, so they know when to expect a reminder.
3. About a year after the course, the employer is offered the yearly refresher for the same group, with a link to your dates.
4. Six months before expiry, the employer gets one message listing their people who are due, by name and date.
5. The message has a link to book a place on a public course and a second link to ask for a course at their site.
6. With no answer, reminders go at four months and at two months, and the second contact is copied in.
7. A booking is marked on the row and stops the reminders for those learners.
8. A reply that someone has left removes them from the employer's list. If the learner gave their own email, they get one message offering to rebook.
9. With six weeks left and no answer, the row comes to you for a phone call.
10. After the requalification course, the new certificate date goes on the row and the three years start again.
11. Every week you get the list: learners due in the next six months, employers who haven't answered and places booked.
12. If AI drafts a message to a customer, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with you
Which course a learner needs, what your awarding body allows when a certificate has already expired, and your prices stay with you. Providers differ on what is possible after expiry, so the messages say only what you decide they should say. How many first-aiders an employer needs is the employer's decision, based on their own needs assessment. Messages go to business contacts about a service they bought. A learner's personal email is used only if they agreed to it on the course form, and every message has a way to opt out. Employers who track their own staff cards and training can see [CSCS card and training expiry reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/cscs-card-and-training-expiry-reminders/). For another yearly visit to the same customers, see [fire extinguisher service reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/fire-extinguisher-service-reminders/).

## Law firm file closing: a checklist for every finished matter, and a date for every closed file
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/law-firm-file-closing-and-retention-tracking/

A file closing workflow starts when a matter is marked finished. It gives the fee earner a short checklist, drafts the closing letter for a person to approve, and records the review and destruction dates your policy sets for that matter type. Each month it lists matters that finished but were never closed, and closed files whose dates are coming up.

Opening a file has a process. Closing one usually doesn't. The work ends, the last bill goes out, and the file stays "open" for years because nobody had a reason to close it. Checklists published by bar associations follow the same pattern: check nothing is left to do, return the client's original documents, send a closing letter, and set a destruction date at the moment the file is closed. None of it is legal work, and all of it is easy to skip on a busy day. This page shows how a small firm can make closing happen every time, with the decisions left to its lawyers.

### What goes wrong without a closing step
- Matters finished two years ago still show as open, so the list of live work can't be trusted
- The client never got a letter saying the firm's work has ended
- Original wills, deeds and certificates sit in a file nobody will open again
- A small balance is left in the client account with no instruction about it
- No destruction date was set, so boxes and folders are kept forever, or cleared out by guesswork
- When a former client asks for their file, nobody knows if it still exists

### The closing checklist, and who answers each line
The lines below are the ones most published checklists share. Yours will follow your own policy, your regulator's rules and your insurer's guidance.
| Line on the checklist | Who answers it |
| --- | --- |
| Nothing is left to do, and no date is still running | The lawyer who ran the matter |
| Final bill sent and paid, or the balance written off | Accounts |
| No money left in the client account for this matter | Accounts, with a lawyer's sign-off |
| Original documents returned, or stored with the client's agreement | The lawyer or their assistant |
| Closing letter sent | Drafted for you, approved by the lawyer |
| Matter type, review date and destruction date recorded | Filled in from your policy, confirmed by a person |

### How the workflow runs
1. A matter is marked finished in your case software, or the final bill is paid. Either can be the start.
2. The lawyer who ran the matter gets the checklist as a short form, with the matter's details already filled in.
3. Accounts get their two lines at the same time, so nobody waits for anybody.
4. The closing letter is drafted from your template: the work has ended, what is being returned, how long the file is kept and how to ask for it.
5. The lawyer reads the letter, changes what needs changing and approves it. Nothing goes to a client without that.
6. The review and destruction dates are worked out from your own policy for that matter type, and a person confirms them.
7. When every line is answered, the matter is marked closed and the dates go on the closed-file list and the firm's calendar.
8. A checklist that is still open after two weeks is sent again, and after four weeks it goes to the partner in charge.
9. Every month the partners get two lists: matters with no activity that were never closed, and closed files whose review date is in the next three months.
10. At the review date, a lawyer decides: destroy, keep longer, or return to the client. The decision and its date are recorded.

## R&D claim notification: every client's six-month date on one list, and a question asked before it passes
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/rd-claim-notification-deadline-tracking-accountants/

A claim notification workflow keeps one row per company client with its period end and the date six months later. Some companies have to tell HMRC that they plan to claim R&D tax relief before they claim it. GOV.UK sets the limit at six months after the end of the period of account. The companies caught by this are the ones you are least likely to think of: clients who have never claimed, or who last claimed years ago. Their accounts are often prepared seven or eight months after the year end, when the date has already gone. Deciding whether a client's work counts is the adviser's job. Asking every client the question in time is office work, and it can run on its own.

### Why the notification date is missed
- The date falls before most clients send their year-end records
- The client has never claimed, so nobody thinks to ask
- A client who claimed years ago is assumed to be covered
- The director doesn't call the work research, so never mentions it
- A changed year end moves the date and the diary isn't updated
- The question is asked at the accounts meeting, months too late

### What the list holds for each client
One row per company, with dates counted from the period end you already hold. Your practice software stays as it is. Whether a company needs to notify depends on its claim history, and the test has details that the adviser applies. The list only shows what is known and what is still open.

| Adviser's decision and the date the form was submitted | A decision closes the row for that period |

### How the workflow runs

5. A no is recorded with the date, and the row is closed for that period.
6. With no answer, a reminder goes after two weeks and again a month later.
7. The adviser decides whether a notification is needed, submits the form and records the date and reference.
8. Two months before the date, clients who still haven't answered go on a call list.
9. Every week the partners get the list: dates in the next 60 days, answers waiting for an adviser and clients who are silent.
10. If AI drafts an email to a client, a person checks it before it is sent.

## S corp elections: every client's Form 2553 date, every owner's signature and the IRS letter on one list
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/s-corp-election-deadline-tracking-accountants/

An S corp election workflow keeps one row per client with the tax year the election is for and the last day to file. It asks you which clients to review, collects each owner's signature on the form, records the day it was filed and waits for the IRS acceptance letter. Each week you see what is unsigned, what is filed and what has no letter yet.

An S corporation election has a short window. The IRS instructions for Form 2553 say it must be filed no more than two months and 15 days after the start of the tax year it takes effect, or any time during the year before. For a calendar-year business that lands in the middle of March, the busiest weeks of the year. The talk with the client happens in the fall, the form needs every owner's signature, and the new client who formed an LLC in January calls in April. Whether to elect is your advice. Tracking the date, the signatures and the acceptance letter is office work.

### Where elections go wrong
- The client agreed in a November call and nobody opened a task
- One owner's signature is missing and the form sits in a folder
- A new business has its own date, counted from the day it started
- The form was sent, and nobody kept proof of the day
- The acceptance letter went to the client, who never forwarded it
- Payroll was never set up, because nobody told the payroll provider

### What the list holds for each election
One row per client and election. Your tax software and client files stay where they are. The last day to file is worked out from the start of the tax year, and you check it for each client, because a new business or a fiscal year changes the count.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Client, entity type and the accountant responsible | An LLC and a corporation start from different places |
| Tax year the election is for, and its first day | The filing window is counted from this day |
| Last day to file | The date every reminder works back from |
| Each owner who has to sign, and whether they have | One missing signature holds the whole form |
| Date filed, how it was sent and proof of sending | If the IRS has no record, you can show the day |
| IRS acceptance letter: received or not | The election isn't finished until the letter is on file |
| Next steps: payroll set up, client told what changes | The election is the start of the work, not the end |

### How the workflow runs
1. Each fall, you get the list of business clients that are not S corporations, to mark the ones you want to review.
2. For each marked client, a task opens for the accountant, and the client is offered a time to talk.
3. When a client decides to elect, the row opens with the tax year and the last day to file.
4. The accountant prepares Form 2553 and approves it.
5. Each owner gets the form to sign electronically, with a plain note on what it is.
6. An owner who hasn't signed is reminded after three days and again after a week. After that, the accountant is told.
7. When all signatures are in, the accountant files the form and records the date and the proof of sending.
8. A new business client is added the day they sign up, with the date counted from when the business started.
9. If no acceptance letter is recorded after the time you set, the accountant gets a task to follow up.
10. When the letter arrives, it is filed, and the client and your payroll contact get the next-steps message you approved.
11. Every week from January you get the list: unsigned forms, forms ready to file and days left for each.
12. If AI drafts a message to a client, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with you
Whether a client should elect, whether the business is eligible, what goes on the form and what to do about a late election stay with the accountant. The IRS has a procedure for relief when an election is late, with conditions, and that call is yours too. The workflow counts days and chases signatures. It gives no tax advice and files nothing with the IRS. State rules differ, so any state election is a step you add. For the payments that follow, see [quarterly estimated tax payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/quarterly-estimated-tax-payment-reminders/). For a filing that comes back rejected, see [e-file rejection follow-up](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/e-file-rejection-client-follow-up/).

## FBAR season: every client asked, every account listed and every filing confirmed on one list
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/fbar-deadline-reminders-for-clients/

An FBAR workflow asks every client one question each January: did you have a foreign account last year? Clients who say yes get a short form for each account. Reminders go out until the details are in, the accountant reviews and files, and the confirmation is saved. Each week you see who hasn't answered, whose details are missing and what is filed.

The FBAR is easy to miss because it isn't part of the tax return. It is filed with FinCEN, on its own form, and the client who opened an account abroad three years ago doesn't think to mention it. The question sits on page six of the organizer, ticked "no" out of habit. The client who does say yes sends a photo of one statement and nothing about the other two accounts. The IRS says the report is due April 15, with an automatic extension to October 15. Deciding who has to file is your work. Asking everyone, every year, and chasing the account details is office work.

### Where FBARs go wrong
- The question is asked once, at onboarding, and never again
- A client inherits or opens an account abroad and tells nobody
- The client sends a year-end balance when you need the highest value in the year
- A joint account or an account the client only signs on is left off
- The return is filed in March and the FBAR is forgotten until fall
- The filing confirmation is never saved to the client's file

### What the list holds for each client
One row per client, and one line per account for clients who answer yes. Your tax software and client files stay where they are. The IRS says a US person files when the combined value of their foreign financial accounts was over $10,000 at any time in the calendar year, and the test is made again every year. Whether a client meets it, and which accounts count, is the accountant's decision.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Client and the accountant responsible | Someone owns each answer |
| This year's answer: yes, no, or not answered | A missing answer is not a no |
| Each account: bank, country, account number and type | The form needs every account, not only the largest |
| Highest value in the year, and the currency | The year-end balance is not the figure asked for |
| Joint owners, or signing authority only | These change who reports and how |
| Signed authorization for you to file | You can't file for the client without it |
| Date filed and the confirmation saved | If a question comes later, you can show the day |

### How the workflow runs
1. In January, every client gets a short message with one question about foreign accounts in the past year, in the plain words you approved.
2. A client who answers no is recorded with the date of the answer.
3. A client who answers yes gets a form with one section per account, already filled with last year's accounts to confirm or change.
4. A client who hasn't answered is reminded after a week and again after two. After that, the accountant is told.
5. Missing details are asked for by name: the highest value for one account, the country for another.
6. When the details are complete, the accountant gets a task to review them and decide whether a report is due.
7. The client gets the authorization to sign electronically, and is reminded until it is signed.
8. The accountant files with FinCEN and saves the confirmation. The row is marked filed with the date.
9. Every week from February you get the list: no answer, details missing, ready to review, filed.
10. On April 1, anything not filed is listed for the accountant, with what is still missing for each.
11. Clients still open after April 15 stay on the list through the extension, with a reminder schedule you set, until October.
12. If AI drafts a message to a client, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with you
Whether a client is a US person, which accounts count, how values are converted, whether a report is due and what to do about a missed year stay with the accountant. The workflow asks questions, collects answers and counts days. It gives no tax advice and files nothing with FinCEN. Account details are private, so the form and the list live in the accounts you already use, and only the people you choose can open them. Other foreign asset forms have their own rules and are steps you add. For other forms clients wait on, see [K-1 tracking](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/k1-tracking-tax-preparers/). For the payments that follow the return, see [quarterly estimated tax payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/quarterly-estimated-tax-payment-reminders/).

### When is the FBAR due?
The IRS says April 15 of the year after the calendar year reported, with an automatic extension to October 15. You don't need to ask for the extension. Check the date each year, because it moves when April 15 falls on a weekend or holiday.

Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/driver-cpc-periodic-training-tracking/

- A new card arrives and nobody records the new expiry date

### What the list holds for each driver
One row per driver. Your transport software and driver files stay where they are. GOV.UK says a course counts for 5 years from the day it was taken, and only approved courses with approved centres count. 7. After the course the driver is asked to confirm it was done. The hours are added when the office has checked.
8. Three months before a card date, anyone still short is listed for the manager every week until booked.
9. When the new card arrives, the driver sends a photo and the row gets the new date.
10. Every month you get one list: on track, short of hours, booked, and cards due in the next year.
11. If AI drafts a message to a driver, a person checks it before it is sent.

| Customer, site and supervisor | So the reminder reaches the person who can release the wearer |
| Wearer's name and job | People move between jobs with different masks |
| Make, model and size of the facepiece | A test covers the facepiece that was tested |
| Date and type of the last fit test | The annual date is counted from here |
| Medical clearance: yes or no, and the date | The evaluation comes before the fit test |
| Status: due, booked, tested, left the company | You can see what is open at each customer |

### How the workflow runs
1. Your past test records are added once, one row per wearer, from your forms or your testing software's export.
2. About six weeks before the first dates at a customer come up, the safety contact gets an email with the list of wearers who are due.
3. The email asks three things: who has left, who has joined, and whether any mask has changed.
4. New wearers and changed masks are added to the same visit, so they don't wait a year.
5. The customer picks a date from the times you offer. Your team confirms it.
6. A week before the visit, the customer gets the list again, with a note on who still needs medical clearance.
7. Wearers get a short reminder the day before, with your instructions for the day.
8. After the visit, your tester's records are filed against each row and the next date is set.
9. Anyone who missed the visit goes on a short list, and the customer is offered a catch-up date.
10. No answer after a week brings a reminder. After two, your team gets a task to call.
11. Every week you get one list: due in 60 days, booked, missed, and customers who haven't replied.
12. If AI drafts a message to a customer, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with you
The fit test itself, the choice of test method, and any advice on which respirator suits a job stay with your trained people. Medical clearance stays with the licensed health care professional. The workflow keeps dates, writes messages and files records. It doesn't decide who may wear a respirator. A test is also needed when a wearer's face changes in a way that could affect the fit, and the customer has to tell you about that. Some states run their own OSHA-approved plans and can add rules, so check the ones your customers work under. For other dated safety records, see [forklift operator evaluation reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/forklift-operator-evaluation-reminders/) and [bloodborne pathogens training reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/osha-bloodborne-pathogens-training-reminders-dental-offices/).

## Health surveillance recalls: every worker seen by the date your clinicians set
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/health-surveillance-recall-reminders-occupational-health/

A health surveillance recall workflow keeps one row per worker with the checks they are on and the next date your clinician set. It writes to each employer about six weeks ahead with the list of who is due, books the clinic day, chases changes to the list, and records who attended. Clinical findings stay in your clinical system.

You run health surveillance for sixty employers: hearing checks, hand-arm vibration, skin and breathing checks. Each worker has their own next date, set by your clinician after the last appointment. One employer has 140 workers on four checks at three sites. The dates are in your clinical system, the contact names are in a spreadsheet, and the clinic diary is somewhere else. An employer who isn't reminded doesn't call. They find out a year later, usually when someone asks to see the health records.

### Where recalls go wrong
- The recall is run once a year per employer, but workers' dates are spread over the year
- The employer's list of who is exposed to what is two years old
- New starters wait for the next annual visit, with no first check on file
- A clinician asks to see someone again in six months, and it's written only in the notes
- Twelve people miss the clinic day and nobody books a second one
- The reminder goes to an HR contact who has left

### What the list holds, and what it doesn't
One row per worker and check. The list is for booking, so it holds dates and attendance only. Clinical findings and anything confidential stay in your clinical system. HSE's guidance says the employer keeps a health record of the outcome of surveillance, for the period the relevant regulations set, for example 40 years under COSHH. Your outcome reports to the employer go out the way they do today.

## SWPPP inspections: every site inspected on its schedule, with the report and the fixes on file
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/swppp-inspection-reminders-and-reports/

A SWPPP inspection workflow keeps one row per site with the schedule from its permit. It reminds the inspector before each routine inspection, asks for a rain check after a storm, collects the report from a phone form with photos, and follows each problem until someone marks it fixed. Each week you see what is late.

A construction stormwater permit sets how often a site must be inspected and what goes in the report. Under EPA's Construction General Permit, the standard choice is at least every 7 calendar days, or every 14 days plus an inspection within 24 hours of a storm of 0.25 inches or more. Most states issue their own permit with their own schedule. You have nine open sites under two superintendents. The inspections happen, mostly. The reports are on paper in the trucks, the silt fence that was down on Tuesday is still down, and the rain on Saturday is nobody's job.

### Where stormwater inspections slip
- The routine inspection is on one person's calendar, and that person is on vacation
- It rains over the weekend and nobody checks whether the storm counts
- The report is filled in on paper and reaches the binder two weeks later
- A problem is written on the report and nobody is told to fix it
- The fix is done, but no date or photo shows it
- A site is stabilized, the notice to end coverage isn't filed, and the inspections quietly stop

### What the list holds for each site
One row per site. The schedule comes from that site's own permit and its SWPPP, and a person on your team enters it. The workflow follows the row and never guesses the rule.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Site, permit and permit number | State and EPA permits set different schedules |
| Routine schedule, as your permit states it | The reminders follow this |
| Rain rule: how much rain, and how soon to inspect | Taken from the permit, not from memory |
| Inspector, and a back-up | Vacations happen every year |
| Last inspection and next one due | You can see a late site at a glance |
| Open problems and who must fix them | A report with no follow-up fixes nothing |
| Status: active, stabilized, coverage ended | So inspections stop only when a person says so |

### How the workflow runs
1. Each open site is added once, with the schedule and the rain rule from its permit.
2. The inspector gets a reminder the day before each routine inspection, with a link to the report form.
3. The form follows your report template: date, weather, each control checked, problems found, photos and a signature.
4. A submitted report is filed in the site's folder as a PDF, and the next date is set.
5. If no report arrives by the end of the due day, the back-up and the superintendent are told the next morning.
6. After rain, the inspector is asked to enter the reading from the site's rain gauge. If it reaches the amount on the row, a rain inspection is opened with its own deadline.
7. Each problem on a report becomes a task for the named crew or subcontractor, with the photo and a due date you set.
8. The task stays open until someone sends a photo of the fix. A person on your team checks it and closes it.
9. When a site is stabilized, a person changes its status. The workflow never ends inspections by itself.
10. Every week you get one list: late inspections, open problems and how old they are, and sites close to the end.
11. If AI drafts a message to a subcontractor, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with you
Reading the permit, deciding who is qualified to inspect, judging whether a control is working and choosing the fix stay with you and your inspector. The rain reading comes from your own gauge or the source your permit allows. The workflow reminds, files and follows up. It doesn't inspect a site, and it gives no legal advice about your permit. Permits are reissued and changed from time to time, so check the current version for each site. For other site paperwork, see [construction daily site reports](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/construction-daily-site-reports/) and [building permit and inspection tracking](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/building-permit-inspection-tracking-contractors/).

## Clearinghouse annual queries: every CDL driver queried before the 12 months run out
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/clearinghouse-annual-query-tracking/

A Clearinghouse annual query workflow keeps one row per CDL driver with the date of the last query and the consent on file. It reminds the office weeks before a driver's 12 months end, asks for a missing consent form, and records the new date once your team has run the query. Your team runs every query and makes every decision.

Under 49 CFR 382.701, an employer of CDL drivers queries the FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse at least once a year for each driver it employs. FMCSA counts this on a rolling 12 months, and a pre-employment query starts the clock. That means every driver has a different date. A fleet of fourteen drivers hired across six years has fourteen dates, and most small fleets try to fix that by querying everybody in one week each winter. Then a driver hired in March is forgotten, or the consent form for a limited query can't be found.

### Where annual queries slip
- Everyone is queried in one batch, and drivers hired later in the year fall outside it
- The date of the last query lives in one person's memory or in an old email
- The driver's consent for limited queries was signed on paper and nobody can find it
- A limited query shows that information exists, and the full query needs the driver to log in and consent from the road
- The query plan has run out and nobody noticed until the day of the batch
- A driver leaves and comes back, and nobody knows which date counts

### What the list holds for each driver
One row per CDL driver. A person on your team enters the dates from your Clearinghouse query history, and the workflow follows the row.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Driver, hire date and status | Only current drivers are reminded |
| Last query date and type (pre-employment, limited or full) | The 12 months run from this date |
| Next query due | The reminders follow this |
| Limited query consent: on file, and until when | A limited query needs it first |
| Where the signed consent is saved | So anyone can find it in an audit |
| Who runs queries, and a back-up | One person on vacation shouldn't stop it |
| Result recorded by your team: done, or full query needed | The row shows what still has to happen |

### How the workflow runs
1. Each CDL driver is added once, with the last query date taken from your Clearinghouse history.
2. A new hire's row starts from the pre-employment query date your team enters.
3. About six weeks before a driver's date, the office gets a reminder with the driver's name and the consent status.
4. If no consent for limited queries is on file, or it is about to end, the driver gets the form to sign and a reminder until it is back.
5. The signed consent is saved in the driver's folder and the row is updated.
6. Your team runs the query in the Clearinghouse and enters the date. The workflow sets the next one.
7. If your team marks that a full query is needed, the driver gets a plain message asking them to log in and respond to the consent request. It says nothing about why.
8. If a date is two weeks away and no query is recorded, the back-up and the owner are told.
9. Every month you get one list: queries due in the next 60 days, consents missing, and anything overdue.
10. If AI drafts a message to a driver, a person checks it before it is sent.

### What stays with you
Running the query, reading the result, and every decision about whether a driver can drive stay with you or your consortium. The workflow never logs in to the Clearinghouse and never sees a result beyond the word your team enters. It keeps dates, asks for forms and reminds people. It is not compliance advice: the rules are in 49 CFR Part 382, and they change from time to time. If you also keep medical cards and motor vehicle records by hand, see [driver qualification file tracking](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/driver-qualification-file-expiry-tracking/). For fuel tax and heavy vehicle use tax dates, see [IFTA and Form 2290 filing reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ifta-and-form-2290-filing-reminders-trucking-clients/).

If your consortium already tracks every driver's date and tells you in time, you may not need this, and we'll say so on the call.

### How often must an employer query the Clearinghouse for a CDL driver?
At least once a year for each CDL driver it employs, under 49 CFR 382.701. FMCSA counts a rolling 12 months from the last query, and a pre-employment query starts the clock.

## Medicare Annual Wellness Visit recall: every eligible patient invited when the date comes
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/medicare-annual-wellness-visit-recall/

An Annual Wellness Visit recall workflow keeps one row per Medicare patient with the date of the last wellness visit and the first date the next one can be booked. It sends a plain invitation to book, follows up with patients who don't reply, sends the pre-visit questionnaire, and shows the front desk who is still open.

Medicare Part B covers a yearly wellness visit once every 12 months. A patient's first one can't take place within 12 months of their Part B enrollment or their "Welcome to Medicare" visit, and Medicare Advantage plans may count the year differently. So every patient becomes eligible on a different day. In a practice with 900 Medicare patients, the visit is usually offered only when the patient happens to come in for something else. - The patient thinks it is a full physical and arrives expecting one
- The health questionnaire is handed over in the waiting room and takes up the visit
- A patient had the visit somewhere else this year and nobody recorded it

One row per Medicare patient, built from a report out of your practice software. It holds dates and booking status only. No diagnoses, results or notes are copied into it.

## HVAC warranty registration: every install registered before the manufacturer's window closes
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/hvac-equipment-warranty-registration-tracking/

An HVAC warranty registration workflow keeps one row per installed system with the install date, the serial numbers and the manufacturer's registration deadline. It collects the serial numbers from the installer on the day, reminds the office before the window closes, and sends the homeowner the confirmation once a person has registered the equipment.

You install a furnace and a condenser on a Tuesday. The crew moves to the next house, and the serial numbers are on a photo in somebody's phone. Many manufacturers give the longer parts warranty only if the equipment is registered within a set window after installation, often 60 or 90 days. In July nobody in the office has a spare hour. Four years later a compressor fails, the homeowner calls, and you both learn the unit was never registered. The registration takes five minutes. What is missing is a list that says which installs are still open and how many days each one has left.

### Where warranty registration slips
- Serial numbers are on a phone photo or a paper job sheet, not in the office
- The installer thinks the office registers, and the office thinks the homeowner does
- Busy season: installs go in faster than anyone can register them
- Each brand has its own portal, its own window and its own rules
- A system has two or three serial numbers and only one gets registered
- The homeowner's email address was never collected, so the portal can't send a confirmation
- Nobody can show the homeowner proof when a part fails years later

### What the list holds for each install
One row per installed system. Your office sets the registration window for each brand you sell, taken from that brand's warranty document.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Customer, address, email and phone | The registration needs them, and so does the confirmation |
| Install date | The window starts here |
| Brand and the window your office set for it | The deadline is worked out from these two |
| Model and serial number of each unit | Outdoor unit, indoor unit and coil are registered separately |
| Photo of each data plate | A person can check a serial number that looks wrong |
| Who registers: your office or the homeowner | No install is left between two people |
| Status: waiting for serials, ready, registered, proof sent | The weekly list is built from this |

### How the workflow runs
1. When a job is marked as installed, a row is opened with the install date and the deadline for that brand.
2. The installer gets a short form on their phone: a photo of each data plate and the serial numbers.
3. If the form isn't filled in by the next morning, the installer is reminded, and after that the service manager is told.
4. The office gets a daily list of installs that are ready to register, with everything needed on one screen.
5. A person on your team registers the equipment on the manufacturer's site and saves the confirmation. If AI reads the serial numbers from the photos first, a person checks them before anything is submitted.
6. The homeowner gets an email with the confirmation and a plain line about what the warranty covers, in wording you approved.
7. Two weeks before a window closes, any install that is still open goes to the service manager.
8. Every week you get one list: installs waiting for serial numbers, installs ready to register, and days left on each.

### What stays with you
The registration itself is done by a person on your team, on the manufacturer's own site. The workflow doesn't log in to a manufacturer portal, doesn't decide what a warranty covers and doesn't promise that a claim will be accepted. Warranty terms and registration windows differ by brand and product line, and some states don't allow a registration requirement at all, so take the window from each manufacturer's warranty document. ## Sales tax exemption certificates: one on file for every exempt customer, and renewed before it runs out
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/sales-tax-exemption-certificate-tracking/

An exemption certificate tracking workflow keeps one row per tax-exempt customer and state, with the certificate on file and its end date where there is one. It asks new customers for a certificate before their first untaxed invoice, requests a new one before an old one runs out, and lists customers who are invoiced without tax and have no current certificate.

Rules on how long a certificate lasts differ by state and by type of certificate, and your customers don't track those dates for you. The fix is plain: one list of exempt customers, the document behind each, and somebody who asks again in time.

### Where exemption certificates slip
- A customer is set to "exempt" in the accounting software before any certificate arrives

- A customer ships to a new state and nobody asks for that state's form
- The form is unsigned, or the business name doesn't match the customer on the invoice
- A customer changes name or is sold, and the old certificate stays on file
- The only full check happens when an auditor asks

| Status: current, due soon, missing, sent to accountant | The monthly list is built from this |

4. A person on your team checks it: right state, signed, name matches. If AI reads the dates and the registration number from the form first, a person confirms them.
5. If something is wrong, the customer gets a short note saying exactly what to fix.
6. Sixty days before an end date or a review date, the customer is asked for a new certificate. A second request goes a month later.
7. If nothing arrives, the row goes to the person who owns the account, with the open invoices next to it.
8. Whether to start charging tax on the next invoice is your decision. The workflow changes nothing in your accounting software.
9. Every month you and your accountant get one list: missing, due soon, and how long each has been open.

### What stays with you
Whether a certificate is valid, which form a state accepts and whether a sale is exempt are questions for your accountant or the state's department of revenue. It makes sure a document exists for every customer you treat as exempt, and that somebody looks at it again on a date. ## Year-end donation receipts: every donor's statement checked, sent in January and answered
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/year-end-donation-receipts-nonprofits/

A year-end donation receipt workflow builds one giving statement per donor from your records, in wording your accountant approved. It finds donors with a missing address or an unmatched gift in December, has a person approve the statements in January, sends each one by email or prints it for mail, and tracks bounces and donor questions until they are closed.

It is the second week of January. Your bookkeeper is a volunteer, or works one day a week. Giving came in through the online platform, by check, in cash envelopes and as two gifts of stock. Donors start asking for their statement because their tax preparer wants it. A donor needs a written acknowledgment from you for any single gift of $250 or more, and without it they can lose the deduction. Nobody fines the organization for a late statement. The donor is the one who pays for it, and donors remember. Most of the work is not the letter. It is finding the gifts with no name, the donors with no address and the couple who gave under two spellings.

### Where year-end statements slip
- Gifts sit in three places: the online giving platform, the bank deposits and a spreadsheet
- The same donor appears twice, under two spellings or two email addresses
- Checks were recorded as one deposit, with no donor names
- A donor moved, and the statement goes to the old address
- Non-cash gifts are in the books with a dollar value and no description
- A dinner ticket or an auction item is counted as a full gift
- Statements go out in February, after donors have asked twice
- Bounced emails are never followed up

### What goes on each donor's row
One row per donor or household. The statement wording is set once with your accountant, and the workflow fills in the gifts.
| On the row | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| Donor or household name, as they want it printed | Couples often give under two names |
| Email and mailing address, with the date last confirmed | Old addresses are found in December, not in February |
| Each gift: date, amount and how it was given | The statement lists gifts one by one |
| Non-cash gifts: a description in words | Your accountant decides how these appear |
| Anything the donor received in return | Tickets, dinners and auction items need a person's eye |
| How the statement goes out: email or mail | The print list is built from this |
| Status: to fix, ready, approved, sent, bounced, question open | You can see what is left on any day |

### How the workflow runs
1. In early December, exports from your giving platform and your books are put on one list, donor by donor.
2. Likely duplicates, gifts with no donor and donors with no address are put on a short fix list for your bookkeeper.
3. Donors whose address hasn't been confirmed this year get a short message asking them to check it.
4. After the last deposit of the year is recorded, a statement is drafted for each donor from the template your accountant approved. If AI helps match names or tidy descriptions, a person checks the result.
5. Your treasurer or bookkeeper reads the statements and approves them. Nothing is sent before that.
6. Approved statements go out by email. Donors who want paper are put on a print list with mailing labels.
7. A bounced email goes back on the fix list the same day, with the donor's phone number next to it.
8. Donor replies go to one inbox. Each question is logged against the donor's row and closed by a person.
9. At the end of January you get one list: sent, bounced, questions open, and statements reissued.

### What stays with you
What the statement says, how non-cash gifts and benefits to the donor are described, and whether a payment was a gift at all are decided by your treasurer and your accountant. The IRS lists what a written acknowledgment must contain in Publication 1771. The workflow doesn't value a gift, doesn't give tax advice to donors and doesn't send a statement nobody approved. It makes sure every donor's gifts are on one row, that a person has read the statement, and that it reaches the donor. For other nonprofit dates, see [Form 990 deadline reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/form-990-deadline-reminders-nonprofit-accountants/) and [grant reporting deadline reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/grant-reporting-deadline-reminders/).
