### How long until Facebook shows the new image?
After you ask the Sharing Debugger to scrape the page again, new shares usually use the new preview straight away. Posts already published may keep the old one.

### Why does WhatsApp still show the old preview?
WhatsApp keeps its own copy for a while and has no public refresh tool. New chats usually pick up changes sooner. Adding a small parameter to the link (like ?v=2) makes it fetch a fresh preview.

### Do I need different images for each platform?
Usually not. One 1200 × 630 image works well across Facebook, LinkedIn, X and WhatsApp.

## How to start a loyalty card scheme for a small business (and make it pay)
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/loyalty-card-scheme-small-business/ (2026-11-22)

A simple stamp card works when the reward is something customers want, the finish line is reachable within a few months, and the rules are printed on the back. Pick the number of stamps from how often people visit (10 for weekly regulars, 5 or 6 for monthly visits), stamp the first box on the day you hand the card over, and count how many cards come back finished.

Loyalty apps cost a monthly fee and ask customers to download something. A paper stamp card costs a few pence, works for every customer on day one, and sits in their wallet as a reminder of you.
Here's how to set one up so it actually brings people back: the numbers to pick, the wording, the one trick that makes more cards get finished, and how to know if it's paying for itself.

### 1. Pick a reward people actually want
The reward is the whole point, so make it something a regular would be pleased to get, and say it in plain words: "a free coffee of your choice", "a free cut", "50% off your next treatment". Vague rewards like "a surprise gift" get fewer people collecting.
Work out the cost honestly. On a 10-stamp coffee card the reward is one free drink after nine paid ones, roughly a 10% discount for your most loyal customers, given only to people who came back nine times.

### 2. Choose how many stamps from how often people visit
A good test: a regular should be able to finish the card within three or four months. If it would take a year, most cards will be lost before they're full.
| Business | Typical visit | Stamps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Café, bakery, sandwich shop | Several times a week | 8 to 10 |
| Car wash, dog groomer, nail bar | Every 2 to 4 weeks | 6 to 8 |
| Hairdresser, barber, beauty salon | Every 4 to 8 weeks | 5 or 6 |
| Shop with occasional purchases | Monthly or less | 5, with a stamp per purchase over a set amount |

### 3. Give the first stamp free
This is the single most useful trick. In a field study by Nunes and Drèze (Journal of Consumer Research, 2006), car wash customers got either an 8-stamp card or a 10-stamp card with 2 stamps already filled. Both needed 8 more washes. 34% of the pre-stamped cards were completed, against 19% of the blank ones, and they were finished faster.
So print a 10-stamp card, stamp the first box (or two) when you hand it over, and say so: "Here's your card, the first one's on us."

### 4. Put the rules on the back
Clear rules stop awkward conversations at the till. Keep them short:
- What earns a stamp: one per visit, or one per purchase over £5 / $5
- How long the card lasts: 12 months from the first stamp is common
- That the reward has no cash value
- A line for the customer's name, so a found card can be returned
- Your phone number and a QR code to your website or booking page

### 5. Stop people faking stamps
Use a self-inking stamp or a hole punch with an unusual shape that only you have, and initial each stamp if you're worried. In practice most small businesses find a few faked stamps cost far less than the extra visits the card brings.

### 6. Check that it pays
1. Count the cards you hand out each month (a tally on a sticky note is enough).
2. Keep every finished card when you give the reward, and count them monthly.
3. Compare: if 100 cards went out and 20 came back full, those 20 customers made 9 paid visits each to earn one reward.
4. If almost nobody finishes, cut the number of stamps or improve the reward before giving up on the idea.

### Free tool: make the card in two minutes
The free [loyalty card maker](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/loyalty-card-maker/) draws a print-ready stamp card: 5 to 12 stamps with the last one as the reward, six stamp pictures (coffee cup, scissors, paw print and more), your colours and logo, and the rules and a QR code on the back. Print 10 on A4 or send the files to a printer. Make matching [business cards](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/business-card-maker/) too, and a [Google review link](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/google-review-link-generator/) to ask the regulars who finish a card for a review.

### Is a paper loyalty card better than an app?
For most small, local businesses, yes to start with. It costs almost nothing, needs no download, and works for every customer straight away. An app makes more sense once you want to send offers to card holders.

### Should the reward be a freebie or a discount?
A freebie of something they already buy is easiest to understand and feels more generous than a percentage. "Your 10th coffee free" beats "10% off" even when the cost to you is similar.

### What if a customer loses their card?
Most businesses simply start a new card, sometimes with a stamp or two as goodwill. Printing a name line and your phone number on the back means a found card often makes its way back.

### Do loyalty cards need terms and conditions?
A few short rules on the back are enough for a simple stamp card: what earns a stamp, how long it's valid and that the reward has no cash value. Keep them fair and apply them the same way to everyone.

## What to put on a business card, and what to leave off
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-put-on-a-business-card/ (2026-11-22)

A business card needs your name, what you do, the business name, and one or two ways to reach you, usually a mobile number and an email or website. Put a QR code on the back that saves your contact to the person's phone. Leave off anything they won't act on: fax numbers, every social account, long addresses and slogans.

A business card has one job: make it easy for someone who met you to get back in touch next week. Most cards fail at that because they try to say everything.
Here's what to include, what to cut, the standard sizes, and the one addition that stops your card ending up forgotten in a drawer.

### What to put on the front
| Line | Example | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Your name | Sarah Jones | People remember people, not businesses |
| What you do | Owner and senior stylist | So they know why to call you |
| Business name or logo | Bloom Hair Studio | What they'll search for later |
| Mobile number | 07700 900123 | The fastest way to reach you |
| Email or website | bloomhair.co.uk | For people who'd rather not call |
| Area or address (optional) | York city centre | Only if customers come to you |

### What to leave off
- Fax numbers and landlines nobody answers
- Every social account you have. Pick the one where customers actually find you, or none
- A list of all your services. One line on what you do is enough
- Slogans and long mission statements
- Personal details you wouldn't want on a noticeboard

### Put a QR code on the back
Most cards are looked at once, then lost. A QR code on the back fixes that: one scan with a phone camera and your name, number, email and website are saved straight into their contacts. That uses the vCard format, the contact file every phone understands.
If you'd rather, point the QR code at your website or booking page instead. Either way, scan it with your own phone before you print a box of 500.

### Sizes and printing
For a handful of cards, print 10 on A4 on thick card (300 gsm or more) and cut carefully. For a box, send print-quality images to any online printer. Keep text at least 3 to 4 mm from the edges so nothing is cut off.
| Where | Standard size | At 300 dpi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| UK, Europe, Israel | 85 × 55 mm | 1004 × 650 pixels |
| US and Canada | 3.5 × 2 in (88.9 × 50.8 mm) | 1050 × 600 pixels |

### Wording tips
1. Write what you do in the words customers use: "Boiler repairs and servicing", not "Thermal comfort solutions".
2. Use one font and two colours at most. Contrast matters more than style.
3. Keep each line short enough to read at arm's length.
4. Make the phone number the easiest thing on the card to read.

### Free tool: make yours in two minutes
The free [business card maker](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/business-card-maker/) draws both sides at print quality: three layouts, five colour themes, your logo, and a QR code that saves your contact or opens your website. Download the images, print 10 on A4 with the back lined up for double-sided printing, or download the contact as a .vcf file. Matching tools: an [email signature](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/email-signature-generator/), a [QR code](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/qr-code-generator/) for flyers, and a [loyalty stamp card](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/loyalty-card-maker/) for regulars.

### Are business cards still worth it?
For local and trade businesses, yes. They're cheap, they work at events, on site and at the till, and with a QR code on the back they put your contact straight into someone's phone.

### Should I put my home address on my business card?
Only if customers need to come to you. Otherwise your area ("Serving Leeds and Bradford") is enough, and safer.

### Matte or gloss?
Matte is easier to write on and looks calmer; gloss makes colours and photos pop. For most trades and services, matte or soft-touch reads as more professional.

### What should the QR code on a business card link to?
Your contact details (so they're saved in one scan) or your booking page. Avoid linking to a homepage that makes people hunt for how to reach you.

## How to sell gift vouchers as a small business, without a gift card system
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/sell-gift-vouchers-small-business/ (2026-11-22)

Decide the amounts or services you'll sell, give each voucher a unique code and a clear expiry date, take payment the way you normally do, and keep one list of every code, its value and whether it's been used. In the US, gift cards generally can't expire within 5 years of purchase. In the UK there's no general minimum expiry, but VAT timing depends on whether the voucher is single-purpose or multi-purpose.

Gift vouchers bring in money before the work is done, and they bring in new customers: the person who receives one often hasn't been to you before. Around birthdays, Mother's Day and Christmas they can be a real boost.
You don't need a gift card platform to sell them. Here's a simple way to run vouchers properly, the rules to know, and how to stop copies being used twice.

### 1. Decide what you'll sell
- Set amounts (£25, £50, £100) work for any business and are easiest to manage
- A named service ("one full colour and cut", "a 60-minute massage") feels more like a present
- If you sell a service, say whether the voucher covers its price on the day or the price when bought

### 2. Make every voucher unique
Each voucher needs its own code, such as BLOOM-7K3Q, plus the value, who it's for, and the expiry date printed clearly. A code on every voucher means a copy or a screenshot can only be used once, because you check it against your list.

### 3. Keep one record
A spreadsheet is enough. When a voucher is redeemed, find the code, check the date, and fill in "Used on". If someone uses part of a money voucher, note the balance left.
| Code | Value | Sold on | Expires | Used on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BLOOM-7K3Q | £50 | 02/12/2026 | 02/12/2027 |  |
| BLOOM-P2MX | Colour and cut | 05/12/2026 | 05/12/2027 | 14/01/2027 |

### 4. Choose the expiry date (and know the rules)
- US: under the federal gift card rules (Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.20), a gift certificate or gift card generally can't expire earlier than 5 years after it was issued or money was last loaded. Some states go further, so check yours.
- UK: there's no general legal minimum, but 12 months is the least customers expect and 24 months feels generous. Print the date on the voucher and stick to it.
- Wherever you are, put the expiry and any conditions on the voucher itself, not only on your website.

### 5. VAT on vouchers in the UK
Since 1 January 2019, HMRC splits vouchers into two kinds. A single-purpose voucher is one where the VAT due is known when it's sold (for example, a voucher for one specific standard-rated service at your salon): VAT is due when you sell it. A multi-purpose voucher can be spent on things with different VAT rates: VAT is due when it's redeemed. HMRC's VAT Notice 700/7 covers this. If you're VAT-registered and unsure which you sell, ask your accountant before the busy season.

### 6. Make selling them easy
1. Add a "Gift vouchers" line to your website, booking page and social bios.
2. Take payment by card, bank transfer or payment link, as you do now.
3. Send the voucher as an image by email or WhatsApp straight away, or print it on card for collection.
4. Remind your customers two or three weeks before key dates.
5. When the voucher is used, welcome the new customer and ask for their details so you can keep in touch (with their consent).

### Free tool: make the voucher in a minute
The free [gift voucher maker](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/gift-voucher-maker/) draws a voucher with the value or service, who it's for and from, a message, your colours and an expiry date, and gives every voucher its own code plus a record line you can paste into your spreadsheet. Download it as an image or print it. To run the rest of your money admin in one place, try the [income and expenses spreadsheet](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/income-and-expenses-spreadsheet/).

### Do I have to give change on a gift voucher?
That's your choice; say it on the voucher. Many small businesses keep the remaining balance on the voucher record instead of giving cash.

### Can I refuse an expired voucher?
If the expiry date and terms were clear when it was sold and they're within the law where you trade, generally yes. Many businesses honour recently expired vouchers anyway as goodwill.

### What happens to vouchers that are never used?
The money stays with you, but how you account for it, and in the UK how VAT applies, depends on the voucher type. Ask your accountant how to treat unused vouchers at year end.

### Should vouchers be printed or digital?
Both work. Digital is instant for last-minute buyers; printed vouchers in an envelope feel more like a present. Offering both sells more.

## What to put on a receipt: a checklist for small businesses
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-put-on-a-receipt/ (2026-11-22)

A receipt should show your business name and contact details, a receipt number, the date, what was paid for, the amount, how it was paid and, if you know it, the customer's name. If you're VAT registered in the UK, add your VAT number, the VAT rate and the VAT amount. For sales of £250 or less including VAT, HMRC allows a simpler VAT invoice.

A receipt is the customer's proof they paid, and your record that money came in. Getting it right takes a minute, and it saves you the "did I pay you for that?" message three months later.
Here's what to include, how a receipt differs from an invoice, the VAT rules for UK businesses, and how long to keep your copies.

### The checklist
| Line | Example | Needed? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Business name and contact | Bloom Hair Studio, 14 High Street, York | Always |
| Receipt number | R-0042 | Strongly recommended |
| Date of payment | 22 November 2026 | Always |
| What was paid for | Cut and colour, conditioning treatment | Always |
| Amount paid | £100.00 | Always |
| Payment method | Card, cash, bank transfer | Recommended |
| Customer name | Emma Wilson | If you know it |
| VAT number, rate and amount | GB123456789, 20%, £16.67 | If VAT registered |
| Balance left to pay | £50.00 still to pay | For part payments and deposits |

### Receipt or invoice?
An invoice asks for payment. A receipt confirms payment has been made. If a customer pays on the spot, a receipt is all you need. If you bill first, send the invoice, then a receipt (or an invoice marked "Paid") when the money arrives.
For deposits and part payments, the receipt should say what has been paid and what's still owed. That one line prevents most payment disputes.

### VAT receipts in the UK
If you're VAT registered and a customer asks for a VAT receipt, it needs your VAT number, the VAT rate and the VAT amount. HMRC's record-keeping notice (VAT Notice 700/21, section 4.5) lets businesses that aren't retailers issue a simplified VAT invoice when the supply is £250 or less including VAT. It must show your name, address and VAT number, the time of supply, a description of what was supplied, and for each VAT rate, the total including VAT and the rate charged.
If your prices include VAT, the VAT is worked out of the total, not added on top. At 20%, the VAT in a £100 total is £100 ÷ 1.2 = £83.33 net, so £16.67 VAT. Not VAT registered? Don't show VAT at all.

### Numbering and keeping copies
1. Use one simple sequence for every receipt, like R-0001, R-0002. Don't restart it each year unless your accountant asks you to.
2. Keep a copy of every receipt you issue, as a PDF or in your accounts software.
3. Note each receipt in one place, such as your income spreadsheet, with the date, amount and payment method.
4. Keep your records for as long as the rules require. In the UK, that's at least 5 years after the 31 January Self Assessment deadline for sole traders, and 6 years for limited companies. In the US, the IRS says to keep records that support income for as long as they may be needed for a tax return, usually at least 3 years.

### Paper slip or PDF?
Most customers are happy with a PDF by email or a photo of the receipt in WhatsApp, and it's quicker for you. Keep a till-slip option for walk-in customers and anyone who asks for paper. An 80 mm receipt printer prints the same receipt as a slip.

### Free tool: a receipt in one minute
The free [receipt generator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/receipt-generator/) makes a receipt with your items, VAT included or added, the payment method, part payments and a "Paid" stamp. Save it as a PDF, print a till slip, or copy it as text for an email. The "Next receipt" button moves the number on for you. To ask for payment first, use the [invoice generator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/free-invoice-generator/), and track what came in with the [income and expenses spreadsheet](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/income-and-expenses-spreadsheet/).

### Is a bank transfer confirmation a receipt?
It proves money left the customer's account, but it isn't your record of what it was for. Send your own receipt that says what was paid for and links it to the invoice or booking.

### Do I have to give a receipt?
Customers expect one and many will ask. VAT-registered businesses in the UK must issue a VAT invoice to VAT-registered business customers. For everyone else, a receipt is simply good practice and good records.

### Can a receipt be handwritten?
Yes, as long as it has the same details: number, date, what was paid for, amount and your business details. A printed or PDF receipt is easier to read and to keep.

### What if I made a mistake on a receipt?
Don't edit the old one. Issue a new receipt with a new number and a note that it replaces receipt R-0041, and keep both in your records.

## How to make a price list that sells
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-make-a-price-list/ (2026-11-22)

Group your services into a few clear sections, write each one in the words customers use, and give a price for every line, using "from" only where the price really varies, with a short note on why. Include any fee everyone has to pay in the price itself. Then put the same list everywhere customers look: your website, Google profile, Instagram and WhatsApp.

"How much is it?" is the most common first message a service business gets. A clear price list answers it before anyone has to ask, and the people who get in touch after reading it are already happy with the price.
Here's how to structure it, how to handle prices that vary, what UK rules say about showing the full price, and where to post it so it actually gets seen.

### Structure: sections, not one long list
- Three to six sections, in the order customers think: "Cuts", "Colour", "Treatments", not your internal codes
- Most popular services first in each section
- Each line: the service, the price, and an optional short note ("includes wash", "60 minutes")
- Your contact line at the bottom: how to book, phone number, website

### Prices that vary
Use "from £70" when the price really depends on something, like hair length or the size of a room, and say what it depends on in the note. A range ("£150-220") works when the spread is narrow. If every line says "from" or "price on request", people assume the worst and message a competitor instead.
For jobs that are always quoted, like a full rewire, show a typical example ("Typical 3-bed rewire: £4,000-6,000") and offer a free quote. A rough number beats no number.

### Show the full price
In the UK, the CMA's price transparency guidance under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 says the total price should normally include any unavoidable, or mandatory, charges. If every customer has to pay a booking fee, a call-out charge or VAT, build it into the price you show rather than adding it at the end. Optional extras can be listed separately.
The same idea is good practice everywhere, and some US states now require total pricing too. For consumers, show prices including VAT or sales tax where that's the norm.

### Make it easy to read
1. Line prices up on the right so people can scan them.
2. Use one font and one accent colour that matches your shop or logo.
3. Leave space between sections. A crowded list looks expensive and confusing.
4. Put the date at the bottom, or update it every time prices change, so old screenshots don't cause arguments.

### Where to put it
| Place | Format | Tip |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Website | Text on a page, not only an image | Search engines and AI assistants can read text |
| Google Business Profile | Services and prices section, plus a photo | Shown when people search your name |
| Instagram | Square or story image, pinned post | Add it to a highlight called "Prices" |
| WhatsApp | Image you send in one tap | Save it as a quick reply for "how much?" |
| In the shop | Printed A4 or A5 | By the till or the waiting area |

### Free tool: make it in five minutes
The free [price list maker](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/price-list-maker/) lays out your sections and prices, with notes, colours and your contact line, and downloads it as an A4 page to print, an Instagram post, or a story for Instagram and WhatsApp status. To share it on social media with a headline, try the [social post maker](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/social-post-maker/), and add a [QR code](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/qr-code-generator/) to the printed copy that links to your booking page. Raising prices? The [price increase letter generator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/price-increase-letter-generator/) writes the message to your regulars.

### Should I put prices on my website?
For most small service businesses, yes. It saves you time answering the same question, and the people who contact you have already accepted the price. If every job is different, show typical prices or ranges.

### Does showing prices lose customers to cheaper competitors?
Price shoppers will find a cheaper option either way. A clear price list with what's included tends to bring people who care about quality and don't want surprises.

### How often should I update my price list?
Whenever a price changes, and check it at least once a year. Update it everywhere at once: website, Google, social media and the printed copy.

### Should prices end in 9?
For services, round numbers (£45, £80) tend to look more premium and are easier to read. Charm prices like £44.99 suit retail goods more than services.

## How to write a cancellation policy for appointments
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-write-a-cancellation-policy/ (2026-11-22)

A good cancellation policy says how much notice you need (24 hours is most common), how to cancel, what happens to a deposit, and what a late cancellation or no-show costs. Keep fees in line with what you actually lose, show the policy before people book, and repeat it in one line in the booking confirmation and reminder.

Every empty slot from a no-show is time you can't sell again. A clear cancellation policy doesn't stop all of them, but it changes behaviour: people who know a slot is held for them, and what a no-show costs, are far more likely to let you know.
Here's what to put in it, how strict to be, the UK rules worth knowing, and how to make it work without awkward conversations.

### What to include
| Part | Example wording |
| --- | --- |
| Notice needed | Please give at least 24 hours' notice to cancel or move. |
| How to cancel | Call 01904 555123 or reply to your reminder. |
| Free changes | Cancelling or moving with 24 hours' notice or more is free. |
| Late cancellation | Cancellations with less notice are charged 50% of the price. |
| No-show | Missed appointments are charged in full. |
| Deposit | A £20 deposit secures your booking and counts towards the price. |
| Late arrival | If you're more than 15 minutes late, we may need to shorten your appointment. |
| Exceptions | Emergencies and illness happen. Get in touch and we'll always be fair. |

### How much notice to ask for
- 24 hours: the usual choice for salons, clinics, tutors and trades. It gives you a real chance to refill the slot
- 48 hours: long or expensive appointments, like a colour, a tattoo session or a half-day job
- 7 days: things you prepare or buy materials for, like events or custom work
- More than 72 hours for a normal appointment tends to put people off booking at all

### Fees and deposits: keep them fair
In the UK, the Consumer Rights Act 2015 says unfair terms in consumer contracts aren't binding on the consumer. A cancellation fee is much easier to defend when it was clearly agreed before booking and reflects what you really lose, for example the price of the slot minus anything you save. Charging more than the appointment itself is likely to be unfair.
In practice, fees you have to chase often go unpaid. A small deposit taken at booking, kept for a late cancellation or no-show and otherwise taken off the bill, works far better. Always check the rules where you trade; this isn't legal advice.

### Bookings made online or by phone (UK)
If a consumer books and agrees the contract at a distance, online or by phone, the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 normally give them 14 days to cancel. You can only start the service within those 14 days if they expressly ask you to, for example by ticking a box or saying so in writing (regulation 36). If they then cancel, they pay for the part of the service already provided.
For most appointment businesses, the simple answer is a line in your booking flow: "By booking a time within the next 14 days, you ask us to start the service in that time." Ask your adviser how this applies to you, especially for courses and packages paid in advance.

### Make it work in practice
1. Show the policy before booking: on your booking page and website, not only in small print afterwards.
2. Put one short line in the confirmation message, and again in the day-before reminder.
3. Make cancelling easy. Someone who can reply "cancel" in a message lets you know; someone who has to call during opening hours often just doesn't turn up.
4. Apply it the same way every time, and use the exceptions line for real emergencies.
5. Keep a waiting list, so a late cancellation becomes a filled slot instead of lost money.

### Free tools: write the policy and the reminders
The free [cancellation policy generator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/cancellation-policy-generator/) writes your policy in three lengths: the full version for your website, a short paragraph for booking confirmations, and one line for SMS. Then the [appointment reminder generator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/appointment-reminder-generator/) writes the confirmation, day-before and same-day messages, with an add-to-calendar link. For the full no-show routine, read [how to reduce no-shows](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reduce-appointment-no-shows/).

### Can I charge a fee for a no-show?
Generally yes, if the fee was clearly agreed before booking and is reasonable for what you actually lose. A deposit taken at booking is the easiest way to collect it.

### Should first-time customers pay a deposit?
Many businesses ask new customers for a deposit and drop it for regulars who have always turned up. It protects you from the bookings most likely to go missing, without punishing loyal customers.

### What if a regular cancels late once?
Most businesses waive it the first time and say so kindly: "No charge this time, but please give us 24 hours' notice next time." The policy gives you the right to charge; you decide when to use it.

### Where should the cancellation policy go?
On your booking page before people confirm, on your website, in the booking confirmation, and as one short line in the reminder message.

## How to track business income and expenses without an accountant's software
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/track-business-income-and-expenses/ (2026-11-24)

Record every sale and every business cost in one place, with the date, who it was with, the amount, a category, and whether you have the receipt. Do it once a week from your bank app, invoices and receipts, then check the monthly totals. Keep the records and receipts for as long as your tax office requires: in the UK that's at least 5 years after the 31 January filing deadline.

Most small business owners don't fall behind on bookkeeping because it's hard. They fall behind because it piles up: a shoebox of receipts in January, a bank statement nobody has looked at since summer, and a panicked call to the accountant before the deadline.
A simple income and expenses record, kept up every week, fixes that. Here's what to record, which categories to use, a routine that takes ten minutes, and when a spreadsheet stops being enough.

### What to record for every transaction
| Column | Why it matters | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Date | Puts it in the right month, quarter and tax year | 14/03/2026 |
| Customer or supplier | Lets you find the invoice or receipt later | Screwfix |
| Description | What it was, in plain words | Copper pipe and fittings |
| Category | Shows where money goes and maps to your tax return | Materials |
| Amount | Gross amount paid or received | £84.00 |
| VAT (if registered) | VAT you charged or can reclaim | £14.00 |
| Receipt kept? | Missing receipts are what accountants chase | Yes |

### Categories that keep it simple
Use the categories your tax return uses, so your totals drop straight in. For UK sole traders, HMRC's allowable expenses are grouped into things like office costs, travel, clothing (uniforms only), staff, things you buy to resell, financial costs, premises, and marketing. In the US, Schedule C has similar lines: advertising, car and truck expenses, supplies, utilities, and so on.
Eight to twelve categories is plenty. If you're unsure where something goes, put it in "Other" with a clear description and ask your accountant once, then use the same category every time after that.

### A 10-minute weekly routine
1. Pick a fixed slot, like Friday afternoon. Little and often beats a weekend in January.
2. Open your business bank account and add every new payment in and out since last week.
3. Match each expense to a receipt. Photograph paper receipts straight away and file them in one folder.
4. Mark any expense where the receipt is missing, and ask the supplier for a copy while it's fresh.
5. Once a month, look at the totals: income, expenses, profit, and VAT to set aside if you're registered.

### How long to keep records
Digital copies are fine in both countries as long as they're clear and complete. If you're not sure which period applies to you, keep everything for 7 years and ask your accountant.
| Where | Rule of thumb | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| UK, self-employed | At least 5 years after the 31 January Self Assessment deadline for that tax year | GOV.UK |
| UK, VAT-registered | VAT records for at least 6 years | GOV.UK |
| US | Generally 3 years from filing, longer in some cases (for example 7 years for bad debt or worthless securities claims) | IRS |

### Making Tax Digital: when a spreadsheet isn't enough on its own
From April 2026, UK sole traders and landlords with qualifying income over £50,000 must keep digital records and send quarterly updates to HMRC using Making Tax Digital compatible software. The threshold drops to £30,000 from April 2027 and £20,000 from April 2028.
You can still keep your records in a spreadsheet, but you'll need bridging software that connects it to HMRC to send the updates. If you're close to the threshold, check with your accountant which software they use before you start the year.

### Free tool: a ready-made spreadsheet
The free [income and expenses spreadsheet](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/income-and-expenses-spreadsheet/) sets this up for you: income and expense sheets with your own categories and year, VAT worked out by formula if you're registered, a monthly summary with profit and your biggest costs, and missing receipts highlighted in red. It downloads for Excel or Google Sheets.
To keep the paperwork that feeds it tidy, use the [invoice generator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/free-invoice-generator/) and [receipt generator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/receipt-generator/), and read [what to put on a receipt](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-put-on-a-receipt/).

### Do I need accounting software as a small business?
Not always. A tidy spreadsheet kept up weekly works for many sole traders. You'll want software once you have staff, stock, lots of invoices, or once Making Tax Digital applies to you.

### Should I use a separate bank account for the business?
Yes, if you can. It makes the weekly routine much faster, because every payment in the account is a business one, and it keeps personal spending out of your records.

### What if I've lost a receipt?
Ask the supplier for a copy, or find the order email. If that fails, record what you can (date, supplier, amount, what it was) and keep the bank statement line as evidence. Ask your accountant whether the cost can still be claimed.

### Is income the same as profit?
No. Income is everything customers paid you. Profit is income minus allowable business expenses, and it's profit that income tax is worked out on.

## How to make business announcement posts people actually read
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/business-announcement-posts/ (2026-11-24)

Put one idea on the image: a short headline people can read in a second, one line of detail, and what to do next, with the dates, price or phone number. Use the same colours every time, include your business name, and make it 1080 x 1350 for the Instagram feed and 1080 x 1920 for stories and WhatsApp status. Post it a week ahead, then again the day before.

Most small business posts aren't ignored because they're ugly. They're ignored because they try to say five things at once, in small text, to people scrolling past on a phone.
Announcement posts, like a sale, holiday opening hours, a new service or a closure, are the easiest to get right, because they have one job. Here's how to write and size them, and when to post them so the people who need to see them do.

### What goes on the image
Everything else (terms, the full menu, the story behind it) goes in the caption, not on the image.
| Part | Keep it to | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Headline | 3-6 words | 20% off all treatments |
| Detail | One line | Monday 1 to Sunday 7 December |
| Action | What to do and how | Book: 07700 900123 |
| Your name | Logo or business name | Studio Noa |

### Five posts every local business needs
- Holiday opening hours: one changed day per line, posted a week before
- Sale or offer: the discount, the dates and how to claim it
- New service or product: what it is, the price, and how to book
- Closure or change: the date, why in a few words, and what customers should do instead
- Thank you or milestone: short and human, with a reason to come back

### Sizes for each place
| Where | Size (pixels) | Shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Instagram feed | 1080 x 1350 | Portrait 4:5, takes up the most space |
| Facebook and Instagram, anywhere | 1080 x 1080 | Square, safe everywhere |
| Stories and WhatsApp status | 1080 x 1920 | Tall 9:16, keep text away from the top and bottom edges |

### Make it readable on a phone
1. Big text, few words. If you have to zoom in, it's too small.
2. Strong contrast between the text and the background: dark on light, or light on dark.
3. The same two or three colours every time, so people recognise you before they read your name.
4. One image, one message. A second announcement gets its own post.

### When to post
For anything with a date, post twice: about a week before, and again the day before or on the morning. Share the same image to your story on the day. For holiday hours, also update the special hours on your Google Business Profile, so Google Search and Maps show the right times, which is where most people check.
Keep a folder of last year's posts. Most announcements come round every year, and changing the dates is quicker than starting again.

### Free tool: make the post in a minute
The free [social post maker](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/social-post-maker/) has templates for a sale, holiday opening hours, a new service, closed today and we're hiring. Change the words, pick your colours and size, and download it for the Instagram feed, a square post, or a story and WhatsApp status. Nothing is uploaded.
For a menu or services post, use the [price list maker](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/price-list-maker/) instead, and read [how to make a price list that sells](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-make-a-price-list/). To see which posts actually bring people to your website, read [how to track which post brings visitors](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/track-which-post-brings-website-visitors/).

### How much text can I put on a post?
As little as you can. A headline, one line of detail and how to act. Anything longer belongs in the caption, where people who want more will read it.

### Should I use a template or design from scratch?
A template, made once in your colours and reused. Consistency matters more than variety: people learn to recognise your posts.

### What's the best time to post?
When your customers scroll, usually early morning, lunchtime and evening. Instagram and Facebook insights show when your followers are online. For dated announcements, timing relative to the date matters more than the hour.

### Can I use the same image on Instagram and Facebook?
Yes. A square or 4:5 portrait image works on both. Make a separate tall version for stories and WhatsApp status.

## How to write an FAQ page that Google and AI assistants can quote
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-write-an-faq-page/ (2026-11-24)

Collect the questions customers really ask, write each one in their words, and answer it in the first sentence with the specific fact: the price, the yes or no, the area, the time. Add one useful detail, keep the same answers on your site, Google profile and price list, and put them in plain text on the page. FAQ schema can still help machines read it, but since 2023 Google only shows FAQ rich results for well-known government and health sites.

A good FAQ page does two jobs. It saves you answering the same five questions on the phone every day, and it gives search engines and AI assistants like ChatGPT, Gemini and Google's AI Overviews a clear, quotable answer when someone asks about a business like yours.
Most FAQ pages do neither, because they're written as marketing. Here's how to write one that works.

### Where to find the right questions
- Your WhatsApp, email and DM history: the questions you answer most
- Notes from phone calls, or ask whoever answers the phone for their top ten
- Reviews: what people praise or complain about tells you what others want to know
- The "People also ask" box when you search your service and town on Google
- Questions people ask just before they book or buy, about price, timing, area and what's included

### How to write each answer
Answer in the first sentence, then add one detail that helps: what's included, an exception, or what to do next. Two to four sentences per answer is enough. AI assistants pick up short, specific, self-contained answers far more often than vague ones.
| Do | Instead of |
| --- | --- |
| "How much is a call-out?" | "Pricing information" |
| "£65 for the first hour, including VAT." | "Our prices are competitive and vary by job." |
| "Yes, we cover Sheffield, Rotherham and Barnsley." | "We serve the wider region." |
| "Usually within 2 working days." | "We aim to respond promptly." |

### Eight questions almost every service business should answer
1. How much does it cost? (a real price or a typical range)
2. Which areas do you cover?
3. How soon can you come, or what's your next free slot?
4. What are your opening hours?
5. How do I book, and do you need a deposit?
6. What's your cancellation policy?
7. Which payment methods do you take?
8. Are you insured, qualified or registered? (with the body's name)

### FAQ schema in 2026: still worth adding?
FAQ schema (FAQPage structured data) is code that marks up your questions and answers. In August 2023 Google announced it would only show FAQ rich results, the expandable questions under a search result, for well-known, authoritative government and health websites. For a plumber or a salon, adding the schema no longer gets you that extra space in Google.
It's still harmless and helps some tools read your page clearly, as long as the questions and answers in the code are exactly the ones visible on the page. What matters most is the visible text: clear questions and direct answers that any search engine or AI assistant can read.

### Keep it in step everywhere
AI assistants compare what different sources say about you. If your website says you open at 8, your Google profile says 9 and your Facebook page says 8:30, they're less likely to state any of them. Use the same prices, hours and areas on your site, your [Google Business Profile](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/business-details-in-google-and-ai-search/), your price list and your social profiles, and update them all at once.

### Free tool: write the FAQ section and the code
The free [FAQ generator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/faq-generator/) suggests the questions customers ask in your type of business, helps you write short, specific answers, and gives you the HTML section and matching FAQ schema to paste into your site. Then check how ready your site is with the [AI search visibility checker](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ai-search-visibility-checker/).

### How many questions should an FAQ page have?
Enough to cover what customers really ask, usually 8 to 15. Better ten specific answers than thirty vague ones. Move long topics to their own page and link to it.

### Should FAQs go on a separate page or on each service page?
Both work. Put general questions (hours, areas, payment) on one FAQ page, and questions about a single service on that service's page, where people are deciding.

### Does FAQ schema still help SEO?
It no longer gets most businesses FAQ rich results on Google, but it does no harm if it matches the visible page. The visible questions and answers are what search engines and AI assistants mainly use.

### Can I copy FAQs from a competitor?
No. Copying their text can breach copyright, and their answers aren't yours: different prices, areas and policies. Use their questions as ideas, then answer them for your own business.

## How to set your hourly rate as a freelancer or sole trader
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-set-your-hourly-rate/ (2026-11-27)

Add what you want to take home in a year, the tax on it, and your yearly business costs. Divide that by the hours you can really bill in a year: weeks you work, times days a week, times the hours you invoice each day (usually 4 to 6, not 8). That's your minimum rate. Then check it against what others charge and what the work is worth to the client.

Most people who start out on their own set their rate by looking at what someone else charges, or by dividing an old salary by 40 hours a week. Both usually come out too low, because they forget holidays, business costs, and the hours that go on quoting, admin and chasing payments.
Here's the sum that gives you a floor you shouldn't go under, with a worked example, and how to decide where to price above it.

### The four numbers you need
| Number | What goes in it | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Take-home pay | What you want to earn in a year, after tax | £40,000 |
| Tax set-aside | Income tax and National Insurance (UK) or self-employment tax (US) on that pay | Ask your accountant |
| Business costs | Software, phone, insurance, equipment, vehicle, accountant, marketing, training | £6,000 |
| Billable hours | Hours a year you actually invoice | 1,150 |

### Billable hours are fewer than you think
Start with 52 weeks and take off holidays, bank holidays and a few sick days: 6 weeks off is realistic for most people. Then count only the hours you can invoice on a normal day. Quoting, travel between jobs, emails, invoicing and learning are real work, but no client pays for them directly.
For most freelancers and trades that leaves 4 to 6 billable hours in an 8-hour day. If you're not sure, track your time for two normal weeks. Guessing 8 is the most common reason a rate comes out too low.

### Worked example
1. Take-home pay plus business costs: £40,000 + £6,000 = £46,000 the business must bring in (before tax, for simplicity).
2. Working weeks: 52 - 6 = 46.
3. Billable days: 46 x 5 = 230.
4. Billable hours: 230 x 5 = 1,150.
5. Minimum hourly rate: £46,000 / 1,150 = £40 an hour. Minimum day rate: £46,000 / 230 = £200.

### Tax: set it aside, don't guess it
In the UK, sole traders pay Income Tax and Class 4 National Insurance on their profit through Self Assessment. In the US, self-employed people pay self-employment tax (15.3% for Social Security and Medicare, on most net earnings) plus income tax. The right figure depends on your profit, allowances and location, so ask an accountant once and use their percentage. Add that set-aside to your take-home figure and the rate in the example goes up, which is why a £40,000 salary and a £40-an-hour rate are not the same thing.
If you're VAT-registered in the UK, your rate to clients is your minimum plus VAT. Don't let VAT eat into the number you worked out.

### Pricing above the minimum
- Check what others in your area and trade charge. If you're far below, you're probably leaving money on the table
- Price the result, not just the hours, for work where you're quick because you're experienced
- Use a day rate or a fixed price for whole jobs, so clients don't watch the clock
- Charge more for urgent, out-of-hours or very small jobs, where the admin costs the same as a big one
- Review the rate once a year, and raise it when costs or demand go up

### Free tool: work it out in a minute
The free [hourly rate calculator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/hourly-rate-calculator/) does the sum: enter your take-home pay, tax set-aside, business costs, weeks off, days a week and billable hours a day, and it shows your minimum hourly and day rates. If the answer means you need to charge more, the [price increase letter generator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/price-increase-letter-generator/) writes the message to your clients, and the [profit margin calculator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/profit-margin-calculator/) shows what the change does to your margin.
Losing a lot of hours to admin? The [admin time calculator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/admin-time-calculator/) shows what those hours cost you in a year.

### Should I charge hourly or a fixed price?
Hourly suits work that's hard to scope. Fixed prices suit jobs you know well, and they reward you for being quick. Many people quote a fixed price worked out from their hourly rate.

### Is my old salary divided by hours a fair rate?
No, it's usually far too low. An employer paid for your holidays, equipment, pension and the hours you weren't productive. On your own, your rate has to cover all of that.

### What if my minimum rate is higher than the market?
Look at costs you can cut and admin you can remove to bill more hours, then check whether you can specialise or add value that justifies a higher price. Pricing below your minimum means working for less than you need.

### How often should I raise my rate?
Review it every year. Small regular increases, given with notice, are easier for clients to accept than a big jump after several years.

## How to tell customers about a price increase without losing them
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-tell-customers-about-a-price-increase/ (2026-11-27)

Tell customers personally and early, a month ahead is a common choice. Say the old price, the new price and the date it starts, give one short honest reason, and thank them. Send it by email so there's a record, with a short WhatsApp or text version for people who don't read email. Check your contract or terms first in case they set a notice period or let the customer cancel.

Most small business owners put off raising prices for years, then do it all at once and feel awkward about it. The customers who leave over a fair, well-explained increase are usually fewer than you fear, and the ones who stay keep paying the new price every month.
Here's what to say, how much notice to give, and examples you can adapt.

### What a good price increase message contains
| Part | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Thanks | Thank you for being a regular customer. |
| The change | From 1 February, fortnightly cleaning goes from £60 to £66. |
| A short reason | Our costs for products and travel have gone up this year. |
| What stays the same | Same cleaner, same day, same checklist. |
| What to do | Nothing needs to change. Any questions, just reply. |

### How much notice to give
First check your contract, terms or subscription agreement. It may set a notice period or a way prices can change. If it says nothing, give enough time for customers to plan: a month is common for regular services, and more for business clients who budget ahead.
In the UK, for consumers, the Consumer Rights Act 2015 lists a term that lets a trader raise the price without giving the consumer the right to cancel among the terms that may be unfair. If you sell ongoing services or subscriptions to consumers, the safest route is clear notice before the new price applies, and letting them cancel if they don't want to continue.

### Reasons that work
- Rising costs: materials, fuel, wages, software. Honest and easy to understand
- More value: a new service, longer appointments, better products
- A yearly review: you look at prices every year, and this is this year's change
- No reason at all is fine too. Never invent one

### Example: short WhatsApp or text version
"Hi Sarah, a quick note from Bright Clean: from 1 February your fortnightly clean will be £66 (currently £60). Same cleaner, same day. Thanks so much for being with us, and any questions just reply. Emma"
Send the full email as well for anyone on a written agreement, so there's a clear record of what was said and when.

### Mistakes that lose customers
1. Surprising them on the invoice. A higher bill with no warning feels like a trick.
2. Apologising too much. Say it clearly and kindly, once.
3. A different message for every customer. Use one wording, then personalise the name and price.
4. Not updating the price list, website and Google profile on the same day, so new customers see old prices.
5. Waiting years and then jumping 30%. Smaller yearly increases are easier to accept.

### Free tool: write the message
The free [price increase letter generator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/price-increase-letter-generator/) writes it for you: enter your business, the service, the old and new price and the start date, choose a warm, brief or formal tone and a reason, and copy the email with its subject line plus a short WhatsApp or SMS version. It works out the percentage too.
Not sure what the new price should be? Work it out with the [hourly rate calculator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/hourly-rate-calculator/) and read [how to set your hourly rate](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-set-your-hourly-rate/). Then update your [price list](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/price-list-maker/) everywhere at once.

### Should I tell new customers the old price?
No. New customers simply get the new price from the date it starts. The notice is for existing customers who are used to the old one.

### Can I keep the old price for my best customers?
Yes, for a while if you like. A common approach is to hold the old price for a few months for long-standing customers, then move everyone to the same price.

### What if a customer complains?
Thank them, restate the reason briefly, and remind them of the value they get. If they leave, part on good terms. Many come back later.

### Is a price increase letter legally required?
It depends on your contract and who your customers are. For ongoing consumer services in the UK, clear notice before the change is the safe approach. This article isn't legal advice: check your terms or ask a solicitor if you're unsure.

## Privacy policy for a small business website: what it must say
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/privacy-policy-small-business-website/ (2026-11-27)

If your website collects any personal information, through a contact form, bookings, a newsletter, payments or analytics cookies, you need a privacy policy. In the UK it must say who you are, what you collect and why, your lawful basis, who you share it with, how long you keep it, people's rights and how to complain to the ICO. In the US, California's law requires one for most sites with California visitors. Link it in your footer and next to every form.

A privacy policy sounds like something only big companies need. But a small business website that takes bookings, has a contact form or runs Google Analytics is collecting personal data, and the rules apply to you too.
The good news: for most small businesses, a clear, honest policy fits on one page. Here's what it has to cover, in plain English.

### Do you need one?
- Contact or enquiry form: yes, you collect names, emails and phone numbers
- Online booking or payments: yes, and your booking or payment provider will usually ask you to link one
- Newsletter or mailing list: yes
- Google Analytics, a Facebook pixel or other tracking: yes, and in the UK and EU you also need consent for those cookies
- A one-page site with only your phone number and no tracking: arguably not, but it's still good practice

### What a UK privacy policy must include
UK GDPR Article 13 sets this list for data you collect directly from people, and the ICO's guidance explains each item. The ICO notes its guidance on the right to be informed is being reviewed after the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, so check its current page.
| Section | In plain words |
| --- | --- |
| Who you are | Business name, address and how to contact you about data |
| What you collect | Names, emails, phone numbers, booking details, payment records, cookies |
| Why | To reply to enquiries, manage bookings, send invoices, send a newsletter |
| Lawful basis | For example contract, legitimate interests or consent, for each purpose |
| Who you share it with | Your website host, booking system, email tool, accountant |
| Transfers abroad | If any provider stores data outside the UK, and how it's protected |
| How long you keep it | For example enquiries for 12 months, invoices for 6 years |
| People's rights | Access, correction, deletion, objection, and how to ask |
| Complaints | The right to complain to the ICO |

### If you have US customers
There's no single federal privacy law for small websites. California's Online Privacy Protection Act (CalOPPA) requires commercial websites that collect personal information from California residents to post a privacy policy saying what they collect, who they share it with and how they respond to "do not track" signals. Since almost any site can have California visitors, most US small businesses treat a privacy policy as required.
Several other states now have their own privacy laws, mostly for larger businesses or those selling data. If you handle health, financial or children's information, get legal advice.

### Cookies: the policy explains, the banner asks
In the UK, the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations (PECR) say you must get consent before setting non-essential cookies, like analytics or advertising pixels. Your privacy policy (or a separate cookie policy) explains which cookies you use and why. A cookie banner asks for consent before they load. Most website builders have a banner setting.

### Where to put it
1. A link in the footer of every page, called "Privacy policy".
2. A short line next to every form: "We use your details to reply to you. See our privacy policy."
3. In your booking confirmation and newsletter sign-up emails.
4. On your Google Business Profile or booking page, if they ask for one.

### Free tool: write it in a few minutes
The free [privacy policy generator](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/privacy-policy-generator/) writes a plain-English policy for you. Tick what your site does (contact form, bookings, payments, emails, analytics), add your details and providers, choose the UK and EU (GDPR) or US version, and copy it as text or HTML. Sections only appear when they apply, so it stays short. Nothing is sent to us.
Automating how you handle client data? Read the [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/).

### Can I copy another business's privacy policy?
No. It wouldn't match what you actually do, and copying the text can breach copyright. A policy has to describe your own data, providers and retention periods.

### How often should I update it?
Whenever you add a new tool that handles customer data, like a new booking system or email platform, and check it once a year. Put the date of the last update at the top.

### Do I need to register with the ICO?
Most UK businesses that process personal data must pay the data protection fee to the ICO, unless they're exempt. The ICO has a short self-assessment to check.

### Is a generated policy legal advice?
No. It's a solid starting point for a typical small business. Read it, make sure it matches what you do, and get advice if you handle sensitive data or do anything unusual.

## Is the text on your website hard to read? Colour contrast in plain English
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/website-text-hard-to-read-colour-contrast/ (2026-11-21)

Contrast is how much text stands out from its background, measured as a ratio from 1:1 (invisible) to 21:1 (black on white). The WCAG accessibility guidelines ask for at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text, buttons and icons at level AA, the level most accessibility rules point to. Light grey text, white text on bright brand colours and text over photos are the usual failures.

A lot of small business websites look elegant on the designer's large, bright screen and hard to read everywhere else: on a phone in sunlight, on an older laptop, or for anyone whose eyesight isn't perfect. Faint text quietly costs enquiries, because people skim, struggle and leave.
Contrast is one of the easiest accessibility issues to measure and fix. Here's what the numbers mean, where problems usually hide, and how to fix them without changing your brand.

### What the numbers mean
The ratio compares how light the two colours are. Black on white is 21:1. A mid grey (#767676) on white is about 4.5:1, right on the AA line. Many accessibility laws and policies, such as the UK public sector rules and Israel's IS 5568, are based on WCAG level AA.
| What | Level AA | Level AAA |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normal text | 4.5:1 | 7:1 |
| Large text (about 24px, or 19px bold) | 3:1 | 4.5:1 |
| Buttons, icons, form borders | 3:1 | - |

### Where low contrast usually hides
- Light grey body text and captions.
- White text on yellow, orange, light green or sky-blue buttons.
- Headlines over photos in the top banner.
- Placeholder text inside form fields, and thin grey field borders.
- Small print: prices, opening hours, legal lines and footers.

### How to fix it without changing your brand
1. Check each text and background pair with a contrast checker.
2. Keep the same hue and make the colour darker (or lighter) until it passes; your brand colour stays recognisable.
3. For white text on a bright colour, use a darker shade of the colour for buttons, or switch to dark text.
4. Put a dark overlay behind text on photos.
5. Check your whole palette once, then use only the pairs that pass.

### How to check your colours in a minute
In Chrome, right-click the text, choose Inspect, and click the small colour square next to the text colour in the Styles panel. It shows the contrast ratio and whether it passes AA and AAA. If it fails, make the text darker (or the background lighter) until it passes. Contrast is one check among many: a full accessibility review also covers headings, image descriptions, keyboard use and forms.

### Does passing contrast make my site accessible?
No. It's one requirement. Accessibility also covers structure, images, keyboard use, forms, captions and more.

### Do logos have to meet contrast rules?
WCAG makes an exception for text that's part of a logo or brand name. Everything else on the page, including buttons, should pass.

### Is AAA required?
Usually not. Most rules point to level AA. AAA is a higher bar that's worth reaching for body text where you can.

### ניגודיות צבעים באתר: מה זה 4.5:1, איפה זה נכשל ואיך מתקנים
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/he/website-color-contrast-accessibility/ (2026-11-21)

ניגודיות היא עד כמה הטקסט בולט מהרקע, ונמדדת ביחס מ-1:1 (בלתי נראה) עד 21:1 (שחור על לבן). הנחיות WCAG ברמה AA, שעליהן מבוסס גם התקן הישראלי לנגישות אתרים (ת"י 5568), דורשות לפחות 4.5:1 לטקסט רגיל ו-3:1 לטקסט גדול, לכפתורים ולאייקונים. הכשלים הנפוצים: טקסט אפור בהיר, טקסט לבן על צבעי מותג בהירים וטקסט על תמונות.
